## FOREWORD

Many difficulties stand in the way, in the West, of a serious and deep study of Eastern doctrines in general, and Hindu doctrines in particular; and the greatest obstacles in this regard are perhaps not those that may come from the people of the East themselves. Indeed, the first condition required for such a study—the most essential of all—is obviously to possess the necessary mindset to understand the doctrines in question; we mean to understand them truly and deeply. Yet, this is an aptitude which, except for very rare exceptions, is totally lacking in Westerners. On the other hand, this necessary condition could be regarded at the same time as sufficient; for when it is fulfilled, the people of the East have not the slightest reluctance to communicate their thought as completely as it is possible to do so.

If there is no other real obstacle than the one we have just indicated, why then have the "Orientalists"—that is, the Westerners who concern themselves with the things of the East—never overcome it? <note>Guénon uses "Orientalist" specifically to refer to academic scholars (philologists, historians) of his era, whom he believed treated living traditions like dead museum specimens.</note> And one could not be accused of exaggeration in asserting that they have indeed never overcome it, when one observes that they have only been able to produce simple works of erudition <note>original: "érudition"; here meaning academic book-learning or the collection of facts without deeper insight.</note>, perhaps estimable from a specialized point of view, but without any interest for the understanding of the slightest true idea. This is because it is not enough to know a language grammatically, nor to be capable of making a correct word-for-word translation, to penetrate the spirit of that language and to assimilate the thought of those who speak and write it. One could even go further and say that the more a translation is scrupulously literal, the more it risks being inaccurate in reality and distorting the thought, because there is no true equivalence between the terms of two different languages, especially when these languages are very distant from one another—distant not so much philologically as by reason of the diversity of the conceptions of the peoples who employ them; and it is this latter element that no amount of academic scholarship will ever allow one to penetrate. For that, something other than a vain "textual criticism" <note>original: "critique de textes"; the academic practice of analyzing the history and variations of a manuscript to determine its original form.</note> extending as far as the eye can see on questions of detail is required; something other than the methods of grammarians and "literary men," and even other than a so-called "historical method" applied to everything

<summary>Guénon argues that the main barrier to understanding Eastern thought is the Western lack of the proper "mindset," asserting that academic scholarship and literal translations fail to capture the true spirit of these doctrines.</summary>
<keywords>Western mindset, Eastern doctrines, Orientalism, translation, philology, textual criticism, historical method, traditionalism</keywords>

indiscriminately. Without doubt, dictionaries and compilations have their relative utility, which we do not intend to dispute, and one cannot say that all this labor is spent in pure loss, especially if one considers that those who provide it would most often be incapable of producing anything else; but unfortunately, as soon as scholarship <note>original: "érudition"; here meaning academic book-learning or the collection of facts without deeper insight.</note> becomes a "specialty," it tends to be taken as an end in itself, instead of being a simple instrument as it normally should be. It is this encroachment of scholarship and its particular methods that constitutes a real danger, because it risks absorbing those who might perhaps be capable of engaging in another kind of work, and because the habit of these methods narrows the intellectual horizon of those who submit to them and imposes an irremediable distortion upon them.

Moreover, we have not yet said everything, and have not even touched upon the most serious side of the question: works of pure scholarship are, in the output of Orientalists <note>Guénon uses this term to describe Western academics (philologists, historians) who study the East through a strictly European lens.</note>, the most cumbersome part, certainly, but not the most harmful; and, in saying that there was nothing else, we meant to imply nothing else that had any value, even of a restricted scope. Certain individuals, in Germany especially, have wanted to go further and—still by the same methods, which can yield nothing further here—have attempted to carry out the work of interpretation. In doing so, they bring to the task the entire set of preconceived ideas that constitutes their own mentality, with a manifest bias toward forcing the conceptions they deal with into the usual frameworks of European thought.

In short, the capital error of these Orientalists, the question of method aside, is to see everything from their Western point of view and through their own mentality, whereas the first condition for being able to correctly interpret any doctrine is naturally to make an effort to assimilate it and to place oneself, as much as possible, at the point of view of those who actually conceived it. We say as much as possible, for not everyone can succeed equally, but at least all can try; yet, far from this, the exclusivism of the Orientalists we are speaking of and their systematizing spirit <note>original: "esprit de système"; referring to the tendency to force complex ideas into rigid, pre-defined academic categories.</note> go so far as to lead them, by an incredible aberration, to believe themselves capable of understanding Eastern doctrines better than the Easterners themselves: a pretension that would be merely laughable if it were not joined with a determined will to "monopolize," in a sense, the studies in question. And, in fact, there are hardly any others concerned with them in Europe, besides these "specialists," except for a certain category of extravagant dreamers and bold charlatans <note>Guénon likely refers here to the Theosophists and various occultist groups of the early 20th century, whom he viewed as misrepresenting Eastern thought as much as the academics did.</note> who could be regarded as a negligible quantity if they did not also exert a deplorable influence in various

<summary>Guénon criticizes Western academics for treating Eastern studies as a mere "specialty" of fact-collecting and for arrogantly attempting to interpret Eastern doctrines using Western intellectual frameworks. He argues that true understanding requires adopting the perspective of the original tradition rather than imposing European categories upon it.</summary>
<keywords>scholarship, Orientalists, Western mentality, Eastern doctrines, exclusivism, specialization, academic bias, interpretation</keywords>

...respects, as we shall have to explain in its proper place in a more precise manner.

To stick here to what concerns the <term>Orientalists: Western scholars who study the languages, history, and cultures of the East, often from a purely academic or "outsider" perspective</term> whom one might call "official," we will further point out, as a preliminary observation, one of the abuses most frequently arising from the use of this "historical method" <note>original: "méthode historique"; a scholarly approach that analyzes ideas strictly as products of their time, often ignoring their eternal or metaphysical validity.</note> to which we have already alluded: it is the error which consists in studying Eastern civilizations as one would study civilizations that have long since disappeared. In the latter case, it is obvious that one is forced, for lack of anything better, to settle for approximate reconstructions, without ever being sure of a perfect match with what actually existed in the past, since there is no way to perform direct verification. But it is forgotten that Eastern civilizations—at least those which interest us at present—have continued down to our own day without interruption, and that they still have authorized representatives <note>Traditional masters or scholars who possess an unbroken chain of oral and written transmission.</note> whose opinion is worth incomparably more for their understanding than all the scholarship in the world. However, to think of consulting them, one would have to avoid starting from that singular principle that one knows better than they do what to think about the true meaning of their own concepts.

On the other hand, it must also be said that Easterners, having—and rightly so—a rather unfavorable idea of European intellectuality, care very little about what Westerners, in a general way, may or may not think of them. Thus, they do not seek in any way to disabuse them; on the contrary, through a somewhat disdainful politeness, they withdraw into a silence that Western vanity easily mistakes for approval. This is because "proselytism" <term>proselytism: the act of attempting to convert others to one's own beliefs or point of view.</term> is totally unknown in the East, where it would be, moreover, without purpose and could only be regarded as a proof of pure and simple ignorance and incomprehension; what we shall say later will show the reasons for this. Regarding this silence for which some reproach Easterners, and which is yet so legitimate, there can only be rare exceptions in favor of some isolated individual presenting the required qualifications and the desired intellectual aptitudes. As for those who abandon their reserve outside of this specific case, one can only say one thing: it is that they generally represent rather uninteresting elements, and that, for one reason or another, they expose only deformed doctrines under the pretext of adapting them to the West; we shall have the opportunity to say a few words about this. What we wish to make understood for the moment, and what we have indicated

<summary>Guénon critiques "official" Orientalists for treating living Eastern traditions as dead historical subjects and ignoring living masters. He explains that Easterners remain silent about their traditions due to a lack of proselytizing spirit and a low opinion of Western intellect.</summary>
<keywords>Orientalism, historical method, Eastern civilizations, European intellectuality, proselytism, intellectual tradition, West vs East</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the author's "Foreword," transitioning from a critique of academic "Orientalists" to a statement of the book's specific purpose. It sets the stage for a comparison between the Western and Eastern (specifically Hindu) mentalities.</meta>

right from the start, is that the Western mentality alone is responsible for this situation. This makes the role of someone who—having found themselves in exceptional conditions and succeeded in assimilating certain ideas—wants to express them in the most intelligible way, yet without distorting them, extremely difficult: he must limit himself to stating what he has understood, insofar as this can be done, while carefully refraining from any concern for "popularization" <note>original: "vulgarisation"; the act of simplifying complex ideas for a general audience, which the author believes often leads to the corruption of the truth.</note>, and without even the slightest desire to convince anyone.

We have said enough to clearly define our intentions: we do not wish to produce a work of scholarship <term>erudition: formal, academic learning or "book-knowledge." Guénon argues that mere research is inferior to direct intellectual understanding.</term> here, and the viewpoint we intend to adopt is much deeper than that. Since truth is not a historical fact for us, it matters very little to us, fundamentally, to determine exactly the origin of this or that idea; such things only interest us because, having understood an idea, we know it to be true. However, certain indications regarding Eastern thought might give some people pause for thought, and this simple result would, on its own, have an unsuspected importance. Moreover, even if this goal could not be achieved, we would still have a reason to undertake an exposition of this kind: it would be to acknowledge, in some way, all that we owe intellectually to the peoples of the East, for which Westerners have never offered us even a partial or incomplete equivalent.

We will therefore first show, as clearly as we can and after some indispensable preliminary considerations, the essential and fundamental differences that exist between the general modes of Eastern thought and those of Western thought. We will then insist more specifically on what relates to Hindu doctrines <note>The metaphysical and spiritual traditions of India, such as Vedanta or Yoga, viewed here as expressions of universal truths.</note>, insofar as these present particular features that distinguish them from other Eastern doctrines—though all have enough common characteristics to justify, on the whole, the general opposition between the East and the West. Finally, regarding these Hindu doctrines, we will point out the inadequacy of the interpretations currently in vogue in the West; for some of them, we should even say their absurdity. As a conclusion to this study, we will indicate, with all necessary precautions, the conditions for an intellectual rapprochement <note>A re-establishment of harmonious relations or understanding between two parties.</note> between the East and the West, conditions which, as is easy to foresee, are far from being currently fulfilled on the Western side: thus, it is only a possibility that we wish to show here, without believing it to be in any way susceptible to a realization <insert>at this time</insert>.

# CHAPTER ONE
## EAST AND WEST

The first thing we must do in the study we are undertaking is to determine the exact nature of the opposition that exists between the <term>East</term> <note>original: "Orient"</note> and the <term>West</term> <note>original: "Occident"</note>, and first of all, for that, to specify the meaning we intend to attach to the two terms of this opposition. We could say, as a first approximation—perhaps a bit summary—that the East, for us, is essentially Asia, and that the West is essentially Europe; but even this requires some explanation.

When we speak, for example, of the <term>Western or European mentality</term>, using one or the other of these two words interchangeably, we mean by that the mentality proper to the <term>European race</term> <note>In the early 20th-century context of this writing, "race" was often used to describe a broad cultural and linguistic group—what we might today call a "civilization"—rather than just biological descent.</note> taken as a whole. We will therefore call "European" everything that relates to this race, and we will apply this common denomination to all individuals descended from it, in whatever part of the world they may be found: thus, Americans and Australians, to name but those, are for us Europeans, in exactly the same capacity as the men of the same race who have continued to inhabit Europe. It is quite obvious, in fact, that the act of having moved to another region, or even being born there, cannot by itself modify the race, nor, consequently, the mentality which is inherent to it; and even if the change of environment is likely to determine certain modifications sooner or later, these will only be secondary modifications, not affecting the truly essential characteristics of the race, but sometimes, on the contrary, bringing some of them out more clearly. Thus, one can easily observe, among Americans, the development pushed to the extreme of some of the tendencies that constitute the modern European mentality.

A question arises here, however, which we cannot dispense with indicating briefly: we have spoken of the European race and its own mentality; but is there truly a European race? If one means by that a primitive race, having an original unity and a perfect

<summary>In this opening chapter, the author begins defining the "East" and "West," arguing that "Western" refers to a specific mentality shared by the European race and its descendants worldwide, including Americans.</summary>
<keywords>East, West, European mentality, cultural identity, civilization, modernization, racial definitions</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter One regarding the definition of the "European race" and the "Western mentality." The previous page ended mid-word, discussing how environmental changes only cause secondary modifications, not affecting the fundamental unity of the group.</meta>

homogeneity, one must answer in the negative, for no one can dispute that the current population of Europe was formed by a mixture of elements belonging to very diverse races, and that there are quite marked ethnic differences, not only from one country to another, but even within each national grouping. However, it is nonetheless true that European peoples present enough common characters for them to be clearly distinguished from all others; their unity, even if it is acquired rather than primitive, is sufficient for us to speak, as we do, of a <term>European race</term>. 

However, this race is naturally less fixed and less stable than a "pure race"; the European elements, when mixing with other races, will be more easily absorbed, and their ethnic characters will disappear rapidly; but this applies only to cases where there is mixing, and, when there is only juxtaposition, it happens on the contrary that the mental characteristics—which are those that interest us most—appear in a way with more relief. These mental characteristics are, moreover, those for which European unity is the clearest: whatever the original differences might have been in this regard as in others, a <term>common mentality</term> has gradually formed among all the peoples of Europe in the course of history. This is not to say that there is not a special mentality for each of these peoples; but the peculiarities that distinguish them are only secondary in relation to a common background upon which they seem to be superimposed: they are, in short, like <term>species of the same genus</term> <note>The author uses a biological metaphor here to suggest that while nations (species) differ, they all belong to the same broader category (genus) of European civilization.</note>. No one, even among those who doubt that one can speak of a European race, will hesitate to admit the existence of a <term>European civilization</term>; and a civilization is nothing other than the product and the expression of a certain mentality.

We will not seek to specify the distinctive traits of the European mentality right now, for they will emerge sufficiently from the rest of this study; we will simply indicate that several influences have contributed to its formation: the one that played the preponderant role is undeniably the Greek influence, or, if you will, the <term>Greco-Roman influence</term>. The Greek influence is almost exclusive regarding the philosophical and scientific points of view, despite the appearance of certain special and properly modern tendencies, which we will speak of later. As for the Roman influence, it is less intellectual than social, and it asserts itself especially in the conceptions of the <term>State</term>, of <term>law</term> <note>original: "droit"</note>, and institutions; moreover, intellectually, the Romans had borrowed almost everything from the Greeks, so that, through them, it is not...

It is also necessary to point out the importance, specifically from a religious point of view, of the **Jewish influence**, which we will also find, moreover, in a certain part of the East; here is an element extra-European in its origin, but which is nonetheless, in part, a constituent of the current **Western mentality**.

If we now consider the **East**, it is not possible to speak of an **Oriental race**, or an **Asian race**, even with all the restrictions we applied to the consideration of a "European race." We are dealing here with a much more extensive whole, comprising much more numerous populations and with much greater ethnic differences; one can distinguish within this whole several races, more or less pure, but offering very distinct characteristics, each of which has its own civilization, very different from the others: there is no single **Oriental civilization** as there is a Western civilization; there are in reality **Oriental civilizations**. There will therefore be reason to say specific things for each of these civilizations, and we will indicate hereafter the major general divisions that can be established in this regard; but, despite everything, one will find there—if one focuses less on the form than on the substance—enough common elements or rather common principles that it is possible to speak of an **Oriental mentality**, as opposed to the **Western mentality**.

When we say that each of the races of the East has its own civilization, this is not absolutely exact; it is only strictly true for the **Chinese race** alone, whose civilization has its essential basis precisely in **ethnic unity**. For other Asian civilizations, the principles of unity upon which they rest are of a completely different nature, as we shall have to explain later, and this is what allows them to embrace within this unity elements belonging to extremely diverse races. We say **Asian civilizations**, for those we have in view are all so by their origin, even when they have spread over other lands, as the **Islamic civilization** <note>original: "civilisation musulmane"</note> especially has done. Moreover, it goes without saying that, apart from the Islamic elements, we do not regard as Oriental those peoples who inhabit Eastern Europe, nor even certain Asian regions neighboring Europe: one must not confuse an **Oriental** with a **Levantine**, who is rather the complete opposite, and who, in mentality at least, has the characteristics

<meta>This page concludes the previous discussion regarding the constituent elements of different civilizations and begins a comparative analysis of the relationship between the East and the West. It specifically addresses the fundamental imbalance and lack of symmetry between these two cultural spheres.</meta>

...essentials of a true Westerner.

One cannot help but be struck at first glance by the disproportion between the two entities that respectively constitute what we call the **East** and the **West**; if there is an opposition between them, there cannot truly be equivalence, nor even symmetry, between the two terms of this opposition. In this regard, there is a difference comparable to that which exists geographically between **Asia** and **Europe**, the latter appearing only as a mere extension of the former; likewise, the true situation of the West in relation to the East is essentially that of a branch detached from the trunk <note>original: "un rameau détaché du tronc." This metaphor is central to the author's argument that Western civilization is a secondary, derivative offshoot of a much older and more foundational Eastern tradition.</note>, and this is what we must now explain more fully.

# CHAPTER II
## THE DIVERGENCE

If one considers what is commonly called **classical antiquity** <note>This refers primarily to the civilizations of ancient Greece and Rome, which are traditionally viewed as the foundations of Western culture.</note>, and if one compares it to **Eastern civilizations**, one easily observes that it is less distant from them, at least in certain respects, than is modern **Europe**. The difference between the **East** and the **West** <note>original: "l'Orient et l'Occident." Throughout his work, the author uses these terms to represent two fundamentally different worldviews: the traditional, stable East and the modern, changing West.</note> seems to have been always increasing, but this divergence is, in a sense, one-sided. It is one-sided because it is the West alone that has changed, while the East, generally speaking, has remained substantially as it was during that era which we are accustomed to regarding as "ancient," and which is nevertheless still relatively recent.

**Stability**, one might even say **immutability**, is a characteristic that people quite readily recognize in Eastern civilizations—particularly that of **China**—but it is perhaps less easy to agree on its interpretation. Europeans, since they began to believe in "**progress**" and "**evolution**"—that is to say, for a little over a century—want to see in this stability a mark of inferiority. We, on the contrary, see it as a state of **equilibrium** <note>The author suggests that "stability" is not stagnation, but rather a successful achievement of balance that the West has lost.</note> which Western civilization has proven itself incapable of reaching. This stability is evident in small things as well as great ones; one can find a striking example in the fact that "**fashion**," with its continual variations, exists only in Western countries. In short, the Westerner, and especially the modern Westerner, appears essentially changing and inconstant, aspiring only to movement and agitation, whereas the Easterner presents exactly the opposite character.

If one wished to represent schematically the divergence of which we speak, one should not draw two lines moving away from each side of an axis; rather, the **East** should be represented by the axis itself, and the **West** by a line starting from that axis and moving away from it like a branch separating from the trunk, as we said previously. This symbol would be all the more accurate because, fundamentally—at least since so-called historical times—the West has never lived intellectually (insofar as it has possessed an intellectuality at all) except through borrowings made from the East, whether directly or indirectly. <term>Evolution</term>: Used here not just biologically, but as a social theory that cultures develop from "primitive" to "complex" forms.
<term>Equilibrium</term>: A state of physical or intellectual balance; used by the author to describe the lasting power of Eastern traditions.

**Greek civilization** itself is far from having had that originality that those who are incapable of seeing anything beyond it delight in proclaiming; these individuals would even go so far as to claim that the Greeks slandered themselves whenever they happened to acknowledge what they owed to **Egypt**, **Phoenicia**, **Chaldea** <note>An ancient region in southern Mesopotamia, often used here to refer to the broader Sumero-Babylonian culture.</note>, **Persia**, and even **India**. Despite all these civilizations being incomparably older than that of the Greeks, certain people, blinded by what we might call "**classical prejudice**" <term>classical prejudice</term> <note>The intellectual bias that views ancient Greece as the sole starting point of "true" civilization and rational thought, often dismissing earlier contributions from the East.</note>, are quite ready to maintain, against all evidence, that it was the older civilizations that borrowed from the latter and underwent its influence. It is very difficult to argue with such people, precisely because their opinion rests only on prejudice; however, we shall return more fully to this question. It is true that the Greeks did possess a certain originality, but it is not at all what is commonly believed; it consists of little more than the form in which they presented and explained what they borrowed, modifying it more or less successfully to adapt it to their own mentality—a mentality quite different from that of the **Orientals** <note>original: "Orientaux." In this context, the peoples of the East.</note>, and even already opposed to it in more than one way.

Before going further, we should clarify that we do not intend to contest the originality of **Hellenic civilization** <note>The culture of ancient Greece.</note> from certain points of view that are, in our opinion, more or less secondary—from the point of view of art, for example—but only from the strictly **intellectual** point of view, which is, moreover, much more reduced there than among the Easterners. This **diminution of intellectuality**—this "shrinking," so to speak—can be clearly stated in relation to the Eastern civilizations that still survive and which we know directly. It is likely the same in relation to those that have disappeared, based on everything we can know of them, and especially based on the analogies that clearly existed between the former and the latter. Indeed, the study of the **East** as it still is today—if one were willing to undertake it in a truly direct manner—would be capable of helping to a large extent in understanding **antiquity**, because of that character of fixity and stability we have indicated; it would even help in understanding **Greek antiquity**, for which we do not have the resource of direct testimony. This is because we are dealing there with a civilization that is quite truly extinct, and the modern Greeks could in no way be regarded as the legitimate continuators of the ancients, of whom they are likely not even the authentic descendants <note>A controversial historical view held by the author, suggesting a rupture in both bloodline and tradition between ancient and modern Greece.</note>.

# CHAPTER III
## THE CLASSICAL PREJUDICE

We have already indicated what we mean by the "classical prejudice": it is specifically the bias of attributing the origin of all civilization to the **Greeks** and **Romans**. Basically, one can hardly find any other reason for it than this: Westerners, because their own civilization indeed barely dates back beyond the Greco-Roman era and derives almost entirely from it, are prone to imagining that it must have been the same everywhere; they find it difficult to conceive of the existence of civilizations that are very different and of much older origin. One could say that they are, intellectually, incapable of crossing the Mediterranean. Furthermore, the habit of speaking about "civilization" in an absolute way contributes to a large extent to maintaining this prejudice: "civilization," understood in this way and assumed to be unique, is something that has never existed; in reality, there have always been, and there still are, "civilizations." 

Western civilization, with its special characteristics, is simply one civilization among others, and what is pompously called "the evolution of civilization" is nothing more than the development of this particular civilization since its relatively recent origins—a development which, moreover, is far from having always been regularly "progressive" in all respects. What we said above regarding the so-called **Renaissance** and its consequences could serve here as a very clear example of an **intellectual regression** <note>The author uses this term to describe a decline in the ability to grasp metaphysical truths, despite progress in material or scientific fields.</note>, which has only continued to worsen until our own time.

For anyone who wishes to examine things with impartiality, it is manifest that the **Greeks** truly borrowed almost everything from **Easterners**, at least from an intellectual point of view, as they themselves frequently admitted. However much they may have been liars <note>This may be an allusion to the ancient "Cretan paradox," where Greeks were stereotyped by contemporaries as being prone to embellishment or deception.</note>, they at least did not lie on this point; besides, they had no interest in doing so—quite the contrary. Their only originality, as we said previously, lies in the way they presented things, according to a faculty of adaptation that cannot be denied them, but which is necessarily limited to the extent of their understanding; this is, in short, an originality of a purely <term>dialectical</term> <note>Dialectics here refers to the method of logical argumentation and the formal structure of language used to express ideas, rather than the core ideas themselves.</note> order. Indeed, the

modes of reasoning, which derive from general modes of thought and serve to formulate them, are different among the Greeks than among the Easterners; one must always be careful of this when pointing out certain analogies—real though they may be—such as that of the Greek **syllogism** <term>syllogism: a form of logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore, Socrates is mortal).</term>, for example, with what has been called, more or less accurately, the Hindu syllogism. One cannot even say that Greek reasoning is distinguished by any particular rigor; it only appears more rigorous than others to those who are exclusively accustomed to it, and this appearance arises solely from the fact that it always confines itself to a more restricted, more limited, and therefore better-defined domain. What is truly specific to the Greeks, on the other hand—though little to their advantage—is a certain dialectical subtlety of which **Plato's** dialogues offer numerous examples. In these, we see the need to indefinitely examine the same question from every angle, approaching it from the most trivial sides, only to arrive at a more or less insignificant conclusion; one must believe that modern Westerners are not the first to be afflicted with "intellectual myopia" <note>intellectual myopia: a metaphor for "nearsightedness" of the mind, or the inability to see the "big picture" of universal truths beyond small, logical details.</note>.

There is perhaps no reason, after all, to excessively reproach the Greeks for having narrowed the field of human thought as they did; on one hand, this was an inevitable consequence of their mental constitution, for which they cannot be held responsible, and on the other hand, they at least placed within the reach of a portion of humanity certain knowledge that might otherwise have remained completely foreign to them. It is easy to see this by observing what Westerners are capable of today when they find themselves directly in the presence of certain Eastern conceptions and attempt to interpret them according to their own mentality: everything they cannot reduce to "classical" forms escapes them entirely, and everything they do manage to reduce, for better or worse, is thereby distorted to the point of being rendered unrecognizable.

The so-called "Greek miracle," as its enthusiastic admirers call it, reduces down to very little in the end; or at least, where it implies a profound change, that change is a downfall: it is the individualization of conceptions, the substitution of the rational for the pure intellectual, and of the scientific and philosophical point of view for the metaphysical point of view. It matters little, moreover, whether the Greeks knew better than others how to give certain knowledge a practical character, or whether they drew consequences of such a character from it, whereas those who had preceded them had not <note>The sentence ends abruptly here, likely continuing on the following page to explain that earlier civilizations prioritized pure knowledge over practical applications.</note>

done; it is even permissible to conclude that they have thus given knowledge a less pure and less disinterested purpose, because their turn of mind allowed them to remain only with difficulty and as if exceptionally in the realm of principles. This "practical" tendency, in the most ordinary sense of the word, is one of those that would become increasingly marked in the development of Western civilization, and it is visibly predominant in the modern era; the only exception that can be made in this regard is in favor of the **Middle Ages**, which was much more oriented toward pure **speculation** <note>speculation: here used in its classical sense of deep theoretical contemplation rather than "guessing."</note>.

Generally speaking, **Westerners** are, by their nature, very little inclined toward **metaphysics**; a comparison of their languages with those of **Easterners** would in itself provide sufficient proof, if indeed **philologists** <term>philologists: scholars who study the history, development, and "spirit" of languages.</term> were capable of truly grasping the spirit of the languages they study. On the other hand, Easterners have a very marked tendency to disregard applications, and this is easily understood, for anyone who essentially devotes themselves to the knowledge of **universal principles** <term>universal principles: fundamental truths that apply to all of reality, beyond the physical or material world.</term> can take only a mediocre interest in specialized sciences, and can at most grant them a passing curiosity—certainly insufficient to lead to numerous discoveries in that line of thought. When one knows—with a mathematical certainty, so to speak, and even more than mathematical—that things cannot be otherwise than they are, one is necessarily dismissive of experimentation. This is because the observation of a particular fact, whatever it may be, never proves anything more or other than the pure and simple existence of that fact itself; at most, such an observation may sometimes serve to illustrate a theory as an example, but by no means to prove it, and to believe otherwise is a serious illusion.

Under these conditions, there is obviously no reason to study the **experimental sciences** for their own sake, and, from a metaphysical point of view, they—like the objects to which they apply—have only a purely accidental and **contingent** <term>contingent: something that depends on circumstances and could be otherwise, as opposed to something that is "necessary" or absolute.</term> value. Often, one does not even feel the need to extract particular laws, which could nevertheless be derived from principles as a special application to a given field, if one felt the effort was worth it. We can thus understand everything that separates Eastern "savoir" (knowledge) from Western "recherche" (research); yet one may still be surprised that research has come, for modern Westerners, to constitute an end in itself, independent of its possible results.

Moreover, as a corollary <note>corollary: a proposition that follows naturally from one already proven.</note> to what preceded, it is clear that no one has ever been further than the **Easterners**, without exception, from having a "cult of nature" like that of Greco-Roman antiquity. This is because nature has never been for them anything more than the world of appearances; to be sure, these appearances also possess a reality, but it is only a transitory and non-permanent reality—contingent <note>contingent: dependent on something else; not necessary or absolute.</note> and not universal. Thus, "**naturalism**," in all the forms it can take, can only constitute a deviation—and even a true intellectual monstrosity—in the eyes of men who might be called *metaphysicians by temperament*.

It must be said, however, that the **Greeks**, despite their tendency toward "naturalism," never went so far as to attach the excessive importance to experimentation that the moderns attribute to it. Throughout all of antiquity, even in the West, one finds a certain disdain for experimental experience. It would perhaps be quite difficult to explain this otherwise than by seeing in it a trace of Eastern influence; for the Greeks, such a disdain had partially lost its justification <note>original: "raison d'être"</note>, since their concerns were hardly **metaphysical**, and aesthetic considerations often took the place of the deeper reasons that eluded them. 

It is these latter aesthetic considerations that are most commonly used to explain this fact; but we believe there is something else at play, at least originally. In any case, this does not prevent us from finding already among the Greeks, in a certain sense, the starting point of the **experimental sciences** as moderns understand them—sciences in which the "practical" tendency unites with the "naturalist" tendency. Neither of these can reach their full development except at the expense of pure thought and **disinterested knowledge** <term>disinterested knowledge: knowledge pursued for its own sake, for the sake of truth alone, rather than for practical application or personal gain.</term>. 

Thus, the fact that Easterners never attached themselves to certain specialized sciences is in no way a sign of inferiority on their part; intellectually, it is quite the opposite. This is, in short, a normal consequence of the fact that their activity has always been directed in an entirely different direction and toward an entirely different end. It is precisely the various directions in which human mental activity can be exercised that give each **civilization** its specific character by determining the fundamental direction of its development. At the same time, this is what gives the **illusion of progress** to those who, knowing only one civilization, see exclusively the direction in which it develops, believe it to be the only one possible, and do not realize that this development in one area may be largely

If we consider the intellectual order—which is the only essential element of Eastern civilizations—there are at least two reasons why the Greeks, in this respect, borrowed everything from them. By this, we mean everything that is truly valid in their concepts. One of these reasons, the one we have emphasized most so far, is derived from the relative ineptitude of the Greek mentality in this regard; the other is that Hellenic <note>Hellenic: relating to the language, culture, and history of ancient Greece.</note> civilization is of a much more recent date than the main Eastern civilizations. # CHAPTER IV
## THE RELATIONS OF ANCIENT PEOPLES

<meta>[Return]</meta>

It is quite generally believed that relations between Greece and India only began, or at least only acquired significant importance, at the time of the conquests of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE), King of Macedon, whose empire reached as far as the Punjab region of India.</note>; for everything that is certainly prior to this date, people therefore speak simply of fortuitous resemblances between the two civilizations, and, for everything that is posterior, or supposed posterior, they naturally speak of Greek influence, as required by the special logic inherent to the "classical prejudice" <note>classical prejudice: the academic bias that assumes Western (Greek and Roman) culture is the primary source of all significant civilization and knowledge.</note>. This is yet another opinion which, like many others, is devoid of any serious foundation, for relations between peoples, even distant ones, were much more frequent in antiquity than is ordinarily imagined. In short, communications were not much more difficult then than they were just one or two centuries ago, and more precisely until the invention of railways and steamships; people undoubtedly traveled less commonly than in our time, less often and especially less quickly, but they traveled in a more profitable way, because they took the time to study the countries they passed through, and sometimes they even traveled precisely for the sake of this study and the intellectual benefits that could be derived from it. Under these conditions, there is no plausible reason to treat as "legend" what is reported to us regarding the travels of the Greek philosophers, especially since these travels explain many things that would otherwise be incomprehensible. The truth is that, long before the earliest times of Greek philosophy, the means of communication must have had a development of which moderns are far from having an accurate idea, and this in a normal and permanent way, quite apart from the migrations of peoples which undoubtedly only ever occurred in a discontinuous and somewhat exceptional manner.

Among other proofs that we could cite in support of what we have just said, we will indicate only one, which specifically concerns the relations of the Mediterranean peoples, and we will do so because it involves a fact that is little known or at least little noticed, to which no one seems to have paid—

Such is the profound difference that exists between philosophical thought, in the European sense of the word, and metaphysical thought; but we shall have the opportunity to [return to it]...

# CHAPTER V
## QUESTIONS OF CHRONOLOGY

Questions relating to chronology are among those that most embarrass Orientalists <term>Orientalists: Western scholars specialized in the study of Asian cultures, languages, and history.</term>, and this embarrassment is generally quite justified; but they are wrong, on the one hand, to attach an excessive importance to these questions, and, on the other, to believe that they can arrive at definitive solutions through their ordinary methods, when in fact they only result in more or less fanciful hypotheses, upon which they are, moreover, far from agreeing among themselves. 

There are, however, some cases that present no real difficulty, at least as long as one is willing not to complicate them at will with the subtleties and quibbles of an absurd "criticism" and "hypercriticism" <note>This refers to the "Higher Criticism" movement of the 19th century, which sought to apply rigorous, often skeptical, historical analysis to ancient texts.</note>. Such is notably the case with documents which, like the ancient Chinese annals, contain a precise description of the state of the sky at the period to which they refer; the calculation of their exact date, based on certain astronomical data, allows for no ambiguity. Unfortunately, this case is not universal—it is even almost exceptional—and other documents, Hindu documents in particular, for the most part offer nothing of the sort to guide research. Fundamentally, this simply proves that their authors had not the slightest concern with "dating their work" in order to claim any kind of priority. 

The claim to intellectual originality, which contributes in large part to the birth of philosophical systems, is, even among Westerners, an entirely modern thing that the Middle Ages still ignored; pure ideas and traditional doctrines have never constituted the property of this or that individual, and the biographical details of those who expounded and interpreted them are of very minimal importance. Moreover, even regarding China, the remark we just made applies hardly, in truth, except to historical writings; but these are, after all, the only ones for which chronological determination presents a real interest, since this determination itself has meaning and scope only from the viewpoint of history. It must be noted, on the other hand, that to increase the difficulty, there exists in India, and doubtless also in certain extinct civilizations, a chronology, or more exactly something that has

He notes that while astronomical data allows for the dating of some Chinese texts, Indian texts often lack such markers because their authors did not value intellectual "originality."</summary>

<keywords>chronology, Orientalism, Chinese annals, Indian literature, traditional doctrines, intellectual history, astronomical dating</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the critique of Western Orientalism, specifically addressing how scholars misinterpret symbolic time cycles as literal years and how Eurocentric bias leads them to downplay the antiquity of Eastern and Egyptian civilizations in favor of a Greek origin for all knowledge.</meta>

the appearance of a chronology, based on symbolic numbers, which should by no means be taken literally as numbers of years; and do we not encounter something similar even in biblical chronology? However, this alleged chronology applies exclusively, in reality, to **cosmic periods** <term>cosmic periods: vast cycles of time in traditional doctrines, such as the Hindu Yugas, which describe the unfolding of the universe rather than human history</term>, and not to **historical periods**; between the one and the other, no confusion is possible, except through the effect of a rather gross ignorance, and yet one is forced to recognize that Orientalists have given only too many examples of such misunderstandings.

A very general tendency among these same Orientalists is that which leads them to reduce as much as possible, and often even beyond any reasonable measure, the antiquity of the civilizations with which they are dealing, as if they were uncomfortable with the fact that these civilizations could have existed and been in full development at such distant epochs—so much earlier than the most remote origins that can be assigned to current Western civilization, or rather to those from which it directly proceeds. Their bias in this regard seems to have no other excuse than this, which is truly quite insufficient. Furthermore, this same bias has also been exercised on things much closer to the West, in all respects, than are the civilizations of China and India, or even those of Egypt, Persia, and Chaldea. Thus, efforts have been made, for example, to "rejuvenate" the Hebrew ***Kabbalah*** <term>Kabbalah: The ancient Jewish tradition of mystical and esoteric interpretation of the Bible</term> in such a way as to be able to assume an Alexandrian and Neoplatonic <term>Neoplatonic: A school of mystical philosophy based on Plato's teachings that flourished in the 3rd century AD</term> influence, when it is almost certainly the reverse that actually occurred. This is always for the same reason: namely, simply because it is agreed **from the outset** <note>original: "a priori"</note> that everything must come from the Greeks, that they held a monopoly on knowledge in antiquity—just as Europeans imagine they hold it now—and that they were (again, just as these same Europeans claim to be today) the educators and inspirers of the human race. And yet Plato, whose testimony should not be suspected in this instance, did not fear to report in the ***Timaeus*** <note>One of Plato's dialogues, where he recounts the story of Atlantis and the origins of the world</note> that the Egyptians treated the Greeks as "children." Orientals would still have many reasons to say the same of Westerners today, if the scruples of a perhaps excessive politeness did not often prevent them from going that far. We remember, however, that this very assessment was aptly formulated by a Hindu who, hearing the conceptions of certain European philosophers explained for the first time, was so far from being filled with wonder that he declared those were ideas good at most for an eight-year-old child!

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of Eurocentric scholarship, specifically addressing the tendency to credit the Greeks as the original inventors of philosophy rather than "adapters" of much older Eastern traditions. Those who might find that we diminish the role played by the Greeks too significantly, by treating them almost exclusively as "adapters," might object that we do not know all of their ideas, and that many things have not reached us. This is certainly true in some cases, particularly concerning the **oral teaching** of the philosophers; but is not what we know of their ideas nonetheless largely sufficient to allow us to judge the rest? Analogy, which alone provides us with the means to go, to a certain extent, from the known to the unknown, can only prove us right here. Moreover, according to the **written teaching** we possess, there are at least strong presumptions that the corresponding oral teaching—in what was precisely special and **“esoteric,”** <term>esoteric: from the Greek *esoteros* meaning "inner"; refers to secret teachings reserved for an initiated inner circle</term> that is to say, "more internal"—was, like that of the **“mysteries”** <term>mysteries: secret religious rites of ancient Greece, such as those at Eleusis, which were hidden from the general public</term> with which it must have had many connections, even more strongly tinged with Eastern inspiration. Furthermore, the very "interiority" of this teaching can only guarantee that it was less distant from its source and less distorted than any other, because it was less adapted to the general mentality of the Greek people; otherwise, its comprehension would obviously not have required a special preparation—especially a preparation as long and difficult as was, for example, the one in use in the **Pythagorean schools** <term>Pythagorean schools: the philosophical and religious communities founded by Pythagoras, known for their rigorous discipline and years of required silence</term>.

Moreover, archaeologists and **Orientalists** <term>Orientalists: 19th and early 20th-century Western scholars who specialized in the languages and cultures of the "Orient" or East</term> would be poorly placed to invoke an oral teaching, or even lost works, against us, since the **“historical method”** <term>historical method: a research approach that prioritizes tangible physical evidence, often rejecting anything that cannot be proven by a dated document or artifact</term> to which they are so attached has as its essential character to take into consideration only the monuments they have before their eyes and the written documents they have in their hands; and it is precisely there that the total insufficiency of this method is shown. Indeed, there is a remark that must be made, but which is too often lost sight of, and it is this: if one finds a manuscript for a certain work whose date can be determined by any means, this proves well enough that the work in question is certainly not *later* than that date, but that is all; it in no way proves that it could not be much *earlier*. It may very well happen that more ancient manuscripts of the same work are discovered later; and furthermore, even if none are discovered, one has no right to conclude that none exist, nor even less that none have ever existed. If some still exist, in the case of a civilization that has lasted until our time, it is at least likely that, most often, they are not left to chance...

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of Western academic methods. It addresses why ancient Eastern texts are often not available as physical "original" manuscripts, contrasting the living traditions of the East with the archaeological remains of dead civilizations.</meta>

of an archaeological discovery like those one can make when dealing with a vanished civilization. Furthermore, there is no reason to assume that those who preserve these documents will feel obliged, at one time or another, to part with them for the benefit of Western scholars—especially since their preservation may involve interests we will not emphasize here, but compared to which curiosity, even when decorated with the epithet **"scientific,"** is of very little value.

On the other hand, regarding vanished civilizations, one is forced to realize that, despite all research and discoveries, there are a multitude of documents that will never be found, for the simple reason that they were accidentally destroyed. As accidents of this kind were, in some cases, contemporary with the civilizations in question and not necessarily subsequent to their extinction—and as we can still frequently witness similar occurrences around us—it is extremely probable that the same must have also occurred, more or less, in other civilizations that have continued until our time. Indeed, there is all the more chance of this having been the case as a longer succession of centuries has passed since the origin of these civilizations.

But there is something more: even without accidents, ancient manuscripts can disappear in a quite natural way—normal, in a sense—through simple wear and tear. In such cases, they are replaced by others that are necessarily of a more recent date, and these are the only ones whose existence can subsequently be confirmed. One can form an idea of this, in particular, by what constantly happens in the **Muslim world**: a manuscript circulates and is transported, according to need, from one center of learning to another, and sometimes to very distant regions, until it is seriously enough damaged by use to be nearly out of service. An exact copy is then made—as precise as possible—which will henceforth take the place of the old manuscript. This copy will be used in the same way and will itself be replaced by another when it, in turn, deteriorates, and so on.

These successive replacements can certainly be very inconvenient for the specialized research of **Orientalists** <term>Orientalists: 19th and early 20th-century Western scholars who studied the languages, history, and cultures of the Near and Far East, often through a Eurocentric lens</term>; but those who carry out these replacements care little for this inconvenience, and even if they were aware of it, they certainly would not consent to change their habits for such a small matter. All these remarks are so obvious in themselves that they might not even be worth the trouble of formulating, if the **preconceptions** <note>original: "parti pris"</note> we have pointed out among the Orientalists did not blind them to the point of entirely hiding this evidence from them.

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of the Western "historical method," shifting focus from the physical survival of manuscripts to the primacy of oral tradition over written records.</meta>

Now, there is another fact that the supporters of the **"historical method"** <term>historical method: a scholarly approach that treats texts primarily as chronological artifacts, often disregarding the spiritual or timeless context the authors intended</term> can hardly take into account without being in disagreement with themselves: it is that oral instruction preceded written instruction almost everywhere, and that it was the only method in use during periods that may have been very long, even if their exact duration is difficult to determine. Generally speaking, a traditional writing is, in most cases, only the relatively recent fixing of a teaching that was first transmitted orally, and to which it is very rare that one can assign an author; thus, even if one were certain to be in possession of the original manuscript—of which there is perhaps no example—one would still need to know how long the previous oral transmission lasted, and that is a question which is likely to remain, more often than not, without an answer. 

This exclusivity of oral instruction may have had multiple reasons, and it does not necessarily imply the absence of writing, the origin of which is certainly very distant—at least in its ideographic form, whereas the phonetic form is merely a degeneracy caused by a need for simplification. We know, for example, that the teaching of the **Druids** <term>Druids: the high-ranking priestly and educational class in ancient Celtic societies</term> always remained exclusively oral, even at a time when the **Gauls** surely knew how to write, since they regularly used a Greek alphabet in their commercial relations; likewise, Druidic teaching has left no authentic trace, and it is at most only possible to reconstruct, more or less accurately, a few very limited fragments. 

It would, moreover, be an error to believe that oral transmission must inevitably alter the teaching over time; given the interest represented by its total preservation, there is, on the contrary, every reason to think that the necessary precautions were taken so that it would always remain identical, not only in substance, but even in form. One can see that this maintenance is perfectly achievable by what still takes place today among all the **Eastern peoples**, for whom the fixation by writing has never led to the suppression of oral tradition, nor been considered capable of entirely replacing it. 

Curiously, it is commonly admitted that certain works were not written down from their origin; this is notably accepted for the **Homeric poems** in classical antiquity, and for the **songs of heroic deeds** <note>original: "chansons de geste," epic poems from the Middle Ages</note> in the Middle Ages; why then would one no longer admit the same thing when it concerns works relating, no longer to a simply literary order, but to the order of **pure intellectuality**, where oral transmission has much deeper reasons? It is truly useless to insist further upon this,

There remains one last point that we would like to indicate in this chapter: it is that, while it is often quite difficult to situate a certain period of an ancient people's existence exactly in time, it is sometimes almost as difficult, strange as it may seem, to situate it in space. By this, we mean that certain peoples may have, at various epochs, emigrated from one region to another, and nothing proves to us that the works left by the ancient **Hindus** or the ancient **Persians**, for example, were all composed in the countries where their descendants live today. Furthermore, nothing proves this to us even in cases where these works contain the designation of certain places—names of rivers or mountains that we still know—for these same names could have been applied successively in the various regions where the people in question stopped during their migrations. There is something quite natural in this: do modern Europeans not frequently have the habit of giving names borrowed from their country of origin to the cities they found in their colonies and to the geographical features they encounter there? 

There has sometimes been discussion as to whether the **Hellas** <term>Hellas: the ancient name for Greece</term> of Homeric times was truly the Greece of more recent eras, or if the biblical **Palestine** was truly the region we still designate by that name; discussions of this kind are perhaps not as vain as is usually thought, and the question at least deserves to be raised, even if, in the examples we have just cited, it is quite probable that it should be resolved in the affirmative. On the other hand, concerning **Vedic India** <term>Vedic India: the era associated with the oldest sacred texts of India, the Vedas, believed by some to have originated far outside the Indian subcontinent</term>, there are many reasons to answer such a question negatively; the ancestors of the Hindus must have, at an indeterminate time, inhabited a very northern region <note>This refers to the "Arctic Home" theory, popular in early 20th-century scholarship, which suggested Indo-European origins in the far north</note>, since, according to certain texts, the sun would circle the horizon without setting; but when did they leave this primitive home, and after how many stages did they arrive from there in present-day India? 

These are interesting questions from a certain point of view, but we are content to point them out without claiming to examine them here, as they do not fall within our subject. The considerations we have dealt with so far are merely preliminaries that seemed necessary before addressing the questions properly relating to the interpretation of **Oriental doctrines**; and, for these latter questions, which are our object...

# CHAPTER VI
## LINGUISTIC DIFFICULTIES

The most serious difficulty for the correct interpretation of Eastern doctrines arises—as we have already indicated and as we intend to explain further in what follows—from the essential difference that exists between the modes of Eastern thought and those of Western thought. This difference is naturally expressed by a corresponding difference in the languages intended to express these respective modes. From this comes a second difficulty, derived from the first, when it comes to rendering certain ideas into Western languages, which lack appropriate terms and which, above all, are very little metaphysical <term>metaphysical: relating to the study of fundamental reality and concepts beyond the physical world</term>. Moreover, this is ultimately only an intensification of the difficulties inherent in all translation, which are found even, to a lesser degree, when passing from one language to another that is very close philologically <term>philologically: the branch of knowledge that deals with the structure, historical development, and relationships of languages</term> as well as geographically. Even in this latter case, terms regarded as equivalents, which often share the same origin or derivation, are sometimes very far, despite this, from offering an exact equivalence of meaning. This is easily understood, for it is evident that every language must be particularly adapted to the mentality of the people who use it, and every people has its own mentality, more or less widely different from that of others. This diversity of ethnic mentalities is only much less when considering peoples belonging to the same race or linked to the same civilization. In this case, the common mental traits are certainly the most fundamental, but the secondary characters superimposed upon them can give rise to variations that are still quite significant. One might even wonder whether, among individuals speaking the same language within the limits of a nation comprising diverse ethnic elements, the sense of words in that language does not take on different shades from one region to another, especially since national and linguistic unification is often recent and somewhat artificial. It would be nothing surprising, for example, if the common language inherited in each province, in substance as much as in form, some particularities of the ancient dialect which it has come to—

# CHAPTER ONE
## THE GREAT DIVISIONS OF THE EAST

We have already stated that, although one can contrast the **Eastern mentality** in its entirety with the **Western mentality**, one cannot, however, speak of an *Oriental civilization* in the same way as one speaks of a *Western civilization*. There are several distinctly different Eastern civilizations, each of which possesses—as we shall see hereafter—a principle of unity unique to itself, which differs essentially from one civilization to another. However, as diverse as they may be, they all share certain common traits, principally regarding their modes of thought; it is precisely this which allows us to say that there exists, in a general sense, a specifically Eastern mentality.

When one wishes to undertake any study, it is always appropriate, for the sake of order, to begin by establishing a classification based on the natural divisions of the subject one proposes to study. This is why, before any other consideration, it is necessary to situate the different Eastern civilizations in relation to one another. In doing so, we shall stick to the broad outlines and the most general divisions, which are sufficient at least for an initial approximation, as our intention here is not to enter into a detailed examination of each of these civilizations taken individually.

Under these conditions, we can divide the East into three major regions, which we shall designate—according to their geographical situation relative to Europe—as the Near East, the Middle East, and the Far East. For us, the **Near East** <note>In the author's era, the "Near East" (Proche-Orient) was a term often used for the Ottoman Empire and surrounding Islamic territories.</note> encompasses the entirety of the Muslim world; the **Middle East** is essentially constituted by India; as for the **Far East**, it is that which is usually designated by this name—namely, China and Indo-China. It is easy to see, at first glance, that these three general divisions correspond well to three great civilizations that are completely distinct and independent. These are, if not the only ones existing in the whole of the East, at least the most important ones and those whose domain is by far the most extensive. Within each of these civilizations, one could, moreover—

The **Near East**, which begins at the borders of Europe, extends not only over the part of Asia nearest to it, but also, at the same time, over all of North Africa; it therefore includes, truth be told, countries which, geographically, are just as Western as Europe itself. The **Berber** populations of North Africa have never merged with the **Arabs** living on the same soil, and it is easy to distinguish them, not only by the special customs they have preserved or by their physical type, but also by a kind of mental physiognomy unique to them; it is quite certain, for example, that the <term>Kabyle<gloss>A Berber ethnic group from the mountainous regions of northern Algeria.</gloss></term> is much closer to the European, in certain respects, than the Arab is. Alongside this Arabic group, we shall distinguish two other main ones, which we may call the **Turkish group** and the **Persian group**, although these designations are perhaps not rigorously exact. # CHAPTER II
## PRINCIPES OF UNITY IN ORIENTAL CIVILIZATIONS

It is very difficult today to find a principle of unity for Western civilization; one might even say that its unity, which always rests naturally on a collection of tendencies constituting a certain mental conformity, is no longer truly anything more than a mere unity of fact. This unity lacks a principle, just as this civilization itself has lacked one ever since the traditional bond of a religious nature was broken during the era of the Renaissance and the Reformation. This bond was precisely its essential principle, and in the Middle Ages, it made the West what was called "Christendom." <note>The term "Christendom" (French: *Chrétienté*) refers here to the socio-political and spiritual unity of Europe under the Catholic Church before the 16th-century religious schisms.</note> Western intellectuality <term>Intellectuality: In this context, the author refers not just to academic intelligence, but to the capacity for metaphysical and traditional knowledge.</term> could not have at its disposal—within the limits in which its specifically restricted activity is exercised—any traditional element of another order that might be capable of substituting for that religious bond. We mean that such an element could not be conceived of in this environment other than in a religious mode, except for a few exceptions incapable of being generalized. As for the unity of the European race, as a race, it is, as we have indicated, too relative and too weak to serve as a basis for the unity of a civilization. There was, therefore, a risk from that point on of having multiple European civilizations without any effective or conscious link; and, in fact, it was from the moment the fundamental unity of "Christendom" was broken that one saw formed in its place—through many vicissitudes and uncertain efforts—the secondary, fragmentary, and diminished units of "nationalities." <note>The author views the rise of the "nation-state" as a symptom of the breakdown of a higher spiritual unity.</note> Yet Europe still preserved, even in its mental deviation and as if despite itself, the imprint of the unique formation it had received over previous centuries; the very influences that had brought about the deviation had been exerted everywhere in a similar fashion, though to varying degrees. The result was still a common mentality, leading to a civilization that remains common despite all its divisions. However, instead of legitimately depending on a principle—whatever that might be—it was henceforth to be, so to speak, at the service of an "absence of principle," condemning it to an irremediable intellectual decline. <note>original: "déchéance intellectuelle"</note> One can certainly maintain that this was the price of the material progress toward which the Western world has tended exclusively ever since, for there are paths of...

<summary>This chapter analyzes the loss of spiritual and intellectual unity in Western civilization following the Renaissance and Reformation, noting the shift from the religious unity of "Christendom" to fragmented nationalist identities.</summary>
<keywords>Western civilization, Christendom, Renaissance, Reformation, nationalism, intellectual decline, material progress, unity of principle</keywords>

--- Page 48 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous page regarding the fragmentation of the West. It specifically contrasts the modern Western concept of "nationality" with the traditional religious unity found in the Middle Ages and the contemporary Islamic world.</meta>

...development which are irreconcilable; but, regardless, it was truly, in our opinion, paying a very high price for this much-boasted progress. <note>The author is referring to the "progress" of the Renaissance and Reformation, which he argues destroyed the traditional unity of Europe.</note>

This very brief overview allows us to understand, first of all, why there can be nothing in the East comparable to what Western nations are: it is because the emergence of nationalities is, in short, a sign of partial dissolution within a civilization, resulting from the loss of what constituted its deep unity. Even in the West, we repeat, the conception of **nationality** is essentially a modern thing; one could find nothing analogous in everything that existed before—neither the Greek city-states, nor the Roman Empire (which arose, moreover, from the successive extensions of the original city), nor its more or less indirect medieval continuations, nor the confederations or leagues of peoples in the Celtic manner, nor even the states organized hierarchically according to the feudal type.

On the other hand, what we have said about the ancient unity of "Christendom"—a unity essentially traditional in nature, and moreover conceived according to a special mode which is the **religious mode**—can be applied, almost in its entirety, to the conception of the unity of the Muslim world. Islamic civilization is indeed, among Oriental civilizations, the one closest to the West, and one could even say that, by its characteristics as by its geographical situation, it is, in various respects, intermediary between the East and the West; thus its tradition appears to us as being capable of being viewed under two profoundly distinct modes, one of which is purely Oriental, but the other, which is the properly religious mode, is common to it and Western civilization.

Moreover, Judaism, Christianity, and **Islam** <note>original: "Islamisme." # CHAPTER III
## WHAT IS TO BE UNDERSTOOD BY TRADITION?

In the preceding sections, we have had constant occasion to speak of tradition, of traditional doctrines or conceptions, and even of traditional languages, and it is indeed impossible to do otherwise when one wishes to designate what constitutes the truly essential core of Eastern thought <note>Guénon uses "Eastern thought" to describe civilizations that have maintained a link to ancient, sacred principles, unlike the modern West.</note> in its various modes; but what, more precisely, is tradition? Let us say at the outset, to clear up a confusion that might occur, that we do not take this word in the narrow sense in which Western religious thought sometimes opposes "tradition" and "scripture," understanding by the first of these two terms, in an exclusive way, that which has only been the object of oral transmission. On the contrary, for us, tradition, in a much more general sense, can be written as well as oral, although, usually—if not always—it must have been primarily oral at its origin, as we have explained; but, in the current state of things, the written part and the oral part everywhere form two complementary branches of the same tradition, whether it be religious or otherwise, and we have no hesitation in speaking of "traditional scriptures," which would obviously be contradictory if we gave the word "tradition" only its most specialized meaning; moreover, etymologically, tradition is simply "that which is transmitted" <note>original: "ce qui se transmet"; derived from the Latin *tradere*, meaning to hand over or deliver.</note> in one way or another. Furthermore, we must also include in tradition—as secondary and derivative elements, yet important for a complete notion of it—the entire set of institutions of different orders which have their principle in the traditional doctrine itself.

Viewed in this way, tradition may seem to merge with civilization itself, which is, according to certain sociologists, "the set of techniques, institutions, and beliefs common to a group of men during a certain time" <insert>[[1]](https://example.com)</insert>; but what, exactly, is this last definition worth? We do not believe, in truth, that civilization is capable of being generally characterized in a formula of this kind, which will always be too broad or too

As for Western civilization, we have said that it is, on the contrary, devoid of any traditional character, with the exception of its religious element, which is the only one to have preserved that character there. This is because social institutions, to be called traditional, must be effectively attached, as if to their principle, to a doctrine that is itself traditional—whether that doctrine be <term>metaphysical</term> <note>In this context, "metaphysics" refers to the knowledge of universal, infinite, and changeless principles, rather than just a branch of academic philosophy.</note>, or religious, or of any other conceivable kind.
