# CHAPTER IV
## TRADITION AND RELIGION

It seems quite difficult to agree on an exact and rigorous definition of religion and its essential elements. Etymology <note>The study of the origin of words and the way in which their meanings have changed throughout history.</note>, often precious in such instances, provides us here with only meager help, for the indication it furnishes is extremely vague. Religion, according to the derivation of this word, is "that which binds" <note>original: "ce qui relie"; likely referring to the Latin *religare*, meaning to tie or bind back.</note>; but should we understand by this that which binds man to a superior principle, or simply that which binds men to one another? Considering Greco-Roman antiquity—from which we received the word, if not the very thing it designates today—it is almost certain that the notion of religion shared in this double meaning, and that the second meaning often played the predominant role. Indeed, religion, or at least what was then understood by the word, was indissolubly one with the whole of social institutions. The recognition of the "gods of the city" <note>The *dii publici*; the official deities of a Greek or Roman city-state whose worship was a civic duty.</note> and the observation of legally established cult forms constituted fundamental conditions and guaranteed stability. It was this, moreover, which gave these institutions a truly traditional character. However, there was already from that time, at least in the classical period, something misunderstood in the very principle upon which this tradition should have intellectually rested. One can see here one of the first manifestations of the metaphysical <note>Metaphysics here refers to the knowledge of universal, eternal principles, as opposed to the physical or social world.</note> inaptitude common to Westerners—an inaptitude which has, as a fatal and constant consequence, a strange confusion in the modalities of thought. Among the Greeks in particular, rites and symbols—the heritage of older and already forgotten traditions—had quickly lost their precise original meaning. The imagination of this eminently artistic people, expressing itself according to the individual fancy of its poets, had covered them with an almost impenetrable veil. This is why we see philosophers such as Plato declare expressly that they do not know what to think of the oldest writings they possessed regarding the nature of the gods [2].

The symbols had thus degenerated into simple allegories <note>A story or image that can be interpreted to reveal a hidden meaning, typically a moral or political one, rather than a direct spiritual truth.</note>, and, due to an invincible tendency toward anthropomorphic <note>Attributing human characteristics or behavior to a god, animal, or object.</note> personifications, they were

This explains how a man who changed his city was required at the same time to change his religion, and could do so without the slightest scruple: he had to adopt the customs of those among whom he settled, and he henceforth owed obedience to their legislation, which became his own; of this legislation, the established religion formed an integral part, exactly in the same way as the governmental, judicial, military, or other institutions. Among the Romans, it was much the same as among the Greeks, with this difference, however: their misunderstanding of the symbolic forms they had borrowed from the traditions of the **Etruscans** <note>A sophisticated civilization in ancient Italy that preceded and deeply influenced the Romans, especially in religious rituals.</note> and various other peoples arose not from an aesthetic tendency invading all domains of thought (even those which should have been most closed to it), but rather from a complete incapacity for everything of a properly intellectual order. This radical insufficiency of the Roman mentality, which was almost exclusively directed toward practical matters, is too visible and, moreover, too generally recognized for it to be necessary to insist upon it; the Greek influence, exerted later on, was only to remedy this to a very limited extent. It is only through a direct examination of what actually exists that it is possible to obtain precise information.

Thus, there are sociologists who claim, for example, that "what characterizes religious phenomena is their **obligatory force**" <insert>[3]</insert>. It should be noted that this obligatory character is far from belonging to the same degree to everything that is equally religious, and that it can vary in intensity, whether for different practices and beliefs within the same religion, or generally from one religion to another; but, even admitting that it is more or less common to all religious facts, it is very far from being unique to them, and the most elementary logic teaches that a definition must apply, not only "to everything being defined," but also "to the defined alone." <note>This refers to the classical logical rule *omni et soli definito*: a definition must cover everything the term includes and exclude everything it does not.</note> In fact, obligation—imposed more or less strictly by an authority or a power of any nature—is an element found almost constantly in everything that constitutes **social institutions** properly so-called; in particular, is there anything that presents itself as more rigorously obligatory than **legality**? Moreover, whether legislation is directly linked to religion as in **Islam**, or whether it is on the contrary entirely separate and independent as in current **European States**, it possesses this character of obligation just as much in one case as in the other; it always possesses it necessarily, simply because that is a condition of possibility for any form of social organization. Who then would dare to seriously maintain that the legal institutions of modern Europe are invested with a religious character? Such a supposition is manifesty ridiculous, and if we dwell on it a little longer than might perhaps be appropriate, it is because we are dealing here with theories that have acquired, in certain circles, an influence as considerable as it is unjustified. To finish on this point, it is not only in the societies that people have agreed to call **"primitive"**—wrongly, in our view—that "all social phenomena have the same constraining character," to one degree or another. This observation forces our sociologists—speaking of these so-called **"primitive"** societies whose testimony they love to invoke all the more because verifying it is so difficult—to admit that "religion is everything there, unless one prefers to say that it is nothing there" <insert>[4]</insert>! It is true that they immediately add this restriction for this second alternative (which seems to us to be the correct one): "if one wishes to consider it as a **special function**"; but precisely, if it is not a "special function," it is no longer religion at all.

Certainly, a ritual element is found in every religion, but this element is not sufficient on its own to characterize religion as such; here, just as before, the proposed definition is much too broad, because there are rites that are not in the least religious, and there are even several kinds of them.

There are, in the first place, rites that have a purely and exclusively social character—civil, if you will: this case should have been found in Greco-Roman civilization, had there not been the confusions we previously mentioned <note>The author argues that in ancient Rome, the distinction between "sacred" and "profane" was often blurred in a way that differs from modern Western concepts.</note>; it exists currently in Chinese civilization, where no such confusion exists, and where the ceremonies of **Confucianism** are effectively social rites, without the slightest religious character: it is only in this capacity that they are the object of official recognition, which, in China, would be inconceivable under any other condition. 

This is what the **Jesuits** established in China in the 17th century understood very well; they found it quite natural to participate in these ceremonies and saw nothing in them incompatible with **Christianity** <note>This refers to the "Chinese Rites Controversy," a historical dispute within the Catholic Church over whether Chinese folk religion and Confucian rituals were religious or merely cultural/social.</note>. Contemporary sociologists commit exactly the same mistake that the opponents of the Jesuits once made when they accused them of submitting to the practices of a religion foreign to Christianity: having seen that there were rites there, they naturally thought that these rites must be religious in nature, like those they were accustomed to seeing in their European environment.

The same sentimental factor, which is secondary in doctrine, becomes preponderant—and even nearly exclusive—within **morality**. The principle that morality depends upon dogma is an assertion that is primarily theoretical; in practice, this morality, whose reason for being can only be purely social, could be regarded as a kind of legislation—the only kind that remains within the jurisdiction of religion in societies where civil institutions are independent of it. 

Finally, the **rites** which together constitute **worship** <note>original: "le culte"</note> have a dual nature:
*   An **intellectual character**, insofar as they are regarded as a symbolic and sensible expression of the doctrine.
*   A **social character**, insofar as they are regarded as "practices" requiring the participation of all members of the religious community, in a way that can be more or less obligatory. 

The name "worship" should properly be reserved for religious rites; however, in practice, it is also commonly (though somewhat incorrectly) used to designate other rites, such as purely social ones—for example, when one speaks of "ancestor worship" in China. 

It is noteworthy that in a religion where the social and sentimental elements outweigh the intellectual element, the roles of dogma and worship simultaneously diminish more and more. 1.  In a **religious mode**, when it is linked in principle to a dogma to which it is subordinated.
2.  In a **philosophical mode**, when it is regarded as independent; we shall return to this second form later.

# CHAPTER V
## ESSENTIAL CHARACTERISTICS OF METAPHYSICS

While the religious point of view essentially implies the intervention of an element of a sentimental nature <note>The author uses "sentimental" here to describe aspects of faith, devotion, and emotion that characterize religious practice, contrasting them with the "intellectual" nature of metaphysics.</note>, the metaphysical point of view is exclusively intellectual. However, even though this distinction has a very clear meaning for us, it might seem to many to insufficiently characterize this latter point of view—one which is quite unfamiliar to Westerners—unless we take care to provide further clarification. Science and philosophy, as they exist in the Western world, also lay claim to "intellectuality." If we do not admit that these claims are well-founded, and if we maintain that there is a profound difference between all speculations of that kind and metaphysics, it is because pure intellectuality <term>intellectuality (pure)</term> <note>In this context, "pure intellectuality" refers to a direct, non-discursive knowledge of universal principles, rather than just logical reasoning or academic study.</note>, in the sense we intend, is something quite different from what is usually understood by that term in a more or less vague way.

We must first declare that, when we employ the term "metaphysics" as we do, we care little for its historical origin. This origin is somewhat doubtful and would be purely accidental if we were to accept the opinion—which seems quite unlikely to us—that the word was first used simply to designate what came "after physics" <note>original: "après la physique"</note> in the collection of Aristotle’s works. Nor do we need to concern ourselves with the various and often improper meanings that some have seen fit to attribute to this word at one time or another. These are not sufficient reasons for us to abandon the term; as it stands, it is perfectly suited to what it should normally designate, at least as much as any term borrowed from Western languages can be. Indeed, its most natural sense, even etymologically, is that which designates what is "beyond physics." Here, we must understand "physics" <note>original: "physique"</note> as the ancients always did: as the study of the whole of nature, viewed in a quite general way, and not simply as one specific science among others, according to the restricted meaning used by moderns. It is therefore with this interpretation that we take this...

the term metaphysics, and it must be clearly understood once and for all that, if we hold to it, it is solely for the reason we have just indicated, and because we believe that it is always regrettable to have recourse to neologisms <note>The author refers to "neologisms" as newly coined words. He prefers to use traditional terms like "metaphysics," even if they have been distorted by modern philosophy, rather than inventing a new vocabulary.</note> outside of cases of absolute necessity.

We will now say that metaphysics, thus understood, is essentially the knowledge of the universal, or, if one prefers, of the principles of a universal order <term>universal order</term> <note>In this context, the "universal" refers to that which is beyond the reach of individual, physical, or material experience, concerning the timeless principles that govern all existence.</note>, to which alone the name of principles properly belongs; but we do not wish to give by this a truly formal definition of metaphysics, which is strictly impossible, because of this very universality that we regard as the first of its characteristics, the one from which all others derive. In reality, only that which is limited can be defined, and metaphysics is, on the contrary, in its very essence, absolutely unlimited, which, obviously, does not allow us to enclose its notion in a more or less narrow formula; a definition would be all the more inaccurate here the more one strove to make it precise.

It is important to notice that we have said *knowledge* and not *science*; our intention, in this, is to mark the profound distinction that must necessarily be established between *metaphysics*, on the one hand, and, on the other, the various *sciences* in the proper sense of the word, that is to say, all the particular and specialized sciences, which have as their object this or that determined aspect of individual things. This is, therefore, at its core, the very distinction between the *universal* and the *individual*, a distinction which must not be taken for an opposition, for there is no common measure between these two terms, nor any possible relationship of symmetry or coordination. Furthermore, there can be no opposition or conflict of any kind between *metaphysics* and the *sciences*, precisely because their respective domains are profoundly separate; and it is exactly the same, for that matter, regarding religion. It must be well understood, however, that the separation in question does not relate so much to things themselves as to the points of view <note>The author emphasizes that "metaphysics" and "science" can look at the same object, but they see it differently: science sees the individual, physical details, while metaphysics sees the underlying universal principle.</note> under which we consider things; and this is particularly important for what we will have to say more specifically about the way in which the relations between the different branches of the Hindu doctrine <term>Hindu doctrine</term> <note>The author uses this term to refer to the traditional body of knowledge from India, such as the Vedas and Upanishads, which he views as purely metaphysical.</note> must be conceived. <meta>This page continues the author’s distinction between knowledge and science, further defining the scope of metaphysics as a field that transcends the limitations of individual experience and the scientific method.</meta>

considered from the universal point of view, which, moreover, is not a special point of view, as much as that which cannot be considered from another perspective in an individual mode can be. In this way, it can be said that the domain of metaphysics encompasses everything, which is necessary for it to be truly universal, as it must essentially be; and the proper domains of the various sciences nonetheless remain distinct from that of metaphysics, for the latter, not placing itself on the same ground as the particular sciences, is in no way their analog, so that there can never be any reason to establish a comparison between the results of the one and those of the others. On the other hand, the domain of metaphysics is by no means—as some philosophers think who hardly know what is at issue here—what the various sciences may leave outside of themselves because their current development is more or less incomplete, but rather that which, by its very nature, eludes the grasp of these sciences and immensely exceeds the scope to which they can legitimately lay claim. The domain of every science always falls within the realm of <term>experience</term> <note>The author uses "experience" here to refer to anything that can be observed or felt through the senses or the mind within the physical world.</note>, in any one of its various modalities, while that of metaphysics is essentially constituted by that of which no experience is possible: being "beyond physics," we are also, and by that very fact, beyond experience. Consequently, the domain of each particular science can extend indefinitely, if it is capable of it, without ever reaching even the slightest point of contact with that of metaphysics.

The immediate consequence of what precedes is that, when speaking of the object of metaphysics, one must not have in view something more or less analogous to what the special object of such or such a science might be. It is also that this object must always be absolutely the same, that it cannot be in any degree something changing and subject to the influences of time and place; the <term>contingent</term> <note>In philosophy, "contingent" refers to things that happen to be true but could have been otherwise—the accidental or non-essential parts of reality.</note>, the accidental, the variable, belong properly to the domain of the individual; they are even characteristics that necessarily condition individual things as such, or, to speak even more rigorously, the individual aspect of things with its multiple modalities. Therefore, when it comes to metaphysics, what can change with time and place are only the <term>modes of exposition</term> <note>The author distinguishes between the unchanging "truth" of metaphysics and the "exposition"—the language, culture, and symbols used to explain it to different people at different times.</note>, that is to say, the more or less external forms in which metaphysics may be clothed, and which are susceptible to various adaptations; and it is also, obviously, the state of knowledge or ignorance of men, or at least of the generality of them...

<summary>The author defines the domain of metaphysics as absolutely universal and entirely distinct from the sciences, arguing that metaphysics deals with unchanging principles beyond the reach of sensory experience.</summary>

...them, with regard to true metaphysics; but the latter remains always, at its core, perfectly identical to itself, for its object is essentially one, or more exactly "without duality" <note>original: "sans dualité." This is a translation of the Sanskrit term *Advaita*, a key concept in Hindu philosophy meaning that ultimate reality is a single, undivided whole.</note>, as the Hindus say, and this object—always for the very reason that it is "beyond nature"—is also beyond change: this is what the Arabs express by saying that "the doctrine of Unity is unique" <note>original: "la doctrine de l’Unité est unique." This refers to the Islamic concept of *Tawhid*, asserting the absolute oneness of the Divine.</note>. Moving even further into the order of consequences, we can add that there are absolutely no possible discoveries in metaphysics; because, since it concerns a mode of knowledge that does not have recourse to the use of any special or external means of investigation, everything that is susceptible to being known could have been known equally by certain men in every era. This is indeed what emerges from a deep examination of traditional metaphysical doctrines. 

Moreover, even if one were to admit that the ideas of evolution and progress might have a certain relative value in biology and sociology—which is far from being proven—it would be no less certain that they have no possible application regarding metaphysics. Thus, these ideas are completely foreign to the peoples of the East, just as they were, for that matter, until towards the end of the 18th century, to Westerners themselves, who today believe them to be essential elements of the human spirit. This implies, let us note well, the formal condemnation of any attempt to apply the "historical method" to that which is of a metaphysical order. Indeed, the metaphysical point of view itself is radically opposed to the historical point of view (or what is so-called), and one must see in this opposition not only a question of method, but also and above all—which is much more serious—a true question of principle. Because the metaphysical point of view, in its essential immutability, is the very negation of the ideas of evolution and progress, one might say that metaphysics can only be studied metaphysically. 

There is no need to take into account here such contingencies as individual influences, which, strictly speaking, do not exist in this regard and cannot be exerted upon the doctrine. Since the doctrine is of a universal order, and is therefore essentially <term>supra-individual</term> <note>The author uses this term to describe truths that exist independently of human minds, personalities, or historical figures.</note>, it necessarily escapes their action. Even the circumstances of time and place can—we insist once more—influence only the external expression, and in no way the very essence of the doctrine. Finally, in metaphysics, it is not at all a matter of "beliefs" or "opinions" which are more or less variable and changing because they are more or less doubtful (as is the case in the realm of the relative and the contingent), but exclusively a matter of permanent and <term>immutable</term> <note>Unchanging over time; unable to be modified.</note> certitude.

Indeed, because metaphysics does not participate in any way in the relativity of the sciences, it must imply absolute certainty as an intrinsic character; this is true first by virtue of its object, but also by its method—if indeed this word can still be applied here—otherwise this method, or whatever other name one might wish to call it, would not be adequate to the object. Metaphysics therefore necessarily excludes any conception of a hypothetical character, from which it follows that metaphysical truths, in themselves, cannot be in any way contestable; consequently, if there can sometimes be room for discussion and controversy, it will never be except as the result of a defective exposition or an imperfect understanding of these truths. Furthermore, any possible exposition is necessarily defective here, because metaphysical conceptions, by their universal nature, are never totally expressible, nor even imaginable, since they can only be reached in their essence by pure and "informal" <term>informal (informelle): in this context, it refers to a state of being or knowledge that exists beyond "form," meaning it is not bound by mental images, shapes, or the constraints of the material world</term> intelligence; they immensely surpass all possible forms, and especially the formulas in which language would try to enclose them—formulas that are always inadequate and tend to restrict them, and thereby to distort them. These formulas, like all symbols, can only serve as a starting point, a "support" so to speak, to help conceive what remains inexpressible in itself; it is up to each individual to strive to conceive it effectively according to the measure of one's own intellectual capacity, thus compensating, precisely in that same measure, for the fatal imperfections of formal and limited expression. It is moreover evident that these imperfections will reach their maximum when the expression must be made in languages which, like European languages—especially modern ones—seem as poorly suited as possible to the exposition of metaphysical truths. As we were saying earlier, regarding the difficulties of translation and adaptation, metaphysics—because it opens onto unlimited possibilities—must always reserve a place for the inexpressible, which, in fact, is the very essence of it.

We can now realize what the distinction between metaphysical knowledge and scientific knowledge is in its deepest sense: the first belongs to the <term>pure intellect (intellect pur): a higher faculty of direct, non-logical spiritual intuition</term>, which has the **universal** as its domain; the second belongs to **reason**, which has the **general** as its domain, for, as Aristotle said, “there is no science but of the general.” <note>original: "il n’y a de science que du général." This is a fundamental principle of Aristotelian logic: science deals with categories and laws that apply to groups, not with unique, individual instances.</note> One must not, therefore, confuse the **universal** and the **general**, as happens all too often with Western logicians; they, for that matter, never truly rise above the general, even when they incorrectly give it the name of "universal." The point of view of the sciences, as we have said, is of the individual order; this is because the general is not opposed to the individual, but only to the particular, and it is, in reality, merely the individual extended. However, the individual can receive an extension, even an indefinite one, without thereby losing its nature and without escaping its restrictive and limiting conditions. This is why we say that science could extend indefinitely without ever joining metaphysics, from which it will always remain profoundly separated, because only metaphysics is the knowledge of the universal.

We believe we have now sufficiently characterized metaphysics, and we could hardly do more without entering into the exposition of the doctrine itself, which could find no place here; moreover, these details will be completed in the following chapters, particularly when we speak of the distinction between metaphysics and what is generally called by the name of "philosophy" in the modern West. All that we have just said is applicable, without any restriction, to any of the traditional doctrines of the East, despite great differences in form which may hide the identity of the underlying substance from a superficial observer: this conception of metaphysics is true at once of **Taoism**, of **Hindu doctrine**, and also of the profound and <term>extra-religious (extra-religieux): refers here to the "inner" or esoteric side of a tradition, such as Sufism, which deals with universal truths beyond specific religious rituals</term> aspect of Islam. <note>original: "Islamisme." However, what we indicated regarding **Aristotle** and the **Scholastic** doctrine <note>The "Scholastics" were medieval philosophers and theologians, such as Thomas Aquinas, who tried to reconcile Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> shows that, at the very least, there was truly metaphysics there to a certain extent, if not...

# CHAPTER VI
## RELATIONSHIPS BETWEEN METAPHYSICS AND THEOLOGY

The question we wish to consider now does not arise in the East, due to the absence of the strictly religious viewpoint—to which theological thought is naturally inherent <note>Guénon argues that Eastern traditions are "purely metaphysical" or "traditional" rather than "religious," as the Western concept of religion implies specific social and dogmatic structures not found in the same way in India or China.</note>; at least, it could hardly arise except regarding Islam, where it would more precisely be the question of the relationships that must exist between its two essential aspects: the religious and the extra-religious, which one could rightly call theological and metaphysical. In the West, on the contrary, it is the absence of the metaphysical viewpoint that means the same question generally does not arise; it has only been able to arise in practice for the <term>Scholastic doctrine: the system of philosophy and theology taught in medieval European universities, most notably by Thomas Aquinas</term>, which was indeed both theological and metaphysical, although, in this second aspect, its scope was restricted, as we have previously indicated; but it does not seem that a very clear solution was ever provided. There is all the more interest in treating this question in a completely general way, and what it essentially implies is, at heart, a comparison between two different modes of thought: pure metaphysical thought and specifically religious thought.

The metaphysical viewpoint, as we have said, is the only one that is truly universal, and therefore unlimited; every other viewpoint is, consequently, more or less specialized and bound, by its own nature, to certain limitations. We have already shown that this is indeed the case, notably for the scientific viewpoint, and we will also show that the same applies to various other viewpoints usually grouped under the common and rather vague label of "philosophical," and which, moreover, do not differ very deeply from the scientific viewpoint strictly speaking, even though they present themselves with greater and completely unjustified claims. Now, this essential limitation—which is obviously capable of being more or less narrow—exists even for the theological viewpoint; in other words, theology is also a special viewpoint, though naturally not in the same way as that of the sciences, nor within limits assigning it such a restricted scope;

In fact, these confusions did not fail to occur, and they were even able to go as far as a reversal of the relationships that should normally exist between metaphysics and theology; for even in the Middle Ages—which was nevertheless the only period when Western civilization received a truly <term>intellectual: here meaning the direct knowledge of universal principles, rather than just "academic" or "rational" study</term> development—it happened that metaphysics (which was, moreover, insufficiently detached from various considerations of a merely philosophical order) was conceived as being dependent upon theology. This remark provides a sufficient excuse for the mistake committed then, and it is certain that the Greeks—even to the extent that they engaged in true metaphysics—would have been able to err in exactly the same way, if indeed there had been among them something corresponding to what theology is in the Judeo-Christian religions. This essentially brings us back to what we have already said: that Westerners, even those who were truly metaphysicians to a certain degree, have never known <note>Guénon uses the term "total metaphysics" to describe a knowledge that is not restricted by the categories of Western logic or the boundaries of specific religious dogmas.</note> total metaphysics.

This would still be possible even in the current Western world, though undoubtedly with greater difficulty, due to the general tendencies of the <note>original: "mentalité"</note> mentality which create an environment as unfavorable as possible in this regard. In any case, it is appropriate to add that if there were such exceptions, no written testimony of them exists, and they have left no trace in what is commonly known. This, however, proves nothing in a negative sense, and it is not even surprising, given that if cases of this kind did effectively occur, it could only have been thanks to very particular circumstances, upon the nature of which it is not possible for us to insist here.

To return to the very question currently occupying our attention, we shall recall that we have already indicated what distinguishes, in the most essential way, a metaphysical doctrine from a religious dogma: it is that, while the metaphysical point of view is purely **intellectual**, the religious point of view implies, as a fundamental characteristic, the presence of a **sentimental** element which influences the doctrine itself, and which does not allow it to maintain the attitude of a purely disinterested speculation. This is indeed what occurs in theology, though in a more or less marked way depending on which of the different branches it is divided into. This sentimental character is nowhere more emphasized than in the specifically *mystical* form of religious thought; and let us say in this regard that, contrary to a far too widespread opinion, <term>mysticism: a religious practice seeking direct, emotional union with the divine</term>, by the very fact that it cannot be conceived outside of the religious point of view, is totally unknown in the East. The influence of this sentimental element obviously harms the intellectual purity of the doctrine, and it marks, all things considered, it must be said, a decline compared to metaphysical thought. This <term>decline: here used to mean a descent from universal principles into more limited, human emotions</term> was, moreover, somewhat inevitable and even necessary in a sense where it occurred mainly and generally—that is, in the Western world—if the doctrine was to be adapted to the mentality of the men to whom it was specifically addressed, and in whom sentimentality predominated over intelligence. This predominance has, furthermore, reached its highest point in modern times. We can now see how the theological point of view is merely a particularization of the metaphysical point of view—a particularization that implies a proportional alteration. It is, if you will, an application to <term>contingent conditions: specific circumstances that depend on time, place, or human nature rather than being universal</term>, an adaptation whose mode is determined by the nature of the requirements it must satisfy, since these special requirements are, after all, its only reason for being. 

It follows from this that every theological truth can, through a **transposition** that releases it from its specific form, be traced back to a corresponding metaphysical truth, of which it is merely a sort of translation. However, this does not mean there is an actual equivalence between the two orders of conceptions. We must remember what was said earlier: everything that can be viewed from an individual point of view can also be viewed from a universal point of view, without these two viewpoints being any less profoundly separated. If we then consider things in the opposite direction, it must be said that certain metaphysical truths—but not all—are capable of being translated into theological language. This is because we must account for everything that, being impossible to view from any individual point of view, belongs exclusively to the domain of metaphysics: the universal cannot be entirely enclosed within a special point of view, nor within any form whatsoever, which is ultimately the same thing. like any other formulation, is necessarily only incomplete and partial, and what it leaves out measures precisely all that separates the point of view of theology from that of pure metaphysics. This could be supported by numerous examples; but these examples themselves, to be understood, would presuppose doctrinal developments that we could not dream of undertaking here: such would be, to limit ourselves to citing one typical case among many others, a comparison established between the metaphysical conception of <term>liberation: the state of being free from the cycle of rebirth (Sanskrit: *moksha*)</term> in Hindu doctrine and the theological conception of "salvation" in Western religions. These are essentially different conceptions, which only the misunderstanding of a few <term>Orientalists: 19th and early 20th-century Western scholars who studied the languages and cultures of Asia</term> has attempted to equate, in a manner that is, moreover, purely verbal. Let us note in passing, since the occasion presents itself here, that cases like this must further serve to warn against another very real danger: if one asserts to a Hindu—to whom Western conceptions are otherwise foreign—that Europeans mean by "salvation" exactly what he himself means by ***moksha*** <note>original: "moksha", a Sanskrit term for spiritual liberation</note>, he will certainly have no reason to contest this assertion or to suspect its accuracy. It is exactly the same for the confusions produced by the no less erroneous assimilation of the metaphysical point of view with Western philosophical points of view: we recall the example of a Muslim who very willingly accepted, as a quite natural thing, the designation of "Islamic pantheism" attributed to the metaphysical doctrine of the <term>Supreme Identity: the metaphysical realization of the essential oneness of the individual self with the Absolute</term>, but who, as soon as it was explained to him what <term>pantheism: the belief that the universe and God are identical, which often implies that God is not distinct from the material world</term> truly is in the proper sense of the word—notably in the work of **Spinoza**—rejected such a label with genuine horror.

As for how we might understand what we have called the translation of metaphysical truths into theological language, we will take only one extremely simple and entirely elementary example: this immediate metaphysical truth: "Being is." If one wishes to express this in a religious or theological mode, it will give rise to this other proposition: "God exists." These two would only be strictly equivalent under the dual condition of conceiving of God as the <term>Universal Being: the source and totality of all that is, beyond a personal deity</term>—which is far from always actually being the case—and of identifying existence with pure being, which is metaphysically inaccurate. # CHAPTER VII
## SYMBOLISM AND ANTHROPOMORPHISM

The name “symbol,” in its most general sense, can be applied to any formal expression of a doctrine, whether that expression is verbal or figurative: the word can have no other function or reason for being than to symbolize the idea—that is, in short, to provide, as far as possible, a <term>sensible: perceptible by the senses; material or physical</term> representation of it, which is, moreover, purely <term>analogical: based on a similarity of proportion or relationship rather than a direct identity</term>. Thus understood, symbolism—which is merely the use of forms or images constituted as signs for ideas or <term>suprasensible: things that exist beyond the reach of human senses or physical observation</term> things, and of which language is simply a particular case—is evidently natural to the human mind, and therefore necessary and spontaneous. There is also, in a more restricted sense, an intentional and deliberate symbolism, which crystallizes the teachings of the doctrine into figurative representations; and furthermore, between the two, there are no precise limits, for it is quite certain that writing, at its origin, was everywhere <term>ideographic: a writing system where characters represent ideas or objects directly rather than representing sounds</term>, which is to say essentially symbolic, even in this second sense, although it is perhaps only in China that it has always remained so in an exclusive manner. 

In any case, symbolism, as it is most commonly understood, is used much more constantly in the expression of Eastern thought than in that of Western thought; and this is easily understood if one considers that it is a means of expression far less narrowly limited than ordinary language: suggesting even more than it expresses, it is the best-suited support for possibilities of conception that words would not allow one to reach. This symbolism—in which conceptual indefiniteness does not exclude a completely mathematical rigor, and which thus reconciles seemingly contrary requirements—is therefore, if one may say so, the metaphysical language *par excellence*; and furthermore, symbols that were originally metaphysical were able, through a process of secondary adaptation parallel to that of the doctrine itself, to subsequently become religious symbols. <term>Rites: ritual acts or ceremonies</term>, in particular, have an eminently symbolic character, regardless of the domain to which they belong, and a metaphysical transposition is always possible for the meaning of religious rites, as well as for the theological doctrine to which they are linked; even for...

Regarding simply social rites, if one wishes to seek their profound reason, one must ascend from the order of applications—where their immediate conditions reside—to the order of principles, which is to say, to the traditional source, which is metaphysical in its essence. We do not mean to say, moreover, that rites are nothing but pure symbols; they are that, undoubtedly, and they cannot fail to be so, under penalty of being totally void of meaning, but one must at the same time conceive of them as possessing in themselves an efficacy of their own, as <term>means of realization: methods or practices intended to lead a person toward a higher state of being or understanding</term> acting in view of the end to which they are adapted and subordinated. This is evidently, on the religious plane, the Catholic conception of the virtue of the "sacrament"; it is also, metaphysically, the principle of certain paths of realization of which we shall say a few words later, and it is this which has allowed us to speak of properly <term>metaphysical: relating to that which is beyond the physical or material world; the study of ultimate reality</term> rites. Furthermore, one could say that every symbol, insofar as it must essentially serve as a support for a conception, also has a very real efficacy; and the religious sacrament itself, insofar as it is a <term>sensible: something that can be perceived by the five senses</term> sign, has precisely this same role as a support for the "spiritual influence" which will make it the instrument of a psychic regeneration—whether immediate or deferred—in a manner analogous to how the intellectual potentialities included in a symbol can arouse an effective or merely virtual conception, depending on the receptive capacity of each individual. From this perspective, the rite is still a particular case of the symbol: it is, one might say, an "acted symbol," but on the condition of seeing in the symbol everything that it really is, and not only its external, <term>contingent: something that depends on circumstances; not absolute or necessary</term> shell. Here, as in the study of texts, one must know how to go beyond the "letter" to release the "spirit."

Now, this is precisely what Westerners do not usually do: the errors of interpretation by <term>orientalists: Western scholars who study the languages, cultures, and history of the Near and Far East</term> provide a characteristic example here, for they consist quite commonly in distorting the symbols studied in the same way that the Western mentality, in its generality, spontaneously distorts those it encounters within its reach. The predominance of the sensory and imaginative faculties is the determining cause of the error here: to take the symbol itself for what it represents, through an incapacity to rise to its purely intellectual significance—such is, fundamentally, the confusion in which lies the root of all "idolatry" in the proper sense of the word, the sense that <term>Islamism: here referring to the religion of Islam and its theological perspectives</term> gives it in a particularly clear way. When one no longer sees anything in the symbol but its outward form, its reason for being and its actual efficacy have likewise disappeared; the symbol is no longer anything but a

"idol," that is to say, a vain image, and its preservation is nothing but pure "superstition," so long as no one is found whose understanding is capable—partially or entirely—of effectively restoring to it what it has lost, or at least what it no longer contains except in the state of latent possibility. It is also among the Greeks that we find to its highest degree a tendency that appears inseparable from "idolatry" and the materialization of symbols: the tendency toward <term>anthropomorphism: the practice of attributing human characteristics, emotions, or physical forms to divine beings or principles</term>. They did not conceive of their gods as representing certain principles at all; rather, they truly imagined them as beings in human form, endowed with human feelings, and acting in the manner of men. For them, these gods no longer possessed anything that could be distinguished from the form in which poetry and art had clothed them; they were literally nothing outside of this very form. 

Such a complete anthropomorphization alone could provide the pretext for what has been called—after the name of its inventor—"<term>Euhemerism: the theory, named after the Greek mythographer Euhemerus, that mythological gods were originally historical human beings who became deified through the passage of time and legend</term>," that is to say, the theory according to which the gods were originally nothing but illustrious men. One could not, in truth, go further in the direction of a crude misunderstanding—one even cruder than that of certain modern scholars who wish to see in ancient symbols nothing but a representation or an attempted explanation of various natural phenomena. This type of interpretation, of which the all-too-famous theory of the "solar myth" is the best-known example <note>The "solar myth" theory was popular in 19th-century academia, suggesting most ancient myths were merely allegories for the movement of the sun.</note>. 

The "myth," like the "idol," has never been anything more than a misunderstood symbol: the one belongs to the verbal order as the other belongs to the figurative order. Among the Greeks, poetry produced the former just as art produced the latter; but among peoples to whom—as with the peoples of the East—<term>naturalism: here, the belief that religious symbols and myths refer only to the physical forces of nature</term> and anthropomorphism are equally foreign, neither one nor the other could take birth. Indeed, they could only arise in the imagination of Westerners who wished to make themselves the interpreters of that which they did not understand at all. The naturalist interpretation properly reverses the relationships: a natural phenomenon can, just as well as anything else in the <term>sensible: that which can be perceived by the five senses</term> order, be taken to symbolize an idea or a principle; however, the symbol only has meaning and a reason for being insofar as it is of a lower order than that which is symbolized. The word that designates it is indeed Latin in its form, but not in the meaning it received with Christianity; for *creare* <note>original: "creare" — Latin for "to bring forth" or "to make"</note> originally meant nothing other than "to make," a sense which has always remained, in Sanskrit, that of the verbal root *kri* <note>original: "kri" — a fundamental Sanskrit root meaning "to do," "to make," or "to perform"</note>, which is identical to this word. There has been a profound change of meaning here, and this case is, as we have said, similar to that of the term "religion." It is obviously from Judaism that the idea in question passed into Christianity and Islam; and, as for its essential reason for being, it is at heart the same as that for the prohibition of anthropomorphic symbols.

# CHAPTER VIII
## METAPHYSICAL THOUGHT AND PHILOSOPHICAL THOUGHT

We have said that metaphysics, which is profoundly separated from science, is no less so from everything that Westerners, and especially moderns, designate by the name of philosophy. Under this name, a variety of highly heterogeneous—and even entirely disparate—elements have been gathered together. It matters little here what the Greeks may have originally intended to encompass within the word "philosophy," which seems to have first included for them, in a somewhat indistinct way, all human knowledge within the limits of what they were capable of conceiving; our concern is only with what currently exists in fact under this designation. 

However, it is worth noting first that whenever true metaphysics appeared in the West, efforts were always made to join it with considerations belonging to special and <term>contingent: referring to things that are not absolute or necessary, but depend on specific circumstances</term> points of view, in order to incorporate it with them into a whole bearing the name of philosophy. This shows that the essential characteristics of metaphysics, with the deep distinctions they imply, were never identified with sufficient clarity in the West. 

We will go even further: the fact of treating metaphysics as a branch of philosophy—either by placing it on the same level as any other relative field of study, or even by qualifying it as "first philosophy" <note>original: "philosophie première"; this is the term Aristotle used for the study of being as being, which later became known as metaphysics.</note> as Aristotle did—essentially denotes a misunderstanding of its true scope and its character of universality. The absolute whole cannot be a part of anything, and the universal cannot be enclosed or contained within any system whatsoever. This fact alone is an evident mark of the incomplete character of Western metaphysics, which is, moreover, reduced solely to the doctrines of Aristotle and the <term>Scholastics: the medieval philosophers and theologians who taught in the early European universities, primarily following the teachings of Aristotle</term>. Aside from a few fragmentary considerations that may be found scattered here and there, or things that are not known with enough certainty, one encounters in the West—at least from classical antiquity onward—no other doctrine that is truly metaphysical, even with the restrictions required by the mixture of contingent, scientific, theological, or any other elements; we are not speaking of the...

He critiques the Western tendency to treat metaphysics as a mere branch of philosophy, asserting that its universal nature means it cannot be a subordinate part of any other system.</summary>

Alexandrians, on whom Eastern influences were directly exerted. <note>The Alexandrian school (c. 3rd century BCE – 7th century CE) in Egypt served as a major intellectual crossroads where Greek philosophy met the wisdom of Egypt, Persia, and India.</note>

If we consider modern philosophy as a whole, we can say, in a general way, that its point of view presents no truly essential difference from the scientific point of view: it is always a rational point of view, or at least one that claims to be so, and all knowledge that remains within the domain of reason—whether it is labeled philosophical or not—is properly a knowledge of a scientific order. If such knowledge aims to be something else, it loses all value, even relative value, by claiming a scope that it cannot legitimately possess; this is the case with what we shall call <term>pseudo-metaphysics: a system of thought that uses metaphysical language but remains limited to human reason and logic, failing to reach the universal or the infinite</term>. On the other hand, the distinction between the philosophical domain and the scientific domain is all the less justified because the former includes, among its multiple elements, certain sciences that are just as specialized and restricted as the others, without any character that could differentiate them so as to grant them a privileged rank. Such sciences, like <term>psychology: the study of the individual soul or mental processes</term> or <term>sociology: the study of human social structures</term>, for example, are only called philosophical due to a usage that is not based on any logical reason; philosophy, in short, has only a purely fictitious unity—historical, if you will—without anyone being able to say why the habit was not taken or kept to include any other sciences just as well. Furthermore, sciences that were regarded as philosophical at a certain period are no longer so today; it was enough for them to undergo greater development to exit this poorly defined grouping, without their intrinsic nature being changed in the least. In the fact that certain sciences still remain there, we should see only a vestige of the extension that the Greeks had originally given to philosophy, which indeed included all the sciences.

That said, it is evident that <term>true metaphysics: the knowledge of universal principles that transcend the physical and individual realm</term> can have no more relationship, nor relationships of a different nature, with psychology, for example, than it has with physics or physiology: these are, on exactly the same basis, sciences of nature—that is to say, <term>physical sciences: derived from the Greek word "physis," meaning nature, used here to denote any study of the manifested, changing world</term> in the original and general sense of that word. Metaphysics must necessarily be self-sufficient, being the only truly immediate knowledge, and it cannot be founded on anything else; this is because it is the knowledge of universal principles from which everything else derives, including the objects of the various sciences. These sciences, moreover, isolate their subjects from these principles to consider them according to their own specialized points of view. Such an approach is certainly legitimate on the part of these sciences, as they could not function otherwise or connect their objects to universal principles without exceeding the limits of their own proper domains. 

This last remark shows that one should not dream of founding the sciences directly upon metaphysics either: it is the very relativity of their defining points of view that ensures them a certain autonomy in this regard. Misunderstanding this can only provoke conflicts where none should normally occur. This error, which weighs heavily upon all modern philosophy, was initially that of <term>Descartes: René Descartes (1596–1650), the French philosopher often called the father of modern philosophy, who sought to establish a mathematical-rational basis for all knowledge</term>. Descartes, however, only produced a pseudo-metaphysics <note>original: "pseudo-métaphysique"</note>, and he was only interested in it as a preface to his physics, to which he believed he was providing more solid foundations.

If we now consider logic, the case is somewhat different from the sciences we have looked at so far, all of which can be called experimental, as they are based on the data of observation. Logic is still a specialized science, since it is essentially the study of the conditions proper to the human understanding; but it has a more direct link with metaphysics. In this sense, what we call logical principles are merely the application and specification, within a determined domain, of true principles, which are of a universal order. Regarding logic, one can therefore perform a transposition of the same kind as that which we indicated was possible regarding <term>theology: the study of religious belief and the nature of the divine</term>. 

The same remark can also be made regarding mathematics: although it has a restricted scope—since it is exclusively limited to the single domain of quantity—it applies relative principles to its special object. These may be regarded as a direct determination of certain universal principles. Thus, within the entire scientific domain, logic and mathematics are the fields that offer the most real connections to metaphysics. What we have just said about the relationship between metaphysics and logic might somewhat astonish those who are accustomed to considering logic as dominating, in a sense, all possible knowledge, because a speculation of any kind can only be valid on the condition of conforming rigorously to its laws. However, a distinction must be made here between metaphysics itself, as a **pure intellectual conception**, and its formulated exposition: while the former totally escapes individual limitations and thus escapes reason, the latter—to the extent that it is possible—can only consist of a sort of translation of metaphysical truths into a discursive and rational mode, because the very constitution of all human language does not allow it to be otherwise. Logic, like mathematics for that matter, is exclusively a science of reasoning; metaphysical exposition may take on an analogous character in its form, but in its form only. If it must then conform to the laws of logic, it is because these laws themselves have an essential metaphysical foundation, without which they would be worthless. ...unlimited conceptions as the domain of metaphysics itself.

As for **morality**, having spoken of it from the religious point of view, we have already partially addressed its status; however, we have reserved until now what relates to its properly philosophical conception, insofar as it is clearly distinct from its religious conception. There is nothing within the entire domain of philosophy that is more relative and more **contingent** <note>contingent: something that depends on specific circumstances or social conditions and is not a universal necessity</note> than morality; in truth, it is not even a form of knowledge of a more or less restricted order at all, but simply a collection of more or less coherent considerations whose purpose and scope can only be purely practical, even if people too often harbor illusions in this regard. 

Indeed, it is exclusively a matter of formulating rules applicable to human action, the justification for which lies entirely within the **social order**, for these rules would have no meaning outside the fact that human individuals live in society, forming more or less organized communities. Furthermore, they are formulated from a special point of view which, instead of being merely social as among the **Easterners** <note>original: "Orientaux"; referring here to the traditional civilizations of the East, such as those of India and China, which the author contrasts with the modern West</note>, is the specifically "moral" point of view—a perspective foreign to the greater part of humanity. 

We have seen how this point of view could be introduced into religious conceptions by linking the social order to a doctrine that has been influenced by sentimental elements; but, this case aside, it is difficult to see what else could serve as its justification. Outside of the religious point of view, which gives a sense of meaning to morality, everything relating to this order should logically be reduced to a set of pure and simple **conventions** <note>conventions: agreed-upon rules or social norms established for convenience and social stability rather than derived from absolute truth</note>, established and observed solely for the purpose of making life in society possible and bearable. However, if this conventional character were frankly recognized and accepted, "philosophical morality" would cease to exist. 

It is again **sentimentality** <term>sentimentality: the tendency to base values or actions on human emotion and feeling rather than on objective, intellectual principles</term> that intervenes here. In order to find material to satisfy its special needs, it strives to mistake these conventions—and make others mistake them—for what they are not. From this comes a deployment of various considerations, some remaining clearly sentimental in both form and substance, while others disguise themselves under more or less rational appearances. Furthermore, while morality—like all social contingencies—varies greatly according to time and country, the moral theories appearing in any given environment, however opposed they may seem, all tend toward the justification of the same practical rules: those which are commonly observed in that very environment. This should be enough to show that these theories are devoid of any real value, being built by each...

We have reviewed all the branches of philosophy that present a well-defined character; but there are, moreover, within philosophical thought, all sorts of rather poorly determined elements that cannot properly fit into any of these branches, and whose connection is not formed by any trait of their own nature, but only by the fact of their grouping within a single systematic conception. 

This is why, after having completely separated **metaphysics** <term>metaphysics: the study of universal principles and ultimate reality, which the author argues must be kept distinct from modern "philosophy"</term> from the various so-called philosophical sciences, it must also be distinguished, no less profoundly, from **philosophical systems**. Pure metaphysics is essentially exclusive of any **system**, because any system presents itself as a closed and bounded conception, as a more or less strictly defined and limited whole, which is in no way reconcilable with the universality of metaphysics; and besides, a philosophical system is always "someone’s" system—that is to say, a construction whose value could only be...

Monism can be defined as being essentially characterized by this: because it does not admit that there is an absolute irreducibility, and because it wishes to overcome the apparent opposition, it believes it can succeed by reducing one of its two terms to the other. If we are specifically considering the opposition of spirit and matter, we will thus have, on one hand, <term>spiritualist monism</term> <note>The philosophical view that everything is ultimately composed of spirit or mind, and that "matter" is just an appearance or a product of spirit.</note>, which claims to reduce matter to spirit, and, on the other hand, <term>materialist monism</term> <note>The view that everything is ultimately physical or material, and that "spirit" or "mind" is just a function of matter.</note>, which claims on the contrary to reduce spirit to matter. <term>Monism</term>, whatever it may be, is right to admit that there is no absolute opposition, for in this, it is less narrowly limited than <term>dualism</term>, and it constitutes at least an effort to penetrate deeper into the nature of things; but it happens almost inevitably to fall into another defect, and to completely neglect, if not deny, the opposition which—even if it is only an appearance—nevertheless deserves to be considered as such: it is therefore, here again, the exclusivity of the system that constitutes its primary flaw. On the other hand, by wanting to directly reduce one of the two terms to the other, one never completely escapes the alternative that was posed by <term>dualism</term>, since one considers nothing that lies outside these same two terms which it had made its fundamental principles; and there would even be reason to ask if, these two terms being correlative, one still has its reason for being without the other—if it is logical to preserve one as soon as one suppresses the other. Furthermore, we then find ourselves in the presence of two solutions which, at their core, are much more equivalent than they superficially appear: whether <term>spiritualist monism</term> affirms that everything is spirit, or <term>materialist monism</term> affirms that everything is matter, this ultimately has very little importance, all the more so since each finds itself obliged to attribute to the principle it preserves the most essential properties of the one it suppresses. Thus, the intervention of the metaphysical point of view has the effect of immediately resolving the apparent opposition, and it alone, moreover, allows one to truly do so, where the philosophical point of view showed its powerlessness. What is true for the distinction between spirit and matter is equally true for any other distinction among all those that one could similarly establish between more or less specific aspects of being, which exist in an indefinite multitude. If one can, moreover, simultaneously consider this entire infinity of possible distinctions—which are all equally true and legitimate from their respective points of view—it is because one is no longer locked within a systematization limited to one of these distinctions to the exclusion of all others. Thus, <term>non-dualism</term> is the only type of doctrine that corresponds to the universality of metaphysics. The various philosophical systems can generally, in one way or another, be linked either to dualism or to monism; but "non-dualism" alone, as we have just indicated its principle, is capable of immensely surpassing the scope of any philosophy, because it alone is properly and purely metaphysical in its essence—or, in other words, it constitutes an expression of the most essential and fundamental character of metaphysics itself.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of metaphysical principles, moving from the concept of non-duality to the challenges of expressing universal truths through limited language. absolute <term>indeterminacy</term> <note>The state of being undefined or unlimited. In this context, the author argues that the highest principles cannot be "defined" because definition is a form of limitation.</note> of the most universal principles—and therefore of those which must be considered before all others—is a cause of quite significant difficulties, not in their conception (except perhaps for those who are not at all accustomed to them), but at least in the exposition of metaphysical doctrines. This indeterminacy often forces one to use only expressions which, in their outward form, are purely negative.

It is in this way that, for example, the idea of <term>the Infinite</term> <note>original: "l’Infini." In metaphysics, the Infinite is not a mathematical quantity but the Absolute Totality which has no limits.</note>—which is in reality the most positive idea of all, since the Infinite can only be the absolute whole which, being limited by nothing, leaves nothing outside itself—this idea, we say, can only be expressed by a term of negative form. This is because, in language, every direct affirmation is necessarily the affirmation of *something*, which is to say a particular and determined affirmation. However, the negation of a determination or of a limitation is properly the "negation of a negation," and thus a real affirmation; so it follows that the negation of all determination is equivalent, at its core, to absolute and total affirmation. 

What we say regarding the idea of the Infinite could apply equally to many other extremely important metaphysical notions, but this example suffices for what we intend to make understood here. Furthermore, one must never lose sight of the fact that pure <term>metaphysics</term> is, in itself, absolutely independent of all the more or less imperfect terminologies with which we attempt to clothe it in order to make it more accessible to our understanding.

# CHAPTER IX
## ESOTERICISM AND EXOTERICISM

We have occasionally pointed out, during our preliminary considerations, the distinction—moreover generally well known—that existed in certain philosophical schools of ancient Greece, if not all of them, between what is called **esotericism** and **exotericism**, that is to say between two aspects of the same doctrine, one more interior and the other more exterior: this is the full literal meaning of these two terms. <term>Exotericism</term> <note>From the Greek *exôterikos*, meaning "outer." These were teachings designed for the general public or beginning students.</note>, comprising what was more elementary, more easily understood, and consequently capable of being made more widely available to everyone, is expressed alone in the written teaching, such as it has reached us more or less completely; <term>esotericism</term> <note>From the Greek *esôterikos*, meaning "inner." These were deeper truths reserved for those with the intellectual and spiritual preparation to grasp them.</note>, more profound and of a higher order, and addressed as such only to the regular disciples of the school, specially prepared to understand it, was the subject of a purely oral teaching, on the nature of which it has obviously not been possible to preserve very precise data. Moreover, it must be well understood that, since this was only a matter of the same doctrine under two different aspects, and as if at two levels of teaching, these aspects could in no way be opposed or contradictory, but were rather meant to be complementary: esotericism developed and completed, by giving it a deeper meaning which was only contained there <term>virtually</term> <note>In traditional philosophy, "virtually" means that a thing exists in potential or as a seed, waiting to be fully developed or explained.</note>, what exotericism set forth in too vague, too simplified, and sometimes more or less symbolic a form, even though the symbol too often had, among the Greeks, that purely literary and poetic air which makes it degenerate into simple <term>allegory</term> <note>An allegory is a story where characters or events represent ideas. The author suggests that the Greeks often reduced profound symbols to mere poetic metaphors, losing their deeper metaphysical power.</note>. It goes without saying, on the other hand, that esotericism could, within the school itself, be subdivided in turn into several more or less profound degrees of teaching, the disciples passing successively from one to another according to their state of preparation, and being able to go more or less far depending on the extent of their intellectual aptitudes; but that is about all that one can say for certain.

This distinction between esotericism and exotericism has in no way been maintained in modern philosophy, which is truly nothing more than...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Chapter IX, moving from the specific historical example of Greek schools to a broader structural analysis of inner (esoteric) and outer (exoteric) teachings in Western history, specifically mentioning the Middle Ages, Druidry, and Alchemy.</meta>

deeper than what it is outwardly, and which, for what it has to teach, certainly has no need of any esotericism whatsoever, since everything that is truly profound totally escapes its narrow point of view. Now, the question arises as to whether this conception of two complementary aspects of a doctrine was specific to Greece; in truth, it would be surprising if a division that seems natural enough in principle had remained so exceptional, and, in fact, this is not the case. 

First of all, one could find in the West, since antiquity, certain schools that were generally very closed—and more or less poorly known for this reason—which were, moreover, not philosophical schools at all. Their doctrines were expressed outwardly only under the veil of certain symbols that must have seemed very obscure to those who did not have the key; and this key was given only to members who had taken certain commitments, and whose discretion had been sufficiently tested, at the same time as their intellectual capacity had been assured. 

This case, which clearly implies that we are dealing with doctrines profound enough to be completely foreign to the common mentality, seems to have been especially frequent in the Middle Ages. This is one of the reasons why, when speaking of the intellectuality of that era, one must always make reservations about what may have existed outside of what is known to us with certainty; it is evident indeed that, there as with Greek esotericism, many things must have been lost because they were only ever taught orally. This is also, as we have indicated, the explanation for the almost total loss of the <term>Druidic doctrine</term> <note>The oral teachings of the ancient Celtic priestly class, which were never recorded in writing and thus vanished when the oral lineage was broken.</note>. 

Among these schools to which we have just alluded, we can mention as an example the **alchemists**, whose doctrine was primarily of a **cosmological** <note>In this context, cosmology refers to the study of the laws governing the manifest universe and the "becoming" of nature, rather than just modern astronomy.</note> order; but, moreover, cosmology must always have as its foundation a certain set of more or less extensive **metaphysical** conceptions. One could say that the symbols contained in alchemical writings constitute the exotericism here, while their reserved interpretation constituted the esotericism; but the share of exotericism is then very reduced, and even, since it basically has a true reason for being only in relation to and for the purpose of esotericism, one may wonder whether it is still appropriate to apply these two terms. 

Indeed, **esotericism** and **exotericism** are essentially correlative, since these words are comparative in form <note>The suffixes -erior and -oteric function like "inner" vs "in-most" or "outer" vs "out-most," implying a relationship of degree or position.</note>, so that where there is no exotericism, there is no longer any reason to speak of esotericism either; this latter name cannot therefore, if one wishes to keep its proper meaning, serve to designate indiscriminately every closed doctrine, to

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the distinction between esotericism and exotericism, shifting from historical schools to the inherent nature of thought and expression, particularly in metaphysics and traditional texts like Chinese script.</meta>

the exclusive use of an intellectual elite.

One could no doubt, but in a much broader sense, envision an esotericism and an exotericism within any doctrine whatsoever, insofar as one distinguishes between its conception and its expression. The former is entirely internal, while the latter is merely its externalization. One can thus, strictly speaking—though departing from the usual meaning—say that the conception represents the <term>esotericism</term> <note>from the Greek 'esoteros', meaning inner or hidden</note> and the expression the <term>exotericism</term> <note>from the Greek 'exoteros', meaning outer or public</note>. This is a necessary distinction resulting from the very nature of things. Understood in this way, there is particularly in every metaphysical doctrine something that will always be esoteric, and that is the "inexpressible" part which every truly metaphysical conception essentially contains, as we have explained. This is something that each person can only conceive for themselves, with the help of words and symbols that serve simply as a support for their conception; their understanding of the doctrine will be more or less complete and profound according to the measure to which they actually conceive it. Even in doctrines of another order, whose scope does not extend to what is truly and absolutely inexpressible—which is the <term>mystery</term> <note>original: "mystère". Guénon refers to the etymological root 'muein', meaning to keep silent or close the mouth/eyes, rather than something simply "mysterious" in the modern sense.</note> in the etymological sense of the word—it is nonetheless certain that expression is never completely adequate to conception. Consequently, to a much lesser degree, something similar still occurs: the one who truly understands is always the one who knows how to see further than the words, and one could say that the "spirit" of any doctrine is esoteric in nature, while its "letter" is exoteric. This would be especially applicable to all traditional texts, which, moreover, most often offer a plurality of meanings of varying depth, corresponding to as many different points of view. But, instead of seeking to penetrate these meanings, people commonly prefer to engage in futile research into exegesis and "textual criticism," following the methods laboriously established by the most modern scholarship; and this work, however tedious it may be and whatever patience it requires, is much easier than the other, for it is at least within the reach of all levels of intelligence.

A remarkable example of the plurality of meanings is provided to us by the interpretation of the ideographic characters that constitute Chinese writing: all the significations of which these characters are capable can be grouped around three main ones, which correspond to the three fundamental degrees of knowledge, and of which the first is of the sensible order, the second of the [order...]
