<meta>This page continues the discussion of how different levels of meaning—rational and metaphysical—can be found within a single symbol or expression, particularly within traditional Eastern systems of thought.</meta>

rational, and the third of a purely intellectual or metaphysical order; thus, to limit ourselves to a very simple case, the same character could be used analogically to designate at once the sun, light, and truth. The nature of the context alone allows one to recognize, for each application, which of these meanings should be adopted—hence the numerous errors made by Western translators. One must understand from this how the study of <term>ideograms</term> <note>symbols representing ideas or concepts rather than specific sounds or words, common in Chinese script</note>, whose significance completely escapes Europeans, can serve as the basis for a truly integral education by allowing for the development and coordination of all possible conceptions across all orders. This study could therefore, from different points of view, be revisited at every level of teaching, from the most elementary to the most advanced, each time giving rise to new possibilities of conception; it is a marvelously appropriate instrument for the exposition of a <term>traditional doctrine</term> <note>a system of knowledge rooted in ancient, often sacred, principles passed down through generations</note>.

Let us return now to the question of whether the distinction between <term>esotericism</term> <note>inner or hidden knowledge intended for a specialized group</note> and <term>exotericism</term> <note>outer or public knowledge accessible to the general population</note>, understood this time in its precise sense, can be applied to Eastern doctrines. First of all, in Islam, the tradition is double in essence—both religious and metaphysical—as we have already mentioned. Here, one can very accurately describe the religious side of the doctrine as exoteric, as it is indeed the most outward aspect and the one accessible to all, and its metaphysical side as esoteric, which constitutes its profound meaning and is, moreover, regarded as the doctrine of the elite. This distinction retains its proper meaning since these are the two faces of one and the same doctrine. 

It should be noted, on this occasion, that there is something analogous in Judaism, where esotericism is represented by what is called <term>Qabbalah</term> <note>original: "Qabbalah". From the Hebrew root meaning "to receive," referring to the mystical and esoteric tradition of Judaism.</note>, a word whose original meaning is none other than "tradition," and which applies to the study of the deeper meanings of sacred texts, whereas the exoteric or common doctrine adheres to their most outward and literal meaning. However, this *Qabbalah* is, generally speaking, less purely metaphysical than Islamic esotericism, and it still undergoes, to a certain extent, the influence of the specifically religious point of view; in this, it is comparable to the metaphysical part of <term>scholastic doctrine</term> <note>the philosophical and theological systems taught in medieval European universities</note>, which was insufficiently detached from theological considerations. In Islam, on the contrary, the distinction between the two points of view is almost always very sharp; through the relationship between exotericism and esotericism, this distinction allows us to see here even better than elsewhere how, through metaphysical transposition, theological conceptions receive a profound meaning.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into whether the Western categories of "inner" and "outer" knowledge can be applied to Eastern systems, moving from the previous discussion on Islamic and Chinese symbolic structures to specific Eastern doctrines.</meta>

If we move on to more Eastern doctrines, the distinction between **esotericism** <note>inner knowledge for the few</note> and **exotericism** <note>outer knowledge for the public</note> can no longer be applied in the same way, and indeed there are some to which it is no longer applicable at all. Undoubtedly, regarding China, one could say that the social tradition <note>referring to Confucianism, which focuses on social harmony and ethics</note>, which is common to all, appears as exoteric, while the metaphysical tradition <note>referring to Taoism, which focuses on universal principles beyond the human social sphere</note>, the doctrine of the elite, is esoteric as such. However, this would only be strictly accurate if one considered these two doctrines in relation to the **primordial tradition** <note>the theoretical original source of all spiritual and philosophical wisdom</note> from which they both originate; but, in truth, they are too clearly separated, despite this common source, for one to regard them as being merely two faces of the same doctrine, which is necessary for one to speak properly of esotericism and exotericism. One of the reasons for this separation lies in the absence of that sort of "mixed domain" created by the religious point of view, where the intellectual and social points of view unite—to the extent that they are capable of doing so—though often to the detriment of the former's purity. Yet, this absence does not always have such marked consequences in this regard, as shown by the example of India, where there is also nothing strictly religious, and where all branches of the tradition nevertheless form a unique and indivisible whole.

It is precisely of India that we must speak here, and it is there that it is least possible to envision a distinction like that of esotericism and exotericism, because the tradition there indeed has too much unity to present itself, not only as two separate bodies of doctrine, but even as two complementary aspects of this kind. All that can really be distinguished there is the essential doctrine, which is entirely **metaphysical**, and its various applications, which constitute so many secondary branches in relation to it; but it is quite evident that this is by no means equivalent to the distinction in question. The metaphysical doctrine itself offers no other esotericism than that which may be found in the very broad sense we have mentioned, and which is natural and inevitable in any doctrine of this order: all may be admitted to receive the teaching at all its levels, with the sole reservation of being intellectually qualified to derive an effective benefit from it; we speak here only, of course, of admission to all levels of teaching, but not to all functions, for which other qualifications may also be required; but, necessarily, among those who receive this same...

This is why it is completely improper to speak of "**esoteric Brahmanism**" <note>Brahmanism refers to the ancient social and religious system of India based on the Vedas</note>, as some have wished to do, particularly applying this name to the teaching contained in the ***Upanishads*** <note>the philosophical-speculative texts that form the final part of the Hindu Vedas</note>; it is true that others, speaking for their part of "**esoteric Buddhism**," have done even worse, for they have presented under this label only eminently fanciful conceptions, which relate neither to **authentic Buddhism** nor to any **true esotericism** <note>This is likely a critique of 19th-century movements like Theosophy, which used the term "Esoteric Buddhism" for their own doctrines</note>. In a manual on the history of religions to which we have already alluded—and where one finds, moreover, despite the spirit in which it is written, many of the confusions common in this type of work, especially the tendency to treat as religious those things which in reality are not so at all—we have noted in this regard the following observation: "An Indian thought rarely finds its exact equivalent outside of India; or, to speak less ambitiously, ways of looking at things that are elsewhere esoteric, individual, or extraordinary, are, in **Brahmanism** and in **India**, common, general, and normal" <insert>[7]</insert>. This is fundamentally correct, yet it calls for some reservations, because one cannot qualify as *individual*, any more elsewhere than in India, conceptions which, being of a metaphysical order, are on the contrary essentially **supra-individual** <note>meaning they relate to truths that exist beyond the limits of human personality or individual psychology</note>; on the other hand, these conceptions find their equivalent, though under different forms, wherever a truly metaphysical doctrine exists—that is to say, throughout the **East**—and it is only in the **West** that there is indeed nothing that corresponds to them, even remotely. What is true is that conceptions of this order are nowhere as generally widespread as in India, because one does not encounter elsewhere a people possessing as generally and to the same degree the required aptitudes, even though these are nevertheless frequent among all Easterners, and notably among the Chinese, among whom the metaphysical tradition has despite this kept a much more closed character. What must have contributed above all to the development of such a mentality in India is the purely traditional character of Hindu unity: one can only truly participate in this unity insofar as one assimilates the tradition, and, as this tradition is metaphysical in essence, one could say that if every **Hindu** is naturally a metaphysician, it is because he must be so, in a sense, by definition.

# CHAPTER X
## METAPHYSICAL REALIZATION

In pointing out the essential characteristics of metaphysics, we stated that it constitutes intuitive knowledge—that is, immediate knowledge—opposing it in this regard to the discursive and mediated knowledge of the rational order <note>Discursive knowledge refers to reasoning that moves step-by-step through logic, whereas intuitive knowledge is seen as a direct "grasping" of truth.</note>. Intellectual intuition is even more immediate than sensory intuition, for it lies beyond the distinction between subject and object that the latter allows to persist; it is simultaneously the means of knowledge and knowledge itself, and within it, the subject and the object are unified and identified. Moreover, no knowledge truly deserves the name except to the extent that it results in producing such an identification, which, everywhere else, remains incomplete and imperfect; in other words, there is no true knowledge except that which participates more or less in the nature of pure intellectual knowledge, which is knowledge *par excellence* <note>original: "par excellence," meaning "above all others" or "the supreme example."</note>. Any other knowledge, being more or less indirect, ultimately has only a primarily symbolic or representative value; there is no true and effective knowledge except that which allows us to penetrate the very nature of things, and, if such a penetration can already occur to a certain extent in the lower degrees of knowledge, it is only in metaphysical knowledge that it is fully and totally achievable.

The immediate consequence of this is that knowing and being are at their root one and the same thing; they are, if you will, two inseparable aspects of a single reality—aspects which could not even be truly distinguished where everything is "without duality" <note>This "non-duality" is a central concept in many Eastern traditions, particularly the Advaita Vedanta school of Hindu philosophy, suggesting that the perceived separation between the self and the universe is an illusion.</note>. This suffices to render completely vain all "theories of knowledge" with pseudo-metaphysical <term>pseudo-metaphysical: appearing to be concerned with the fundamental nature of reality but actually limited to human logic or psychology</term> pretensions that occupy such a large place in modern Western philosophy, and which even tend sometimes, as with **Kant** <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), a pivotal German philosopher who argued that we can never know "things-in-themselves," only how they appear to us.</note> for example, to absorb everything else, or at least to subordinate it to themselves; the only reason for the existence of this kind of theory lies in an attitude common to almost all modern philosophers—and moreover stemming from **Cartesian dualism** <note>The philosophy of René Descartes (1596–1650), which famously divided reality into two distinct substances: mind (thought) and matter (extension).</note>—an attitude which consists in artificially opposing *knowing* to *being*, which is the negation of all true metaphysics. <meta>This page continues the critique of Western philosophy's limitations, specifically addressing how modern "theory of knowledge" (epistemology) acts as a barrier to true metaphysical realization. philosophy thus arrives at the point of wanting to substitute the "theory of knowledge" <term>epistemology: the branch of philosophy that investigates the origin, nature, methods, and limits of human knowledge</term> for knowledge itself, and this is, on its part, a true admission of powerlessness; nothing is more characteristic in this regard than this declaration by Kant: "The greatest and perhaps the only utility of all philosophy of pure reason is, after all, exclusively negative, since it is not an instrument for extending knowledge, but a discipline for limiting it" [8] <note>Immanuel Kant, *Critique of Pure Reason*. Kant argued that human reason is limited to the world of experience and cannot know things as they are in themselves.</note>. Do such words not simply amount to saying that the sole claim of philosophers must be to impose the narrow limits of their own understanding upon everyone? This is, moreover, the inevitable result of the "system-building spirit," which is, we repeat, anti-metaphysical to the highest degree.

Metaphysics affirms the fundamental identity of knowing and being, which can only be doubted by those who are ignorant of its most elementary principles; and, as this identity is essentially inherent to the very nature of intellectual intuition, metaphysics does not merely affirm it, it realizes it. At the very least, this is true of "integral" <note>The author uses "integral" to mean a complete, non-fragmented approach to wisdom.</note> metaphysics; but it must be added that what has existed of metaphysics in the West seems to have always remained incomplete in this respect. However, Aristotle clearly established as a principle the identification through knowledge, expressly declaring that "the soul is all that it knows" [9] <note>Aristotle, *De Anima* (On the Soul), Book III. This suggests that in the act of knowing, the mind takes on the form of the object it perceives.</note>; but neither he nor his successors seem to have ever given this affirmation its true scope, by drawing from it all the consequences it entails, so that it remained for them something purely theoretical. This is better than nothing, certainly, but it is nonetheless quite insufficient, and this Western metaphysics appears to us as doubly incomplete: it is already so theoretically, in that it does not go beyond Being <note>In this context, "Being" refers to the first principle of manifestation; the author suggests that true metaphysics must reach "Non-Being" or the Infinite which precedes even Being itself.</note>, as we have explained previously, and, on the other hand, it only envisions things, to the extent that it envisions them at all, in a simply theoretical way; theory is presented there as being, in a sense, self-sufficient and as being its own end, whereas it should normally constitute only a preparation—however indispensable—in view of a corresponding realization.

A remark must be made here regarding the way in which we use this word "theory": etymologically, its primary meaning is that of "contemplation," and, if one took it in this sense, one could say that the whole of metaphysics, with the realization that it implies, is "theory" *above all others* <note>original: "par excellence"</note>; however,

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of knowledge, transitioning from the limitations of Western philosophical systems to the distinction between theoretical knowledge and "effective realization" as understood in Eastern traditions. It specifically addresses how the word "theory" has been narrowed in modern usage.</meta>

Usage has given this word <note>The word being discussed is "theory," derived from the Greek *theoria*, which originally meant contemplation or "seeing" the truth.</note> a somewhat different meaning, and especially a much more restricted one. First, the habit has been formed of opposing "theory" and "practice," and, in its original sense, this opposition—being that of contemplation and action—would still be justified here, since metaphysics is essentially beyond the realm of action, which is the realm of individual contingencies <note>contingencies: things that are not necessary or absolute, but depend on specific circumstances or individual conditions</note>. But the Western mind, being turned almost exclusively toward action and conceiving of no realization outside of it, has generally come to oppose theory and realization. Therefore, we accept this latter opposition in practice, so as not to deviate from received usage and to avoid the confusion that might arise from the difficulty of separating terms from the meanings we are accustomed to attributing to them, whether rightly or wrongly. However, we will not go so far as to call metaphysical realization "practical," for this word has remained inseparable, in common language, from the idea of action it originally expressed, which can in no way apply here.

In any doctrine that is metaphysically complete, such as the Eastern doctrines, theory is always accompanied or followed by an **effective realization**, for which it is only the necessary basis: no realization can be approached without a sufficient theoretical preparation, but the whole theory is ordered toward realization, as the means is toward the end, and this point of view is assumed, at least implicitly, even in the external expression of the doctrine. On the other hand, effective realization may have, in addition to and after theoretical preparation, other means of a very different order, but which are also intended only to provide a support or a starting point, and which have essentially only the role of "adjuvants" <term>adjuvants: auxiliary aids or helpful tools that assist a process but are not the primary cause</term>, regardless of their actual importance. This is, in particular, the reason for the existence of rites of a properly metaphysical character and scope, whose existence we have mentioned. However, unlike theoretical preparation, these rites are never regarded as indispensable means; they are only accessory and not essential, and the **Hindu tradition**, where they nonetheless hold an important place, is quite explicit in this regard; but they can nonetheless, through their own efficacy, greatly facilitate metaphysical realization—that is, the transformation of that virtual knowledge <note>virtual knowledge: knowledge that is understood intellectually but not yet "lived" or fully integrated into one's being</note> which is simple theory, into an effective knowledge.

These considerations may certainly seem very strange to Westerners,

This refers to the ultimate reality that transcends the limitations of human language and conceptual thought.</note>—the same is not true for that which concerns <term>realization</term> <note>original: "réalisation." This is the effective transition from theoretical knowledge to an actual state of being; it is the "making real" of metaphysical truths within oneself.</note>.

<summary>The author explains that discussing the practical "realization" of Indian metaphysics is difficult for Westerners to grasp and notes that while theory can be explained, the actual realization remains largely inexpressible.</summary>

# CHAPTER ONE
## PRECISE SIGNIFICANCE OF THE WORD "HINDU"

Everything stated thus far could serve as an introduction, in an absolutely general way, to the study of all <term>Oriental doctrines</term><note>The author uses "Oriental" to refer broadly to the civilizations of the East (India, China, etc.) which he believes have preserved a "traditional" way of life and thought lost to the modern West.</note>; what we shall say now will concern more particularly the Hindu doctrines. These are specially adapted to modes of thought that, while sharing the common characteristics of Oriental thought as a whole, also present certain distinctive traits. To these traits correspond differences in form, even where the essence is strictly identical to that of other traditions—which is always the case, for the reasons we have indicated, when dealing with <term>pure metaphysics</term><note>Guénon defines "pure metaphysics" as the universal and timeless knowledge of ultimate reality, which is the same in all true traditions despite outward differences in language or symbol.</note>. In this part of our presentation, it is important to clarify, above all else, the exact meaning of the word "Hindu," the more or less vague use of which leads to frequent misunderstandings in the West.

To clearly determine what is Hindu and what is not, we cannot avoid briefly recalling some of the considerations we have already developed: this word cannot designate a race, since it applies equally to elements belonging to various races, nor even less a nationality, since nothing of the sort exists in the East. If we consider India in its totality, it would be comparable to the whole of Europe rather than to this or that European state, and this is true not only because of its size or the numerical importance of its population, but also because of the ethnic varieties it presents; from the North to the South of India, the differences are at least as great, in this respect, as from one end of Europe to the other. Furthermore, there is no governmental or administrative link between the various regions, except for that which Europeans have recently established in a completely artificial manner; this administrative unity, it is true, had already been achieved before them by the <term>Mughal emperors</term><note>original: "empereurs mongols." While the text uses the term "Mongol," it refers to the Mughal Empire, the Persianate-Islamic power that ruled much of the Indian subcontinent between the 16th and 19th centuries.</note>, and perhaps even earlier by others, but it never had more than a fleeting existence in relation to the permanence of Hindu civilization, and it is noteworthy that it was almost always due to the domination of foreign elements,

<summary>This chapter opens by defining the term "Hindu," arguing that it does not represent a race or a nationality, but rather a shared civilization and metaphysical tradition that unifies a diverse subcontinent.</summary>
<keywords>Hinduism, India, definition of Hindu, Oriental doctrines, Mughal Empire, pure metaphysics, traditionalism</keywords>

...or in any case non-Hindus; moreover, it never went so far as to completely suppress the autonomy of individual States, but rather strove to bring them into a federative organization. The conclusion of all this can be formulated as follows: all those who adhere to the same tradition are Hindus, provided, of course, that they are duly qualified to adhere to it really and effectively, and not in a merely external and illusory way; conversely, those who, for whatever reason, do not participate in this same tradition are not Hindus. This is notably the case for the <term>Jains</term><note>Followers of Jainism, an ancient Indian tradition that shares many cultural traits with Hinduism but is considered "non-Hindu" here because it does not recognize the authority of the Vedas.</note> and the <term>Buddhists</term>; in modern times, it is also the case for the <term>Sikhs</term>, who were moreover subject to Muslim influences whose mark is very visible in their specific doctrine. Such is the true distinction, and there could be no other, even though this one is quite difficult to grasp, it must be admitted, for the Western mentality, which is accustomed to basing its judgments on entirely different elements that are completely lacking here. Under these conditions, it is a total nonsense to speak, for example, of "<term>Hindu Buddhism</term>," as is nevertheless done too often in Europe and especially in France; when one wishes to designate Buddhism as it formerly existed in India, there is no other suitable name than that of "Indian Buddhism," just as one can perfectly well speak of "Indian Muslims"—that is to say, the Muslims of India—who are in no way "Hindu." We can see the real gravity of an error such as the one we...

The **tradition** in question was brought into the country that is modern-day India, at a more or less remote period—which would be very difficult to specify—by men coming from the North, according to certain indications we have already reported; moreover, it is not proven that these migrants, who must have stopped successively in various regions, constituted a people properly speaking, at least initially, nor that they originally belonged to a single race. # CHAPTER II
## THE PERPETUITY OF THE VEDA

The name *Veda*, for which we have just indicated the literal meaning <note>original: "sens propre"; as established in the previous chapter, the word comes from the Sanskrit root *vid*, meaning "to know," referring to sacred or traditional knowledge.</note>, is applied generally to all the fundamental writings of the Hindu tradition; moreover, it is known that these writings are divided into four collections bearing the respective names of *Rig-Veda* <note>The "Veda of Adoration," containing hymns to the gods.</note>, *Yajur-Veda* <note>The "Veda of Ritual," containing sacrificial formulas.</note>, *Sama-Veda* <note>The "Veda of Chants," containing melodies and songs.</note>, and *Atharva-Veda* <note>The "Veda of the Atharvans," containing incantations and everyday rituals.</note>. The question of the date at which these collections were composed is one of those that most preoccupies the <term>Orientalists</term> <note>Western scholars of the 19th and early 20th centuries who studied Eastern languages and cultures, often applying European historical frameworks to them.</note>, and they have never managed to agree on its solution, even when limiting themselves to a very approximate estimation of their antiquity. There, as everywhere else, one observes above all—as we have already indicated—the tendency to attribute everything to as recent an era as possible, and also to contest the authenticity of this or that part of the traditional writings, basing all of it on minute analyses of texts, accompanied by dissertations as endless as they are superfluous on the use of a word or a grammatical form.

These are indeed the most habitual occupations of Orientalists, and their ordinary purpose is, in the intention of those who engage in them, to show that the text studied is not as ancient as was thought, that it cannot be by the author to whom it had always been attributed (if there even is one), or at the very least, that it has been <insert>interpolated</insert> <note>Interpolated: In textual studies, this refers to the insertion of new, often unauthorized material into an original text.</note> or has undergone some alteration at a relatively recent date; those who are even slightly familiar with the works of <term>biblical criticism</term> <note>A method of analyzing the Bible as a historical and literary document rather than a divinely inspired text; the author views this as a destructive or reductive approach when applied to sacred traditions.</note> can form a sufficient idea of how these procedures are implemented. It is not surprising that research undertaken in such a spirit results only in piling up volumes of idle discussions, nor that the pitiful results of this "dissolving" criticism, when they become known to the <term>Easterners</term> <note>original: "Orientaux"; the people belonging to the traditional cultures of the East.</note>, contribute greatly to inspiring in them a contempt for the <term>West</term> <note>original: "Occident"; referring to modern European and North American civilization.</note>. In short, what totally escapes the Orientalists are always the questions of principle; and, as these are precisely the ones without which nothing can be understood—since everything else derives from them and should logically be deduced from them—they neglect everything essential because they are incapable of seeing it, and lose themselves irremediably in the most insignificant details or the most arbitrary fantasies.

<summary>This chapter introduces the four Vedas and critiques Western Orientalists for their obsession with dating and deconstructing these texts through "biblical criticism" methods, which ignore the underlying spiritual principles.</summary>
<keywords>Veda, Rig-Veda, Yajur-Veda, Sama-Veda, Atharva-Veda, Orientalism, Biblical Criticism, Hindu Tradition, Western Academia</keywords>

--- Page 118 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the antiquity of the Veda, transitioning from a critique of Western philological methods to an explanation of traditional transmission and the concept of non-human origin.</meta>

The question of the date at which the various parts of the *<term>Veda</term>* <note>Sanskrit: "Knowledge"; the primary sacred scriptures of Hinduism.</note> may have been written seems truly insoluble, and it is, moreover, of no real importance, because, before the more or less distant era when the text was written for the first time, one must consider—as we have already had occasion to remark previously—a period of oral transmission of an indeterminate length. It is probable that the origin of writing in India is significantly older than is commonly claimed, and that Sanskrit characters, furthermore, are not at all derived from a Phoenician alphabet, which they resemble neither in their form nor in their arrangement. Be that as it may, what is certain is that we should see nothing more than an ordering and a definitive fixation of pre-existing traditional texts in the work attributed to Vyâsa—a name that truly designates neither a historical figure nor, even less, a "myth," but rather, as we noted above, an intellectual collectivity. Under these conditions, determining the era of Vyâsa, even assuming it were possible, has only the interest of a simple historical fact, without any doctrinal significance; and it is evident, on the other hand, that this era may comprise a period of a certain number of centuries; it might even never be completed, so that the question of its starting point would be the only one to truly arise, which does not mean that it is possible to resolve it, especially by the specialized methods of Western erudition.

The antecedent oral transmission is often indicated in a text, but without any chronological data, by what is called the *<term>vansha</term>* <note>Sanskrit: "lineage" or "genealogy," referring to the chain of succession through which a teaching is passed from master to disciple.</note> or traditional filiation; this is notably what occurs for most of the *<term>Upanishads</term>* <note>The final parts of the Veda, dealing with metaphysical and philosophical knowledge.</note>. Only, at the origin, one must always have recourse to a direct inspiration, which is also indicated in the *<term>vansha</term>*, for this is not a matter of an individual work; it matters little whether the tradition was expressed or formulated by this or that individual; he is not the author for that reason, since this tradition is essentially of a supra-individual order. This is why the origin of the *<term>Veda</term>* is said to be *<term>apaurushêya</term>* <note>Sanskrit: "not of human origin."</note>, that is to say, "non-human": historical circumstances, no more than other contingencies, exert no influence on the substance of the doctrine, which has an immutable and purely timeless character, and it is furthermore evident that the inspiration of which we have just spoken can occur at any era. The only difficulty here is perhaps to make a theory of inspiration acceptable to Westerners, and

The *Veda*, being the traditional knowledge supreme, is the principle and common foundation of all the more or less secondary and derivative branches of the doctrine; and, for these as well, the question of chronological development is of very little importance. It is necessary to view the tradition in its entirety, and there is no need to ask what, in this tradition, is primitive or is not, since it is a perfectly coherent whole—which does not mean systematic—where all the points of view it comprises can be considered simultaneously as well as successively, and that, consequently, it is of little interest to know the historical order in which they were actually developed. It is even all the less interesting because it would only ever really be about the development of these points of view as they were formulated in writing in the works we may know; for, when one knows how to see beyond the texts and penetrates further into the heart of things, one is forced to recognize that they have always been conceived simultaneously in their very principle; this is why a traditional text may be susceptible to a plurality of interpretations or applications, in correspondence with these different points of view. One cannot assign a specific author to this or that part of the doctrine, any more than one can for the Vedic texts themselves, in which the entire doctrine is contained synthetically, at least as far as it is expressible; and, if a certain known author or commentator has set forth a more or less particular point, that obviously does not mean that no one else had done so before him, and even less that no one had thought of it until then, even if no one had yet formulated it in a definitive text. The exposition can undoubtedly be modified in its external form to adapt to circumstances; but, we can never emphasize it enough, the substance always remains rigorously the same, and these modifications

### CHAPTER III
## ORTHODOXY AND HETERODOXY

Orthodoxy and heterodoxy can be considered not only from a religious point of view—though this is the most common case in the West—but also from the much more general perspective of **tradition** <term>tradition: here used not as mere custom, but as the transmission of universal, unchanging principles</term> in all its modes. Regarding **India**, it is only in this latter way that they can be understood, since there is nothing there that is strictly religious <note>The author often highlights that Indian systems of thought are metaphysical or social in nature, lacking the specific structures of dogma and "faith" found in Western religions</note>, whereas, for the **West**, there is, on the contrary, nothing truly traditional outside of religion. Regarding **metaphysics** and everything that proceeds from it more or less directly, the **heterodoxy** of a conception is essentially nothing other than its **falsehood**, resulting from its disagreement with fundamental principles; and this falsehood is even, most often, a manifest absurdity, provided one is willing to reduce the question to the simplicity of its essential data: it could not be otherwise, since metaphysics, as we have said, excludes everything that presents a hypothetical character, admitting only that which implies true certainty immediately through its comprehension. Under these conditions, **orthodoxy** becomes one with true knowledge, since it resides in a constant agreement with the principles; and, as these principles, for the **Hindu tradition**, are essentially contained in the *Veda* <note>meaning "Knowledge"; the oldest and most authoritative body of sacred texts in the Hindu tradition</note>, it is obviously the agreement with the *Veda* that is the criterion of orthodoxy here.

However, what must be clearly understood is that this is much less a matter of resorting to the authority of written texts than of observing the perfect coherence of the **traditional teaching** in its entirety; agreement or disagreement with the Vedic texts is, in short, only an external sign of the intrinsic truth or falsehood of a conception, and it is the latter which truly constitutes its orthodoxy or heterodoxy. If this is the case, one might perhaps object: why then not simply speak of truth or falsehood? It is because the unity of the traditional doctrine, with all the power inherent to it, provides the surest guide to prevent individual ramblings <note>original: *divagations*, implying intellectual wandering or lack of discipline</note> from taking free rein; the power that tradition holds in itself is sufficient for this, without any need for the constraint exercised by an authority more or less analogous to an authority...

<summary>The author defines orthodoxy in the Indian context as alignment with the fundamental metaphysical principles of the Veda, rather than as a religious dogma. He argues that in metaphysics, orthodoxy is synonymous with truth, while heterodoxy is essentially falsehood or a deviation from the coherence of traditional teaching.</summary>

Where this power of tradition is absent, and where there isn't even an external authority able to substitute for it to a certain extent, one sees only too clearly, through the example of modern Western philosophy, what confusion results from the unrestrained development and expansion of the most hazardous and contradictory opinions; if false conceptions are born so easily and even manage to impose themselves on the common mentality, it is because it is no longer possible to refer to an agreement with principles, for there are no more principles in the true sense of the word. Conversely, in an essentially traditional civilization, principles are never lost from sight, and they only need to be applied, directly or indirectly, in one order or another; conceptions that deviate from them will therefore occur much more rarely; they will even be exceptional, and if they do occur occasionally, their influence will never be very great: these deviations will always remain anomalies just as they were at their origin, and if their gravity is such that they become incompatible with the most essential principles of the tradition, they will find themselves rejected by that very fact outside the civilization where they were born.

To give an example that will clarify what we have just said, we will take the case of **atomism**, to which we will have to return later: this conception is clearly **heterodox** <term>heterodox: originating from the Greek 'heteros' (other) and 'doxa' (opinion); in this context, it refers to ideas that deviate from the foundational principles of the tradition</term>, for it is in formal disagreement with the *Veda* <note>original: *Vêda*; the primary sacred scriptures of Hinduism</note>, and moreover its falsity is easily demonstrable, for it implies within itself contradictory elements; heterodoxy and absurdity are therefore truly synonymous at their root. In India, atomism first appeared in the cosmological school of Kanada <note>original: *Kanâda*; the sage traditionally credited with founding the Vaisheshika school, which explores the nature of the physical universe</note>; it should be noted, moreover, that heterodox conceptions could hardly form in schools devoted to purely **metaphysical** speculation, because, on the ground of principles, absurdity stands out much more immediately than in secondary applications. This atomistic theory was never more than a simple anomaly of little importance among the Hindus, at least as long as nothing more serious was added to it; it therefore had only a very limited expansion, especially if compared to that which it would later acquire among the Greeks, where it was commonly accepted by various schools of "physical philosophy" because traditional principles were already lacking, and where **Epicureanism** <term>Epicureanism: a Greek school of philosophy that sought to achieve peace of mind and advocated for a world-view based on atoms moving in a void</term> especially gave it a considerable reach, the influence of which still affects modern Westerners. In India, **atomism** appeared at first only as a specific cosmological theory <term>cosmological theory: a system of ideas concerning the origin and structure of the physical universe</term>, whose scope, as such, was rather limited; but, for those who accepted this theory, **heterodoxy** on this particular point logically led to **heterodoxy** on many other points, for everything is closely linked within the traditional doctrine. Thus, the conception of atoms as the building blocks of things has as its corollary that of the vacuum in which these atoms must move; from this, sooner or later, was bound to emerge a theory of the "universal void," understood not in a metaphysical sense relating to the "non-manifested" <note>the "non-manifested" refers to the infinite source of all things that exists beyond the physical, perceivable world</note>, but on the contrary in a physical or cosmological sense. This is indeed what occurred with certain Buddhist schools which, identifying this void with *âkâsha* <gloss>ether</gloss>, were naturally led by this to deny the existence of the latter as a bodily element, and to admit only four elements instead of five.

It must also be noted, in this connection, that most Greek philosophers also admitted only four elements, like the Buddhist schools in question, and that, if some nevertheless spoke of ether, they only ever did so in a rather restricted way, giving it a much more specific meaning than the Hindus, and moreover a much less clear one. We have already said enough regarding which side the borrowing must come from when such concordances are observed, and especially when these borrowings are made in an incomplete way, which is perhaps their most visible mark; and let no one object that the Hindus would have "invented" ether after the fact, for more or less plausible reasons, similar to those that cause it to be generally accepted by modern physicists; their reasons are of an entirely different order and are not drawn from experience; there is no "evolution" of traditional conceptions, as we have already explained, and besides, the testimony of the Vedic <note>original: *vêdiques*; referring to the Vedas, the ancient foundational scriptures of India</note> texts is formal regarding both ether and the four other bodily elements.

It seems, therefore, that the Greeks, when they were in contact with Hindu thought, in many cases collected that thought only in a distorted and mutilated form, and even then, they did not always explain it faithfully as they had received it; furthermore, it is possible, as we have indicated, that they found themselves, in the course of their history, in more direct and continuous contact with the Buddhists, or at least with certain Buddhists, than with the Hindus. ## CHAPTER IV

### REGARDING BUDDHISM

**Buddhism**, as we have just said, seems closer, or rather less distant from Western conceptions than other Eastern doctrines, and, consequently, easier for Westerners to study; this is undoubtedly what explains the marked predilection that **Orientalists** <term>Orientalists: Western scholars who study the languages, cultures, and history of Asia, often criticized here for applying Western categories to Eastern thought.</term> show for it. These scholars, in fact, believe they find there something that fits within the framework of their mentality, or which at least does not completely escape it; in any case, they do not find themselves, as in the other doctrines, hindered by a total impossibility of understanding which, without admitting it to themselves, they must nevertheless feel more or less confusedly. Such at least is the impression they feel in the presence of certain forms of **Buddhism**, for, as we shall say shortly, there are many distinctions to be made in this regard; and, quite naturally, they wish to see in those forms which are most accessible to them the true and in a sense "primitive" **Buddhism**, while the others would be, according to them, only more or less late alterations. 

But **Buddhism**, whatever it may be, and even in the most "simplistic" aspects it may have taken on in some of its branches, is still nonetheless Eastern despite everything; thus, **Orientalists** push the assimilation with Western points of view much too far, for example when they want to make it the equivalent of a **religion** in the European sense of the word. This, moreover, sometimes throws them into a singular embarrassment: have not some, not shrinking from a contradiction in terms, declared that it was an "atheistic religion"? <note>The author highlights the internal contradiction in Western scholarship which tries to label Buddhism using Western theological terms that do not apply.</note> In reality, moreover, **Buddhism** is no more "atheistic" than it is "theistic" <term>theistic: relating to the belief in the existence of a creator God who intervenes in the universe.</term> or "pantheistic"; what must simply be said is that it does not place itself at the point of view from which these various terms have meaning; but, if it does not place itself there, it is precisely because it is not a **religion** at all. 

Thus, even that which might seem the least foreign to their own mentality, the **Orientalists** still find ways to distort through their interpretations, and even in several ways; for, when they want to see it as a **philosophy**, they distort it hardly less than when they want to make it a **religion**: if, for example, one

The truth is that **Buddhism** is neither a **religion** nor a **philosophy**, although, especially in those forms preferred by **Orientalists**, it is closer to both in some respects than are the traditional Hindu doctrines. Indeed, these are schools which, having moved outside the regular tradition <note>The author refers here to the Vedic tradition of India, from which Buddhism diverged.</note>, and having thereby lost sight of true **metaphysics**, were inevitably led to substitute for it something that resembles the philosophical point of view to a certain extent, but to a certain extent only. One even finds there at times speculations which, if viewed only superficially, might suggest **psychology**; but, obviously, this is not properly **psychology** at all—a purely Western thing and, even in the West, very recent, since it only really dates back to **Locke** <note>John Locke (1632–1704), an English philosopher often credited with founding modern empiricism and the study of the mind as a "blank slate."</note>; one should not attribute to the **Buddhists** a mentality that proceeds specifically from modern **Anglo-Saxon empiricism** <term>Empiricism: The philosophical theory that all knowledge is derived from sensory experience rather than innate ideas or tradition.</term>. The comparison, to be legitimate, must not go as far as an assimilation and, similarly, regarding religion, **Buddhism** is only effectively comparable to it on one point—certainly important, but insufficient to conclude an identity of thought: this is the introduction of a sentimental element, which moreover can be explained in all cases by an adaptation to the particular conditions of the period in which the doctrines affected by it were born, and which, consequently, is far from necessarily implying that these are all of the same kind. 

The real difference in points of view can be much more essential than a resemblance which, in short, relates mainly to the form of expression of the doctrines; this is what is ignored especially by those who speak of "**Buddhist morality**": what they take for morality—all the more easily as its sentimental side can indeed lead to this confusion—is in reality viewed from an entirely different aspect and has a very different reason for being, which is not even of an equivalent order. One example will suffice to allow one to realize this: the well-known formula: "May all beings be happy," concerns the universality of beings, without any restriction, and not only beings...

Furthermore, it is quite their habit, when they find themselves in the presence of something whose character or origin they cannot exactly determine, to get out of the difficulty by applying a "Buddhist" label to it; this is a rather convenient way of concealing their more or less conscious embarrassment, and they resort to it all the more readily because, by virtue of the factual monopoly they have managed to establish for their own benefit, they are almost certain that no one will come to contradict them. What can such people—who posit as a principle that the only true competence in this field of study is that acquired in their own schools—possibly fear in this regard? It goes without saying, moreover, that everything they thus declare to be "Buddhist" at their whim, as well as that which actually is, is in any case for them only "altered Buddhism." In a manual of the history of religions that we have already mentioned, and where the chapter relating to China generally shows a very regrettable lack of understanding, it is stated that "of primitive **Buddhism**, no trace remains in China," and that the doctrines currently existing there "are Buddhist in name only" <note>[12]</note>. If one understands by "primitive **Buddhism**" what the orientalists present as such, this is quite correct; but one must first know whether we should accept the conception they have formed of it, or if it is not rather their conception which, on the contrary, effectively represents only a degenerate **Buddhism**.

## CHAPTER V
### THE LAW OF MANU

Among the concepts likely to cause great embarrassment to Westerners—because they have no equivalent in the West—we can cite the one expressed in Sanskrit by the word *dharma* <term>Dharma<note>From the Sanskrit root *dhṛ* (to support or bear); it refers to the essential nature of a being, the universal law, or the social and religious duty that sustains the cosmic order.</note></term>. Certainly, there is no shortage of translations proposed by Orientalists <note>Western scholars of Eastern languages and cultures.</note>, but most of them are crudely approximate or even completely erroneous, always due to the confusion of viewpoints that we have previously highlighted. Thus, some attempt to translate *dharma* as "religion," even though the religious point of view does not apply here; yet, at the same time, these scholars must admit that this word does not properly designate the conception of the doctrine itself (which is wrongly assumed to be religious). On the other hand, if we consider the performance of rites—which likewise do not possess a religious character—these are designated as a whole by another word, *karma* <term>Karma<note>Literally "action." In a technical sense within Hindu tradition, it refers to ritual action or the law of cause and effect resulting from actions.</note></term>, which is used in a special, somewhat technical sense, whereas its general meaning is simply "action."

For those who insist on seeing a religion within the Hindu tradition, there would then remain what they believe to be "morality," and it is this which they more specifically call *dharma*. From this, depending on the case, arise various and more or less secondary interpretations such as "virtue," "justice," "merit," or "duty"—all of which are indeed exclusively moral notions, but which, for that very reason, do not in any way convey the concept in question. The moral point of view, without which these notions are devoid of meaning, does not exist in India; we have already insisted upon this sufficiently, and we have even indicated that Buddhism—which alone might seem fit to introduce it—did not go that far down the path of sentimentalism. 

Moreover, let us note in passing that these same notions are not all equally essential to the moral point of view itself. By this, we mean that some are not common to every moral conception: for instance, the idea of "duty" or "obligation" is absent from most ancient moral systems, notably that of the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that emphasized virtue as the only good and living in accordance with reason.</note>; it is only among the moderns, and especially since Kant <note>Immanuel Kant (1724–1804), the German philosopher who made the "categorical imperative" or absolute duty the center of his ethics.</note>, that it has come to play a preponderant role. What is important to note in this regard—because it is one of the most frequent sources of error—is that ideas or viewpoints...

This being said to dismiss the false interpretations, which are the most common, we will try to indicate as clearly as possible what must really be understood by <term>dharma <note>original: "dharma"; from the Sanskrit root meaning "to support" or "to sustain."</note></term>. As shown by the meaning of the verbal root <term>*dhri* <note>original: "*dhri*"; the Sanskrit root *dhṛ*, signifying the act of upholding or supporting the cosmic order.</note></term> from which it is derived, this word, in its most general sense, designates nothing other than a "way of being"; it is, if you will, the essential nature of a being, comprising the entire set of its characteristic qualities or properties, and determining, through the tendencies or dispositions it implies, the manner in which this being behaves, whether as a whole or in relation to each particular circumstance. The same notion can be applied not only to a single being but to an organized collectivity, to a species, to the whole assembly of beings in a cosmic cycle or a state of existence, or even to the total order of the Universe; it is then, to one degree or another, the conformity to the essential nature of beings, realized in the hierarchically ordered constitution of their whole; it is also, consequently, the fundamental balance, the integral harmony resulting from this hierarchization, to which the very notion of "justice" is reduced when stripped of its specifically moral character. Viewed thus as a principle of order—and therefore as an internal organization and disposition for a being or a set of beings—<term>*dharma*</term> can, in a sense, be contrasted with <term>*karma* <note>original: "*karma*"; referring here to external action or manifestation.</note></term>, which is but the action through which this disposition will be manifested externally, provided that the action is normal, that is to say, in conformity with the nature of beings and their states and the relationships derived therefrom. Under these conditions, what is <term>*adharma* <note>original: "*adharma*"; the prefix "a-" denotes negation, thus "non-dharma" or disorder.</note></term> is not "sin" in the theological sense, nor "evil" in the moral sense—notions which are both equally foreign to the <term>Hindu <note>original: "hindou"; here referring to the traditional orthodox Indian perspective.</note></term> mind; it is simply "non-conformity" with the nature of beings, imbalance, the rupture of harmony, the destruction or reversal of hierarchical relationships. No doubt, in the universal order, the sum of all particular imbalances always contributes to the total equilibrium, which nothing could break; but at each point taken separately and in itself, imbalance is possible and conceivable, and whether in social application or elsewhere, there is no need to attribute to it the slightest moral character to define it as contrary, according to its own scope,

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "dharma" from the previous page. The previous page ended by defining dharma as the fundamental foundation or conformity to the essential nature of beings.</meta>

to the "law of harmony" which governs both the cosmic order and the human order. With the meaning of "law" thus specified—and, moreover, freed from all the particular and derived applications to which it might give rise—we can accept this word "law" to translate <term>dharma <note>original: "dharma"; a key Sanskrit term meaning "that which supports," referring to the cosmic and social order.</note></term>. This is undoubtedly still an imperfect translation, but it is less inaccurate than other terms borrowed from Western languages. However, we must emphasize once more that it is by no means a question of a "moral law"; even the concepts of scientific law and social or legal law refer here only to special, specific cases of this broader principle.

The "law" can be viewed in principle as a "universal will," through an analogical transposition; however, such a conception leaves no room for anything personal, let alone anything <term>anthropomorphic <note>assigning human characteristics to non-human things or deities.</note></term>. The expression of this will in each state of manifested existence is designated as <term>Prajâpati <note>original: "Prajâpati"; the "Lord of Creatures" or "Lord of produced beings" in Hindu tradition.</note></term>, or the "Lord of produced beings." In each specific cosmic cycle, this same will manifests as the <term>Manu <note>original: "Manu"; the archetypal legislator or cosmic principle for a specific period of time.</note></term> who gives that cycle its own law. This name, *Manu*, should not therefore be taken as that of a mythical, legendary, or historical figure; it is properly the designation of a principle. We could define this principle, following the meaning of the verbal root <term>*man* <note>the Sanskrit root for "to think" or "to reflect."</note></term>, as "cosmic intelligence" or the "reflected thought of the universal order." 

On the other hand, this principle is regarded as the prototype of man, who is called <term>*mânava* <note>meaning "descendant of Manu," or human.</note></term> insofar as he is considered essentially a "thinking being," characterized by the possession of <term>*manas* <note>original: "manas"; the faculty of thought, mind, or reason.</note></term>—the mental or rational element. The concept of the *Manu* is therefore equivalent, at least in certain respects, to what other traditions—notably the Hebrew <term>Kabbalah <note>original: "Qabbalah"; the mystical school of Judaism.</note></term> and <term>Islamic esotericism <note>original: "l'ésotérisme musulman"; the inner, mystical dimensions of Islam, often referred to as Sufism.</note></term>—call the "Universal Man," and to what <term>Taoism <note>the ancient Chinese philosophical and spiritual tradition.</note></term> calls the "King." 

We have previously seen that the name <term>Vyâsa <note>original: "Vyâsa"; the traditional author of the Vedas and the Mahabharata.</note></term> designates not a man, but a function; however, that is a historical function of sorts, whereas here we are dealing with a cosmic function. This cosmic function only becomes historical in its specific application to the social order, and even then, it does not imply any "personification." In short, the "Law of Manu" for any given cycle or collective group is nothing other than the observation of the natural hierarchical relationships that exist between beings subject to the specific conditions of that cycle or group, along with the set of prescriptions that normally result from them. As for the concept of cosmic cycles, we will not dwell on it here, especially since making it easily intelligible would require quite lengthy explanations; we will simply say

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "law of harmony" and the principle of Manu as the archetypal legislator, transitioning from the cosmic definition of dharma to its social and textual applications.</meta>

only that there is between them not a chronological succession, but a logical and causal link, each cycle being determined in its entirety by its predecessor and determining, in its turn, the successor through a continuous production. This process is subject to the "law of harmony," which establishes the structural analogy between all modes of universal manifestation.

When we arrive at social application, the "law"—taking on its specifically legal meaning—may be formulated in a <term>shâstra <note>original: "shâstra"; a sacred treatise or code of laws and instructions.</note></term> or code. Insofar as this code expresses the "cosmic will" at its particular level, it is attributed to <term>Manu <note>original: "Manu"; the cosmic principle acting as the archetypal legislator for the current age.</note></term>, or more precisely, to the *Manu* of the current cycle. Naturally, this attribution does not make *Manu* the "author" of the *shâstra*, at least not in the ordinary sense where we say a purely human work is by a certain author. Here again, as with the <term>Vedic <note>original: "vêdique"; relating to the Vedas, the oldest and most authoritative scriptures of Hinduism.</note></term> texts, there is no strictly assignable historical origin; moreover, as we have explained, the question of such an origin is of no importance from a doctrinal point of view.

However, there is a major distinction to be noted between these two cases. While the Vedic texts are designated by the term <term>shruti <note>original: "shruti"; literally "that which is heard," referring to direct revelation or pure intellectual intuition.</note></term> as being the fruit of direct inspiration, the <term>dharma-shâstra <note>original: "dharma-shâstra"; a treatise on social and religious duty or "right conduct."</note></term> belongs only to the class of traditional writings called <term>smriti <note>original: "smriti"; literally "that which is remembered," referring to tradition based on reflection and human transmission.</note></term>. The authority of the *smriti* is less fundamental, and it also includes the <term>Purânas <note>original: "Purânas"; ancient texts containing lore, cosmology, and theology.</note></term> and the <term>Itihâsas <note>original: "Itihâsas"; traditional histories or epics, such as the Mahabharata.</note></term>, which Western scholarship views merely as "mythical" or "epic" poems because it fails to grasp the profound symbolic meaning that makes them something entirely different from "literature." 

The distinction between *shruti* and *smriti* essentially corresponds to the difference between pure and immediate intellectual intuition—which applies exclusively to the domain of <term>metaphysical <note>original: "métaphysique"; the branch of philosophy dealing with the first principles of things, beyond the physical world.</note></term> principles—and reflective consciousness of a rational nature. This rational consciousness is exercised upon objects of knowledge belonging to the individual order, which is precisely the case regarding social or other applications. Despite this, the traditional authority of the *dharma-shâstra* does not come from the human authors who may have formulated it—first orally, no doubt, and then in writing—and this is why these authors have remained unknown and undetermined. Its authority comes exclusively from what truly makes it the expression of the "law of *Manu*": that is, its conformity with the natural order of the existences it is intended to govern.

# CHAPTER VI

## PRINCIPLE OF THE INSTITUTION OF CASTES

To support what we set forth in the previous chapter, we will add some clarifications regarding the institution of castes—a matter of primary importance in the "Law of <term>Manu <note>original: "Manu"; the cosmic principle acting as the archetypal legislator for the current human cycle.</note></term>," and one so profoundly misunderstood by the generality of Europeans. We shall first establish this definition: caste, which the Hindus designate interchangeably by one of two words, <term>jâti <note>original: "jâti"; literally "birth," referring to the social group into which one is born.</note></term> and <term>varna <note>original: "varna"; literally "color," but used here in the technical sense of social class or rank.</note></term>, is a social function determined by the specific nature of each human being. The word *varna*, in its original sense, means "color," and some have sought to find there a proof, or at least an indication, of the supposed fact that the distinction of castes was originally based on racial differences; but this is not the case, for the same word has, by extension, the meaning of "quality" in general. From this comes its analogical use to designate the particular nature of a being—what might be called its "individual essence"—and it is precisely this that determines one’s caste, without the consideration of race intervening other than as one of the elements that can influence the constitution of individual nature. As for the word *jâti*, its proper meaning is that of "birth," and people claim to conclude from this that caste is essentially hereditary. This is another error: while it is most often hereditary in practice, it is not strictly so in principle, for the role of heredity in the formation of individual nature may be preponderant in the majority of cases, but it is by no means exclusive; this, moreover, requires some further explanation.

The individual being is regarded, as a whole, as a compound of two elements, which are respectively called <term>nâma <note>original: "nâma"; literally "name," representing the internal, qualitative, or essential aspect of an individual.</note></term>, the name, and <term>rûpa <note>original: "rûpa"; literally "form," representing the external, quantitative, or material aspect of an individual.</note></term>, the form; these two elements are, in short, the "essence" and the "substance" of the individuality, or what the <term>Aristotelian <note>Refers to the school of philosophy following Aristotle, particularly the concepts of "matter" and "form."</note></term> school calls "form" and "matter"—though these terms have a technical meaning very different from their common usage. It must even be noted that the word "form," instead of designating the element we name as such to translate the Sanskrit *rûpa*, designates then on the contrary

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the components that define a person's social and spiritual standing in Hindu tradition. ...the other element, which is properly the "<term>individual essence <note>original: "essence individuelle"</note></term>." We must add that the distinction we have just indicated, although analogous to that of the soul and the body among Westerners, is far from being strictly equivalent: form is not exclusively the bodily form, though it is not possible for us to dwell on this point here; as for the name, what it represents is the collection of all the qualities or characteristic attributes of the being under consideration. There is then reason to make another distinction within the "<term>individual essence <note>original: "essence individuelle"</note></term>": *<term>nâmika <note>original: "nâmika"; derived from the Sanskrit "nâman" (name), referring to individual qualities.</note></term>*, which relates to the name in a narrower sense, or what the particular name of each individual must express, is the set of qualities that belong specifically to them, which they hold from nothing other than themselves; *<term>gotrika <note>original: "gotrika"; derived from "gotra" (lineage or clan), referring to hereditary traits.</note></term>*, which belongs to the race or the family, is the set of qualities that the being holds from their <term>heredity <note>original: "hérédité"</note></term>. One could find an analogical representation of this second distinction in the attribution to an individual of a "given name," which is special to them, and a "family name"; there would, moreover, be much to say about the original meaning of names and what they should normally be intended to express, but, as these considerations do not fall within our current purpose, we shall limit ourselves to indicating that the determination of the true name is identified in principle with that of the <term>individual nature <note>original: "nature individuelle"</note></term> itself. "Birth," in the sense of the Sanskrit *<term>jâti <note>original: "jâti"; literally "birth" or "caste."</note></term>*, is properly the result of the two elements *<term>nâmika</term>* and *<term>gotrika</term>*: one must therefore account for the role of <term>heredity <note>original: "hérédité"</note></term>—and it can be considerable—but also the part by which the individual distinguishes themselves from their parents and other members of their family. It is evident, in fact, that no two beings present exactly the same set of qualities, whether physical or psychic: alongside what is common to them, there is also that which differentiates them; even those who would wish to explain everything in the individual by the influence of <term>heredity <note>original: "hérédité"</note></term> would undoubtedly be quite embarrassed to apply their theory to any particular case; this influence cannot be denied, but there are other elements that must be taken into account, as is done precisely by the theory we have just set forth.

The specific nature of each individual necessarily includes, from the beginning, the entire set of tendencies and dispositions that will develop and manifest throughout their existence, and which will notably determine—since this is what is specifically at issue here—their aptitude for a particular <term>social function <note>original: "fonction sociale"</note></term>. The knowledge of the <term>individual nature <note>original: "nature individuelle"</note></term> must therefore allow for the assignment to each human being the function that suits them by reason of this...

Furthermore, one can say that the negation of this principle implies, theoretically at least, if not always practically, the destruction of any legitimate hierarchy. 

At the same time, we see how absurd the attitude of Europeans is when they are indignant that a person cannot pass from their caste into a higher caste: in reality, this would imply nothing more or less than a change of individual nature. In other words, that person would have to cease being themselves to become another person, which is a manifest impossibility; what a being is potentially from birth, they will remain throughout their entire individual existence. The question of why a being is what they are and is not another being is, moreover, one of those questions that need not be asked; the truth is that each person, according to their own nature, is a necessary element of the total and universal harmony. However, it is quite certain that considerations of this kind are completely foreign to those who live in societies whose constitution lacks a principle and rests on no hierarchy—such as modern Western societies, where any person can fulfill almost indifferently the most diverse functions, including those for which they are least adapted, and where, moreover, material wealth serves almost exclusively as the substitute for any effective superiority.

From what we have said regarding the meaning of *<term>dharma</term>*, it follows that the social hierarchy must analogically reproduce, according to its own conditions, the constitution of the “<term>Universal Man <note>original: "Homme universel"; a metaphysical concept representing the perfected human state and the synthesis of all possible states of being.</note></term>”; by this we mean that there is a correspondence between the cosmic order and the human order. This correspondence, which is naturally found in the organization of the individual—whether viewed in their entirety or even simply in their physical part—must also be realized, in the mode specifically suited to it, within the organization of society. *   The ***Brâhmanas*** represent essentially spiritual and intellectual authority;
*   The ***Kshatriyas*** represent administrative power, including both judicial and military attributes, of which the royal function is merely the highest degree;
*   The ***Vaishyas*** represent the totality of various economic functions in the widest sense of the word, including agricultural, industrial, commercial, and financial roles;
*   As for the ***Shûdras***, they perform all the labor necessary to ensure the purely material subsistence of the community.

It is important to add that the *Brâhmanas* are in no way “priests” in the Western and religious sense of this word: undoubtedly, their functions involve the performance of rites of various kinds, because they must possess the knowledge necessary to give these rites their full effectiveness; but they also, and above all, involve the preservation and regular transmission of the traditional doctrine. Furthermore, among most ancient peoples, the function of teaching—represented by the mouth in the preceding symbolism—was also regarded as the priestly function *par excellence*, precisely because the entire civilization rested upon a doctrinal principle. For the same reason, deviations from the doctrine generally appear to be linked to a subversion of the social hierarchy, as could be seen notably in the cases of attempts made at various times by the *Kshatriyas* to reject the supremacy of the *Brâhmanas*—a supremacy whose reason for being appears clearly through all that we have said regarding the true nature of Hindu civilization. ## CHAPTER VII
# SHIVAISM AND VISHNUISM

Should the Supreme, total, and universal Principle, which the religious doctrines of the West call "God," be conceived as impersonal or as personal? This question can lead to endless and ultimately pointless discussions because it arises only from partial and incomplete conceptions. It would be futile to seek to reconcile these views without rising above the specific theological or philosophical domains that are properly theirs. From a metaphysical <term>metaphysics|The study of the fundamental nature of reality and the first principles of things, transcending the physical world.</term> point of view, it must be stated that this Principle is both impersonal and personal, depending on the perspective from which it is viewed: it is impersonal or, if you will, "supra-personal" in itself; it is personal in relation to universal manifestation <note>The "manifestation" refers to the process by which the infinite Principle produces the finite, visible universe.</note>. However, it must be understood that this "divine personality" does not possess the slightest anthropomorphic <note>Anthropomorphic means attributing human form or characteristics to a non-human being, especially a deity.</note> character, for one must be careful not to confuse "personality" with "individuality." The fundamental distinction we have just formulated—through which the apparent contradictions of secondary and multiple points of view are resolved into the unity of a higher synthesis—is expressed by Far Eastern metaphysics as the distinction between "Non-Being" and "Being." This distinction is no less clear in Hindu doctrine, as is required by the essential identity of pure metaphysics regardless of the diverse forms it may take. The impersonal Principle, which is absolutely universal, is designated as *Brahma* <note>original: "Brahma"</note>; the "divine personality," which is a determination or specification of it involving a lesser degree of universality, is most generally called *Ishwara* <note>original: "Îshwara"</note>. *Brahma*, in its Infinity, cannot be characterized by any positive attribute, which is expressed by saying that it is "beyond all qualification" <note>original: "nirguna"</note>, and also "beyond all distinction" <note>original: "nirvishêsha"</note>. On the other hand, *Ishwara* is said to be "qualified" <note>original: "saguna"</note>, and "conceived distinctively" <note>original: "savishêsha"</note>, because it can receive such attributes. These attributes are obtained by an analogical transposition <note>Analogical transposition is the process of taking a quality found in a creature (like wisdom or power) and applying it to the Divine Principle in an infinite, transcendent sense.</note> into the universal of the various qualities or properties of the beings of which it is the principle. It is obvious that one can thus conceive of an indefinite number of "divine attributes," and that, moreover, any quality could be transposed by considering it in its principle

What we have said regarding symbolism allows us to realize how the misunderstanding that gives rise to anthropomorphism <note>The attribution of human traits or personalities to God.</note> can result in turning "divine attributes" into so many "gods"—that is, entities conceived on the model of individual beings, and to which is attributed a distinct and independent existence. In truth, we know of only one certain example of this error becoming widespread: that of Greco-Roman civilization, and even then, there were at least some exceptions within its intellectual elite. In the East, where the tendency toward anthropomorphism does not exist—aside from individual aberrations that are always possible but rare and abnormal—nothing of the sort could ever occur; this will undoubtedly surprise many Westerners, whose exclusive knowledge of classical antiquity leads them to want to discover "myths" and "paganism" everywhere, yet it is so. However, it should be added that Shaivism, which is less widespread than Vaishnavism and places less importance on external rites, is at the same time "higher" in a sense and leads more directly to pure metaphysical realization. This is easily understood by the very nature of the principle to which it gives prominence; for "transformation"—which must be understood here in its strictly etymological sense <note>original: "transformation" — from the Latin *trans-formatio*, literally meaning a change that goes beyond or across form.</note>—is the passage "beyond form." This passage only appears to be a destruction from the limited and dependent viewpoint of the manifested world; in reality, it is the passage from the manifested to the non-manifested, through which the return to the eternal immutability of the supreme Principle is achieved, outside of which nothing could otherwise exist except in an illusory mode.

Each of the "divine aspects" is regarded as endowed with its own power or energy, which is called *shakti* <term>shakti|The active power or feminine energy of a deity, often personified as a goddess.</term>, and which is represented symbolically in a feminine form: the *shakti* of *Brahmâ* is *Saraswatî*, that of *Vishnu* is *Lakshmî*, and that of *Shiva* is *Pârvatî*. Furthermore, each of the principles we have just mentioned can be further envisioned under a plurality of more specific aspects, and from each of them also derive other secondary aspects—a derivation most often described as a symbolic lineage.
