## CHAPTER VIII
### THE VIEWPOINTS OF THE DOCTRINE

The preceding indications allow us to understand the coexistence, within the essential unity of a single traditional doctrine <term>Traditional Doctrine|A body of spiritual and metaphysical knowledge passed down through generations, which Guénon argues remains consistent in its core principles despite varying outward forms.</term>, of a multiplicity of points of view that in no way affects that unity. Moreover, in all things, everyone obviously brings a sort of perspective of their own into their understanding; consequently, one might say that there are as many ways of understanding, more or less different, as there are individuals. However, this is only true at the starting point because, as soon as one rises above the individual domain, all these differences—which involve no incompatibility—necessarily disappear. In addition to the difference that is thus inherent to the particular nature of various human beings, each person can also place themselves at several points of view to study the doctrine under this or that more or less clearly defined aspect. These aspects can be defined all the more clearly the more they are particularized—that is to say, the further they are removed, in the descending order of applications, from the universality of principles. The totality of possible and legitimate points of view is always contained, in principle and synthetically, within the doctrine itself. What we have already said regarding the plurality of meanings offered by a traditional text suffices to show how these viewpoints can be found there; it will therefore never be a matter of doing anything other than rigorously developing the interpretation of the fundamental doctrine according to these various points of view.

This is precisely what occurs in India, and it is expressed by the Sanskrit word *darshana*, which properly means nothing other than "view" or "point of view," for the verbal root *drish* <note>original: "drish"; the Sanskrit root primarily meaning "to see" or "to perceive."</note>, from which it is derived, has "to see" as its principal meaning. The *darshanas* <term>Darshanas|The six orthodox systems of Hindu philosophy, though Guénon prefers to call them "points of view" to avoid the Western implication of closed, competing systems of thought.</term> are thus truly the points of view of the doctrine, and they are not—as most orientalists <note>Guénon uses this term to refer to 19th and early 20th-century Western scholars who studied the East, often criticizing them for applying Western philosophical categories to Eastern concepts.</note> imagine—competing "philosophical systems" opposing one another. To the full extent that these "views" are strictly orthodox <term>Orthodox|In this context, it refers to alignment with the authority of the Vedas, the core sacred scriptures of Hinduism.</term>, they could not naturally enter into conflict or contradiction. We have shown that every systematic conception—the fruit of the intellectual individualism so dear to modern Westerners—is the negation of metaphysics, which

<summary>Guénon explains that the various schools of Hindu thought, or darshanas, are not conflicting "systems" but rather complementary "viewpoints" that all derive from a single, unified traditional doctrine. He argues that while individuals perceive truth differently at first, these perspectives harmonize as one moves toward universal metaphysical principles.</summary>
<keywords>darshana, traditional doctrine, metaphysics, Hindu philosophy, orthodoxy, intellectual individualism, Sanskrit roots</keywords>

--- Page 149 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument that the diverse viewpoints within Hindu tradition are not contradictory "philosophies" but complementary aspects of a single metaphysical truth. It critiques the 19th and early 20th-century Western academic approach to Eastern thought.</meta>

constitutes the very essence of the doctrine; we have also mentioned the profound distinction between metaphysical thought and philosophical thought, the latter being only a special mode, peculiar to the West, which cannot validly be applied to the knowledge of a traditional doctrine that has been maintained in its purity and integrity. There is, therefore, no such thing as "Hindu philosophy," nor "Chinese philosophy," provided one wishes to keep a somewhat clear meaning for this word "philosophy"—a meaning determined by the line of thought proceeding from the Greeks; and besides, considering above all what philosophy has become in modern times, one must admit that the absence of this mode of thought in a civilization is in no way particularly regrettable. But the Orientalists <term>Orientalists|Western scholars from the 18th to the early 20th century who specialized in the languages and cultures of the East, often criticized by Guénon for applying rigid Western categories to Eastern concepts.</term> wish to see in the *darshanas* <term>Darshanas|Literally 'visions' or 'points of view.' In Indian tradition, these are the six recognized orthodox perspectives through which the Vedas are interpreted.</term> nothing but philosophy and systems, upon which they claim, moreover, to impose Western labels: all this because they are incapable of stepping outside "classical" frameworks, and because they are entirely ignorant of the most characteristic differences between the Eastern mentality and the Western mentality. Their attitude, in the respect we are discussing, is entirely comparable to that of a man who, knowing nothing of current European civilization and having by chance held the teaching programs of a University in his hands, would draw this singular conclusion: that the scholars of Europe are divided into several rival schools, each of which has its own particular philosophical system, the principal ones being those of the mathematicians, physicists, chemists, biologists, logicians, and psychologists; this misunderstanding would certainly be most ridiculous, yet it would hardly be more so than the current conception held by Orientalists; and these latter should not even have the excuse of ignorance, or rather, it is their ignorance itself that is inexcusable. However unlikely it may seem, it is only too certain that questions of principle—which they seem to set aside by prejudice—have never presented themselves to their minds, which are, moreover, too narrowly specialized to still be able to understand them and appreciate their significance; this is a strange case of "intellectual myopia" <note>A term Guénon uses to describe a narrow focus on literal or historical details that misses the broader spiritual or metaphysical reality.</note> to the highest degree; and one can be quite sure that, with such dispositions, they will never succeed in penetrating the true meaning of the slightest fragment of any of these Eastern doctrines that they have given themselves the mission of interpreting in their own way, in conformity with their purely Western points of view.

To return to the true understanding of things, the viewpoints from which the doctrine can be considered are obviously capable of being more

One can therefore always group secondary viewpoints around the principal viewpoints, and it is then these latter alone that one will limit oneself to considering separately, as so many branches of the study of the doctrine; the others give rise therein only to simple subdivisions, which it is, moreover, not even necessary to specify in most cases. It is the major divisions, the principal branches, which are properly the *darshanas* <term>Darshanas|Literally 'visions' or 'points of view.' In Indian tradition, these are the six recognized orthodox perspectives through which the Vedas are interpreted.</term>, in the sense that this word has habitually taken, and, according to the classification generally accepted in India, six are distinguished. One must take care not to confuse these, simply because their number is the same, with what are called the six *Vêdângas*.

The word *Vêdânga* <term>Vêdânga|From 'Veda' (knowledge) and 'anga' (limb). These are six auxiliary disciplines used to support the study and preservation of the Vedas.</term> signifies literally "limb of the *Veda*"; this designation is applied to certain auxiliary sciences of the *Veda*, because they are compared to the bodily limbs by means of which a being acts externally. The fundamental treatises relating to these sciences, of which we are about to give an enumeration, form part of the *smriti* <term>Smriti|'That which is remembered.' Traditional texts of human authorship, as opposed to 'Shruti' (revelation), which include law codes, epics, and auxiliary sciences.</term>, and, by reason of their direct relationship with the *Veda*, they even occupy the first place within it. The *shikshâ* is the science of correct articulation and exact pronunciation, involving—along with the laws of euphony <note>original: "euphonie"; refers to the 'Sandhi' rules in Sanskrit where word endings change to create a harmonious flow of sound.</note> which are more important and more developed in Sanskrit than in any other language—the knowledge of the symbolic value of letters. In traditional languages, indeed, the use of phonetic writing is by no means exclusive of the maintenance of an ideographic meaning, of which Hebrew and Arabic likewise offer examples. The *chhandas* is the science of prosody <note>The study of poetic meters and rhythms.</note>, which determines the application of different meters in correspondence with the vibratory modalities of the cosmic order that they must express; this makes them something entirely different from "poetic" forms in the merely literary sense of the word. Moreover, a profound knowledge of rhythm and its cosmic relationships—from which derives its use for certain preparatory modes of metaphysical realization—is common to all Oriental civilizations, but is, on the contrary, totally foreign to Westerners. The *vyâkarana* is grammar, but one which, instead of presenting itself as a simple collection of rules appearing more or less arbitrary because their reasons are unknown (as usually happens in Western languages), is based instead on conceptions and classifications that are always in close relationship with the logical significance of language. From this arise countless errors on the part of Western scholars of the East <note>Original: "orientalistes." To call an idea "original" or "new" implies it is merely a personal invention or opinion, and therefore likely an error rather than a universal truth.</note>. Furthermore, it is quite evident that a "point of view" has never been the exclusive property of any school, even though, if one is content to view it superficially instead of seeking to grasp its essence, it may sometimes appear to be identified with the conception of the school that developed it most; confusion on this point is another of those natural to Westerners, who are accustomed to attributing all the conceptions familiar to them to individuals, as if they were true "inventions." This is one of the at least implicit postulates of their "historical method," and in our day, the religious point of view itself does not escape the consequences of this special turn of mind, which deploys against it all the resources of that anti-traditional exegesis to which we have already alluded.

# CHAPTER IX
## THE NYAYA

The word *nyâya* properly means "logic," and even "method"; to say, as some do, that it began by designating a school and subsequently became a synonym for logic, is to reverse the natural order of things. Indeed, if one admits that a school must be characterized by a name that possesses a prior meaning, exactly the opposite would have occurred—if, that is, a *<term>darshana</term>* <term>darshana|Literally a "vision" or "point of view"; one of the six orthodox systems of Indian philosophy.</term> could ever be monopolized by any specific school. In fact, it is indeed logic that is at issue, and has always been at issue, regarding this *darshana*. Its development is attributed to Gautama, but this name—which was common to many figures and even families in ancient India and is not accompanied here by even the vaguest biographical information—cannot be linked to a specific individual. What has occurred here is what always happens in the East in such cases: individuals do not matter in relation to the doctrine. It is perfectly possible that there was, at a distant and indeterminate time, a man named Gautama who dedicated himself to the study and teaching of this branch of knowledge that constitutes logic; but this very likely fact is of no interest in itself. The name of this man has only been preserved with a purely symbolic value, to designate, in a sense, the "intellectual aggregate" formed by all those who, during a period whose duration is no less indeterminate than its origin, devoted themselves to the same study. This kind of "collective entity," of which we have already seen an example in <note>Vyâsa is the traditional name given to the compiler of the Vedas and the author of the Mahabharata.</note> Vyâsa, is moreover not a "school," at least in the ordinary sense of the word, but rather a true intellectual function. One could say as much regarding the proper names that appear linked in the same manner to each of the other *darshanas*; these remarks, made once and for all, will dispense us from returning to the subject hereafter.

We have said that the *Nyâya* is essentially logic; but we must add that this term here has a less restricted meaning than it does among Westerners, because what it designates, instead of being conceived as a

Escaping the narrow specialization which is inevitable for logic when viewed in a philosophical mode, and having, moreover, no need to be integrated into any specific system, Hindu logic thereby possesses a much greater scope; to understand this, one should recall here what we said regarding the characteristics of metaphysics: what constitutes the proper object of a speculation is not precisely the things themselves that it studies, but the point of view under which it studies those things. Logic, as we also stated previously, concerns the conditions of human understanding; whatever can be viewed logically is therefore everything that is an object of human understanding, insofar as it is effectively considered from this perspective. Consequently, logic includes within its point of view things considered as "objects of proof," that is to say, of reasoned or discursive knowledge: in the *Nyâya*, this is the meaning of the term <term>padârtha|Literally "the meaning of a word"; in this context, it refers to the fundamental categories or "predicaments" of reality as objects of knowledge.</term>, and, despite certain differences, this is also the true significance of "categories" or "predicaments" <note>original: "prédicaments"; a traditional term in Western logic, derived from the Latin *praedicamenta*, referring to Aristotle's classifications of all possible things that can be predicated of a subject.</note> in ancient Western logic. If the divisions and classifications established by logic have a real ontological <note>Related to the study of the nature of being or existence.</note> value at the same time, it is because there is necessarily a correspondence between the two points of view, provided that one does not establish—as modern philosophy does—a radical and artificial opposition between the subject and the object. Moreover, the logical point of view is analytical because it is individual and rational; it is only as a simple application to the individual order that logical principles, even the most general ones, are derived from metaphysical or universal principles.

The *Nyâya* distinguishes sixteen *padârthas*, the first of which is called <term>pramâna|A legitimate means of attaining right knowledge.</term>, a word that has the usual sense of "proof," and which is even often translated as "evidence"; however, this latter translation is improper in many cases, and it has, furthermore, the disadvantage of suggesting the concept of Cartesian evidence <note>A reference to René Descartes' standard of truth, which requires ideas to be "clear and distinct" to be accepted as true—a concept the author argues is too limited for this context.</note>, which is only truly valid within the mathematical domain alone. To fix the true significance of the word *pramâna*, one must note that its primary meaning is that of "measure"; what it designates here are the legitimate means of knowledge in the rational order—means of which each is, in effect, only applicable to a certain measure and under certain conditions, or, in other words, within a certain particular domain whose extent defines its own scope; and the enumeration of these means of knowledge or proof provides the subdivisions of the first *padârtha*. The other <term>padârthas|Fundamental categories or "objects of knowledge" in the Nyâya system.</term> are less important and relate primarily to the various modalities of reasoning or demonstration; we shall not attempt to provide a complete enumeration of them here, but will content ourselves with specifically pointing out the one constituted by the members of a regular argument.

The argument in question, which is called <term>nyâya|In this restricted sense, it refers to the formal process of logical demonstration; in a broader sense, it refers to the entire school of logic.</term> in a secondary and restricted sense of this term, and which is essentially the model for methodical demonstration, consists, in its fully developed form, of five <term>avayavas|The "members" or constituent parts of a logical argument.</term>: *pratijnâ*, the proposition or assertion to be proved; *hêtu*, the justificatory reason for this assertion; *udâharana*, the example supporting this reason and serving as a kind of illustration by recalling a commonly known case; *upanaya*, the application to the specific case in question, that of the proposition initially stated; finally, *nigamana*, the result or conclusion, which is the definitive affirmation of that same proposition as demonstrated. Such is the complete form of the demonstrative argument, but it is also sometimes given in simplified and abbreviated forms, consisting of either the first three members or the last three; in this latter form especially, it presents a very clear resemblance to the **syllogism** <note>A form of logical reasoning where a conclusion is reached from two premises; for example: "All men are mortal (premise), Socrates is a man (premise), therefore Socrates is mortal (conclusion)."</note> as Aristotle established its theory. Moreover, we find here the equivalent of the "major term" and the "minor term," designated respectively by the names *vyâpaka* or "container" and *vyâpya* or "contained," which refer to the same perspective of logical extension; as for the "middle term," its role is fulfilled by the reason, *hêtu*, which is also called *linga* or the "sign" allowing one to recognize the *vyâpti*, that is to say, the invariable connection that exists between the container and the contained. However, these undeniable analogies—which suggest, as at least a plausible hypothesis, that Aristotle might have had some knowledge of the *Nyâya*—must not make us forget that, as we have already indicated, essential differences remain between the two perspectives: while the Greek syllogism ultimately concerns only concepts or the notions of things, the Hindu argument bears more directly upon the things themselves.

We have said that the separation and opposition of the subject and the object are entirely specific to modern philosophy; but, among the Greeks, the distinction between the thing and its notion already went a little too far, in the sense that logic considered exclusively the relationships between notions, as if things were known to us only through these. Undoubtedly, rational knowledge is indeed an indirect knowledge, and this is why it is susceptible to error; yet, if it did not reach the things themselves to a certain extent, it would be entirely illusory and would not truly be knowledge to any degree; if therefore, under the rational mode, one can say that we know an object through the intermediary of its notion, it is because this notion is still something of the object, that it participates in its nature by expressing it in relation to us. This is why Hindu logic considers not only the way in which we conceive of things, but rather the things themselves insofar as they are conceived by us, our conception being truly inseparable from its object, without which it would be nothing real; and, in this respect, the <term>Scholastic|The school of medieval European philosophy and theology that sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</term> definition of truth as the **conformity of the thing and the intellect** <note>original: *adaequatio rei et intellectus*</note>, at all levels of knowledge, is, in the West, that which comes closest to the position of the traditional doctrines of the East, because it is what is most in conformity with the data of <term>pure metaphysics|A branch of knowledge dealing with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, and identity, outside of the limits of physical experimentation.</term>. Moreover, the Scholastic doctrine, while continuing that of Aristotle in its broad outlines, corrected and completed it on many points; it is regrettable that it did not succeed in freeing itself entirely from the limitations that were the heritage of the Hellenic <note>Greek</note> mentality, and also that it does not seem to have grasped the profound consequences of the principle, already established by Aristotle, of identification through knowledge. It is precisely by virtue of this principle that, once the subject knows an object, however partial and even superficial this knowledge may be, something of the object is in the subject and has become part of its being; whatever the aspect under which we consider things, it is always the things themselves that we reach, at least under a certain relationship, which forms in any case one of their attributes, that is to say, one of the constituent elements of their essence. Let us admit, if one insists, that this is "realism"; the truth is that things are this way, and the word matters little; but, strictly speaking, the special viewpoints of "realism" and "idealism," with the systematic opposition denoted by their correlation, do not apply here at all, where we are well beyond the limited domain of philosophical thought. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of knowledge, moving from the Scholastic definition of truth as "conformity" to a deeper metaphysical realization where the distinction between the knower (subject) and the known (object) is ultimately dissolved into a single, universal principle.</meta>

knowledge presents two inseparable sides: if it is the identification of the subject with the object, it is also, and by that very fact, the assimilation of the object by the subject. In reaching things in their essence, we "realize" them—in the full force of this word—as states or modalities of our own being; and, if the idea, to the extent that it is true and adequate, participates in the nature of the thing, it is because, conversely, the thing itself also participates in the nature of the idea.

Fundamentally, there are not two separate and radically heterogeneous worlds, such as modern philosophy assumes when labeling them "subjective" and "objective," or even superimposed in the manner of the <term>intelligible world|In Platonic philosophy, the realm of perfect, unchanging ideas or forms, accessible only by the intellect.</term> and the <term>sensible world|The physical world we perceive through our senses, which Plato viewed as a mere shadow or reflection of the intelligible world.</term> of Plato. But, as the Arabs say, "existence is unique" <note>original: *l’existence est unique*; this refers to the metaphysical doctrine of *Wahdat al-Wujud*, often translated as the "Unity of Being," which suggests that nothing exists outside of the ultimate Reality.</note>, and all that it contains is but the manifestation, through multiple modes, of one and the same principle, which is Universal Being.

# CHAPTER X
## THE VAISHESHIKA

The name of the *Vaishêshika* is derived from the word *vishêsha*, which means "distinctive character" and, consequently, "individual thing"; this <term>darshana|A Sanskrit term meaning "viewpoint" or "perspective," used to describe the six orthodox systems of Indian philosophy.</term> is thus constituted by the knowledge of individual things as such, envisioned in a distinctive mode, in their contingent existence. While the *Nyâya* <note>The Hindu school of logic and epistemology.</note> considers these things in their relationship with human understanding, the *Vaishêshika* considers them more directly in what they are in themselves; one immediately sees the difference between these two points of view, but also their relationship, since what things are in knowledge is, fundamentally, identical to what they are in themselves; but, moreover, the difference between the two points of view only disappears when they are both surpassed, so that their distinction always has cause to be maintained within the limits of the domain to which they properly apply.

This domain is evidently that of manifested nature, outside of which the individual point of view itself—of which these two *darshanas* represent modalities—no longer has any possible meaning; but universal manifestation can be envisioned in two different ways: either synthetically, starting from the principles from which it proceeds and which determine it in all its modes, and this is what the *Sânkhya* <note>A school of Indian philosophy that focuses on the dualism between consciousness (Purusha) and matter/nature (Prakriti), often through an enumeration of principles.</note> does, as we shall see further on; or analytically, in the distinction of its multiple constituent elements, and this is what the *Vaishêshika* does. This latter point of view can even limit itself to the special consideration of one of the modes of universal manifestation, such as that which constitutes the entirety of the sensible world; and, in fact, it is obliged to limit itself almost exclusively to this, for the conditions of other modes necessarily escape the individual faculties of the human being: one can only reach them "from above," so to speak, that is to say, through that which, in man, surpasses the limitations and relativities inherent to the individual. This clearly moves beyond the distinctive and analytical point of view that we must characterize at present; but one can only completely understand a special point of view on the condition of surpassing it, since this point of view presents itself, not as independent and having its entire reason for being in itself, but as attached to certain principles from which it derives, as an application,

It distinguishes this school from the Nyâya and Sânkhya schools while noting that such individual perspectives must eventually be surpassed to be fully understood through higher principles.</summary>

We have seen that this connection to principles, ensuring the essential unity of the doctrine in all its branches, is a common characteristic of the entire body of traditional knowledge in India; it marks the profound difference that exists between the <term>Vaishêshika|One of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, focusing on the study of the distinct characteristics of the physical world.</term> and the scientific point of view as understood by Westerners—a point of view from which the *Vaishêshika* is, nonetheless, the least distant within that ensemble. In reality, the *Vaishêshika* is notably closer to the point of view that constituted "physical philosophy" <note>original: "philosophie physique" — referring to the ancient Greek study of *physis* or nature in its entirety.</note> among the Greeks; while being analytical, it is less so than modern science, and by that very fact, it is not subject to the narrow specialization that drives the latter to lose itself in the indefinite detail of experimental facts. What we have here is something that is, at heart, more rational, and even, to a certain extent, more intellectual in the strict sense of the word: more rational because, while remaining within the individual domain, it is free from all empiricism; more intellectual because it never loses sight of the fact that the entire individual order is linked to universal principles, from which it derives all the reality of which it is capable. We have said that by "physics," the ancients understood the science of nature in all its generality; this word would therefore be quite appropriate here, but one must take into account, on the other hand, the restriction its meaning has undergone among moderns, which is very characteristic of the change in point of view to which it corresponds. This is why, if one must apply a Western designation to a Hindu point of view, we prefer that of "cosmology" for the *Vaishêshika*; and, moreover, the "cosmology" of the Middle Ages, presenting itself clearly as an application of metaphysics to the contingencies of the sensible order, is even closer to it than was the "physical philosophy" of the Greeks, which almost always takes its principles only from the contingent order, and at most within the limits of the immediately superior, yet still particular, point of view to which the <term>Sânkhya|A school of Hindu philosophy that enumerates the principles of nature, focusing on the distinction between the soul (Purusha) and primordial matter (Prakriti).</term> refers.

Despite this, the very object of the *Vaishêshika* may have determined, among some of those who dedicated themselves specifically to its study, a certain "naturalist" tendency; however, being generally foreign to the Oriental spirit, this tendency was never able to take on the development in India that it had in Greece among the "physical philosophers"; at the very least, only a few schools belonging to the most degenerate forms of Buddhism were to push it to the logical consequences where it led, and this was only possible for them

If we take the word "atom" in its proper sense—that of "indivisible," which modern physicists no longer do, but which must be done here—one can say that an atom, having no parts, must also be without extension; now, a sum of elements without extension will never form an extension; if atoms are what they must be by definition, it is therefore impossible for them to succeed in forming bodies. To this well-known and indeed decisive reasoning, we will add this one, which Shankarâchârya <term>Shankarâchârya|A pivotal 8th-century philosopher and theologian of the Advaita Vedanta school.</term> employs to refute atomism<note>[15]</note>: two things can come into contact through a part of themselves or through their totality; for the atoms, which have no parts, the first hypothesis is impossible; there remains only the second, which amounts to saying that the contact or aggregation of two atoms can only be achieved by their pure and simple coincidence, from which it clearly follows that two atoms joined together are no more, in terms of extension, than a single atom, and so on indefinitely; therefore, as before, any number of atoms will never form a body. Thus, atomism represents nothing but an impossibility, as we indicated when clarifying the sense in which heterodoxy <note>original: "hétérodoxie"; referring to doctrines that do not align with the authority of the Vedas.</note> must be understood; but, with atomism set aside, the viewpoint of the *Vaishêshika*, then reduced to its essentials, is perfectly legitimate, and the preceding explanation...

# CHAPTER XI
## THE *SANKHYA*

The <term>Sânkhya<note>One of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, focusing on a dualism between pure consciousness and primordial matter.</note></term> still relates to the realm of nature—that is to say, of universal manifestation—but, as we have already indicated, it is considered this time synthetically, starting from the principles that determine its production and from which it derives all its reality. The development of this point of view, which is in a sense intermediate between the cosmology of the <term>Vaishêshika<note>The school of philosophy discussed previously, which deals with physics and the classification of entities.</note></term> and metaphysics, is attributed to the ancient sage Kapila; but, in truth, this name does not designate a historical person, and everything said of him presents a purely symbolic character. As for the name of the *Sânkhya*, it has been interpreted in various ways; it derives from *sankhyâ*, which means "enumeration" or "calculation," and also sometimes "reasoning." It properly designates a doctrine that proceeds through the regular enumeration of the different degrees of manifested being, and this is indeed what characterizes the *Sânkhya*, which can be entirely summarized in the distinction and consideration of twenty-five <term>tattwas<note>original: "tattwas"; these are the fundamental principles or "true elements" that constitute reality.</note></term> or true principles and elements, corresponding to these hierarchical degrees.

Placing itself at the point of view of manifestation, the *Sânkhya* takes as its starting point <term>Prakriti<note>The primordial, undifferentiated substance from which the material world emerges.</note></term> or *Pradhâna*, which is the universal substance, undifferentiated and unmanifested in itself, but from which all things proceed by modification; this first *tattwa* is the root or <term>mûla<note>original: "mûla"; meaning the foundation or root of a thing.</note></term> of manifestation, and the following *tattwas* represent its modifications at various degrees. At the first degree is <term>Buddhi<note>The higher, intuitive intellect that reflects pure consciousness.</note></term>, which is also called *Mahat* or the "great principle," and which is the pure intellect, transcendent in relation to individuals; here, we are already within manifestation, but we are still in the universal order. At the next degree, by contrast, we find individual consciousness, <term>ahankâra<note>original: "ahankâra"; literally the "I-maker," or the ego-principle that produces the sense of individuality.</note></term>, which proceeds from the intellectual principle by a "particularizing" determination, if one may put it so, and which in turn produces the following elements. These are, first of all, the five <term>tanmâtras<note>Subtle, non-physical essences or "potentials" of the elements, such as sound-as-such or touch-as-such.</note></term>, which are incorporeal and non-perceptible elementary determinations that will be the respective principles of the five <term>bhûtas<note>The five gross or physical elements: ether, air, fire, water, and earth.</note></term> or corporeal elements. The *Vaishêshika* only had to consider these latter elements, and not the *tanmâtras*, the conception of which is only necessary when one wishes to relate the

sal substance, the first principle of manifestation, which allows us to pass from the simple notion of elements or the conditions of the corporeal modality to the principles of universal existence. Next come the individual faculties, produced by the differentiation of consciousness—of which they are like so many functions—and which are regarded as being eleven in number: ten external and one internal. The ten external faculties comprise five faculties of knowledge <note>original: "facultés de connaissance"; traditionally called the *jñânendriyas*, these are the powers of sensory perception.</note>, which, in the corporeal domain, are faculties of sensation, and five faculties of action <note>original: "facultés d’action"; the *karmendriyas*, such as speech or movement.</note>. The internal faculty is the *manas* <note>original: "manas"; the mind or "inner sense" that coordinates the data from the external senses.</note>, which is both a faculty of knowledge and a faculty of action, and is united directly to the individual consciousness. Finally, we find once more the five corporeal elements, enumerated this time in the order of their production or manifestation: ether, air, fire, water, and earth. Thus, one arrives at twenty-four *tattwas* <note>original: "tattwas"; the fundamental "realities" or principles that constitute the manifested world.</note> comprising *Prakriti* <note>original: "Prakriti"; primordial, undifferentiated substance.</note> and all its modifications.

Up to this point, the *Sânkhya* <note>original: "Sânkhya"; the school of "Enumeration" or "Reasoning."</note> considers things only from the perspective of substance, understood in the universal sense. However, as we indicated previously, there is reason to consider correlatively, as the other pole of manifestation, a principle complementary to that one, which one can call essence. This is the principle to which the *Sânkhya* gives the name *Purusha* <note>original: "Purusha"; the pure, unchanging consciousness or spiritual essence.</note> or *Pumas*, and which it regards as a twenty-fifth *tattwa*, entirely independent of the preceding ones. All manifested things are produced by *Prakriti*, but without the presence of *Purusha*, these productions would have only a purely illusory existence. Contrary to what some believe, the consideration of these two principles does not present the slightest dualistic character: they do not derive from one another and are not reducible to one another, but they both proceed from the Universal Being, in which they constitute the first of all distinctions. Moreover, the *Sânkhya* does not have to go beyond this very distinction, as the consideration of Pure Being does not fall within its specific point of view; yet, because it is not a "system" <note>In this context, the author means a closed, limited philosophical framework.</note>, it leaves open the possibility of everything that surpasses it, and this is why it is in no way dualistic. To relate this to what we have already said concerning dualism, we will add that the Western conception of "spirit" and "matter" corresponds to the distinction between essence and substance only in a very limited domain and as a simple particular application among an infinity of other analogous and equally possible ones. One sees by this how much, without yet being on the ground of pure metaphysics, we are already far from the limitations of ordinary philosophical thought.

We must return once more to the conception of *Prakriti*: it possesses three *gunas* <note>original: "gunas"; the three fundamental qualities or strands—Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—that bind and constitute the material world.</note> or constitutive qualities, which are in perfect equilibrium in its

primordial undifferentiation; every manifestation or modification of substance represents a rupture of this equilibrium, and beings, in their different states of manifestation, participate in the three qualities <note>original: "gunas"; the three fundamental tendencies or "strands" that make up the woven fabric of nature.</note> to varying degrees and, so to speak, according to infinitely varied proportions. These qualities <note>original: "gunas"</note> are therefore not states, but conditions of universal existence to which all manifested beings are subject, and which must be carefully distinguished from the special conditions that determine a particular state or mode of manifestation—such as space and time, which condition the corporeal state to the exclusion of others. The three qualities <note>original: "gunas"</note> are: **purity** <note>original: "sattwa"; conformity to the pure essence of Being or "Sat," identified with intelligible light and knowledge, represented as an ascending tendency.</note>; the **expansive impulse** <note>original: "rajas"; the tendency according to which a being develops within a certain state and at a determined level of existence.</note>; and finally, **darkness** <note>original: "tamas"; assimilated to ignorance and represented as a descending tendency.</note>. One can see how insufficient and even false the current interpretations of the Orientalists <note>The author refers to 19th and early 20th-century Western scholars who studied "the East," whom he often accuses of misinterpreting metaphysical concepts through the lens of Western psychology or morality.</note> are, especially regarding the first two qualities <note>original: "gunas"</note>, for which they attempt to translate the respective designations as "goodness" and "passion," when there is obviously nothing moral or psychological about them. We cannot provide a more complete exposition of this very important conception here, nor speak of the various applications to which it gives rise, notably regarding the theory of elements; we shall content ourselves with noting its existence.

On the other hand, regarding the *Sânkhya* <note>One of the six orthodox systems of Indian philosophy, which focuses on the enumeration of the principles of reality.</note> in general, we do not need to dwell as long as we would have had to if we had not already noted, for the most part, the essential characteristics of this viewpoint alongside those of the *Vaishêshika* <note>Another philosophical school, often associated with logic and a "naturalist" classification of the world.</note> and in comparison with it; but there still remains some ambiguity to clear up. The Orientalists who take the *Sânkhya* for a philosophical system willingly qualify it as a "materialist" and "atheistic" doctrine; it goes without saying that it is the conception of primordial substance <note>original: "Prakriti"</note> that they identify with the notion of matter, which is entirely false, and that, moreover, they take no account of the pure spirit <note>original: "Purusha"; the conscious witness or "Person," the complementary pole to substance.</note> in their distorted interpretation. Universal substance is something quite different from matter, which is at most only a restrictive and specialized determination of it; and we have already had the occasion to say that the very notion of matter, as it was constituted among modern Westerners, does not exist among the Hindus, any more than it existed among the Greeks themselves. It is difficult to see what a...

"materialism" without matter; the atomism of the ancients, even in the West, if it was "mechanistic," was not for all that "materialist," and it is fitting to leave to modern philosophy those labels which, having been invented only for it, could not truly be applied elsewhere. Moreover, although it relates to nature, the <term>Sânkhya</term> <note>One of the six orthodox schools of Indian philosophy; the word literally means "enumeration" or "calculation," referring to its systematic classification of the principles of the universe.</note>, by the way in which it envisions it, does not even risk producing a tendency toward "naturalism" like the one we observed regarding the atomistic form of the <term>Vaishêshika</term> <note>A school of philosophy focusing on the physical world and its constituent "atoms" or particularities.</note>; all the more reason why it can in no way be "evolutionist," as some have imagined, even if one takes "evolutionism" in its most general conception and without making it a synonym for a crude "transformism" <note>The biological theory that species change and evolve over time; the author considers this a physicalist reduction of metaphysical principles.</note>; this confusion of points of view is too absurd for it to be worthwhile to dwell on it further.

As for the reproach of "atheism," here is what one should think of it: the <term>Sânkhya</term> is <term>nirîshwara</term> <note>original: "nirîshwara"; meaning "without a Lord" or non-theistic in its formal structure.</note>, that is to say, it does not involve the conception of <term>Îshwara</term> <note>The "Divine Personality" or the Supreme Lord as a personal God.</note> or of the "divine personality"; but, if this conception is not found there, it is because it does not need to be there, given the point of view in question, no more than it is found in the <term>Nyâya</term> <note>The school of logic and reasoning.</note> and the <term>Vaishêshika</term>. Non-inclusion within a more or less specialized point of view only becomes negation when that point of view claims to set itself up as exclusive—that is, when it constitutes itself as a "system"—which is not the case here. And we might ask the Orientalists <note>The author uses this term for Western scholars who, in his view, often misinterpreted Eastern traditions through the lens of European academic categories.</note> if European science, in its current form, should be declared essentially "atheist" because it does not involve the idea of God within its domain—which it also does not have to do, for there is something there that is beyond its reach. Furthermore, alongside the <term>Sânkhya</term> of which we have just spoken, there exists another <term>darshana</term> <note>Literally "a view" or "point of view"; used to describe the six orthodox systems of Hindu philosophy.</note> which is sometimes regarded as a second branch of the <term>Sânkhya</term>, complementary to the previous one, and which, to distinguish it from the latter, is then described as <term>sêshwara</term> <note>original: "sêshwara"; meaning "with a Lord," acknowledging the Divine Personality.</note>, as it conversely considers the conception of <term>Îshwara</term>; this <term>darshana</term>, which will be discussed now, is the one more usually designated by the name of <term>Yoga</term>, thus identifying the doctrine with the very goal it expressly proposes.

<summary>The author argues that Western labels like "materialism" and "atheism" are misapplied to the Sânkhya school, explaining that its non-theistic structure (nirîshwara) is a matter of scope rather than a denial of the divine. He introduces Yoga as the complementary "theistic" (sêshwara) branch of Sânkhya thought.</summary>

## CHAPTER XII
## YOGA

The word *yoga* properly means "union"; let us say in passing—though the matter is of little importance—that we do not know why many European authors treat this word as feminine, when it is masculine in Sanskrit. What this term primarily designates is the effective union of the human being with the Universal; applied to a <term>darshana</term> <note>One of the six orthodox perspectives or "viewpoints" of Hindu philosophy.</note>, whose formulation into <term>sûtras</term> <note>Aphorisms or "threads" of concise teachings meant to be memorized and expanded upon by a teacher.</note> is attributed to Patanjali <note>A celebrated sage of ancient India, traditionally regarded as the author of the foundational text on Yoga.</note>, it indicates that this *darshana* has as its goal the realization of this union and provides the means to achieve it. While the *Sânkhya* is only a theoretical point of view, it is therefore realization—in the metaphysical sense we have indicated—that is essentially at issue here, regardless of what is thought by those who wish to see in it either "a philosophy," as the official Orientalists do, or even "a method for developing the latent powers of the human organism," as do certain so-called "esoterists" <note>The author is likely critiquing modern occult movements or Theosophists who reduced spiritual practices to psychological or psychic development.</note> who strive to replace the doctrine they lack with daydreams. The point of view in question refers to an entirely different order, incomparably superior to what such interpretations imply, and which equally escapes the understanding of both groups; and this is natural enough, for there is nothing analogous known in the West.

From a theoretical point of view, <term>Yoga</term> <note>The path of spiritual discipline and union.</note> completes the <term>Sânkhya</term> <note>The school of "enumeration" which provides the theoretical framework of cosmic principles.</note> by introducing the conception of <term>Îshwara</term> <note>The Supreme Lord or Universal Being; the personal aspect of the Divine.</note>, who, being identical to the Universal Being, allows for unification: first of <term>Purusha</term> <note>The spiritual principle or "True Self," which Sânkhya views as multiple in its individual manifestations.</note>, a principle that appeared multiple when considered only within particular existences, and then of *Purusha* and <term>Prakriti</term> <note>Primordial substance or Nature; the feminine, productive principle.</note>, the Universal Being situated beyond their distinction since He is their common principle. On the other hand, *Yoga* accepts the development of nature or manifestation as described by *Sânkhya*; but, taking it as the basis for a realization that must lead beyond this contingent nature, it views it in a sense in the reverse order of that development, as a path of return toward its ultimate end, which is identical to its initial principle. In relation to manifestation, the first principle is *Îshwara* or the Universal Being;

this does not mean that this principle is absolutely primary in the universal order, since we have already noted the fundamental distinction that must be made between *Ishwara* <term>Ishwara</term> <note>The "Universal Being" or the personal aspect of the divine in its capacity as creator and ruler.</note>, who is Being, and *Brahma* <term>Brahma</term> <note>The Supreme Principle, which transcends even the concept of Being (Para-Brahma).</note>, who is beyond Being; but, for manifested beings, union with the Universal Being may be regarded as constituting a necessary stage in view of union with the supreme *Brahma*. Moreover, the possibility of going beyond Being—whether theoretically or in terms of realization—presupposes the "total metaphysics" which Patanjali's *Yoga-shâstra* <note>The "Treatise on Yoga," referring to the foundational sutras attributed to the sage Patanjali.</note> does not claim to represent on its own.

Since metaphysical realization consists essentially in identification through knowledge, everything that is not knowledge itself has only the value of accessory means; thus, *Yoga* takes as its starting point and fundamental means that which is called *êkâgrya* <term>êkâgrya</term> <note>Literally "one-pointedness"; the complete focus of the mind on a single object of contemplation.</note>, that is to say, "concentration."

This concentration itself is, as Max Müller <note>Friedrich Max Müller (1823–1900), a pioneering German philologist and Orientalist who was instrumental in bringing Eastern texts to the Western academic world.</note> admits, something entirely foreign to the Western mind, which is accustomed to directing all its attention toward external things and to scattering itself within their indefinitely changing multiplicity; it has even become nearly impossible for it, and yet it is the first and most important of all the conditions for an effective realization. Concentration may take as its support—especially at the beginning—any thought whatsoever, or a symbol such as a word or an image; but subsequently these auxiliary means become useless, as do the rites and other "adjuvants" which may be employed concurrently toward the same goal. It is evident, moreover, that this goal could not be reached by the mere accessory means, extrinsic to knowledge, which we just mentioned last; but it is no less true that these means, while having nothing essential about them, are by no means negligible, for they can have a very great efficacy in facilitating realization and leading, if not to its end, at least to its preparatory stages. Such is the true reason for being of everything designated by the term *hatha-yoga* <term>hatha-yoga</term> <note>A branch of Yoga focusing on physical disciplines and the mastery of vital energies to prepare the body for higher spiritual states.</note>, which is intended, on the one hand, to destroy or rather to "transform" that which, in the human being, acts as an obstacle to their union with the Universal, and, on the other hand, to prepare this union through the assimilation of certain rhythms, principally linked to the regulation of the breath; but, for the reasons we have given previously, we shall not dwell on the modalities of realization. In any case, it must always be remembered that, of all the preliminary means, theoretical knowledge is the only one truly indispensable, and that subsequently, in realization itself, it is concentration which

Finally, action cannot have the effect of making us exit the domain of action, which is what is implied, in its true goal, by a metaphysical realization. However, one can go more or less far in this realization, and even stop at the attainment of higher, but not definitive, states; it is to these secondary degrees that the special observances prescribed by the <term>Yoga-shâstra</term> <note>The "Treatise on Yoga," specifically the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali.</note> primarily refer. The <term>Yogî</term> <note>One who has attained the state of Yoga, or perfect union with the Principle.</note>, in the proper sense of the word, is the one who has realized the perfect and final union; one cannot, therefore, without misuse, apply this name to one who simply devotes themselves to the study of <term>Yoga</term> as a <term>darshana</term> <note>A "point of view" or school of orthodox Hindu philosophy.</note>, nor even to one who effectively follows the path of realization indicated therein, without yet having reached the supreme goal toward which it tends. The state of the true <term>Yogî</term> is that of the being who has reached and possesses in full development the highest possibilities; all the secondary states to which we have alluded also belong to him at the same time and by that very fact, but "as an added bonus," one could say, and without more importance than they have, each in its rank, in the hierarchy of total existence of which they are so many constituent elements. The same can be said of the possession of certain special and more or less extraordinary powers, such as those called <term>siddhis</term> <note>Supernatural or "perfect" powers attained through spiritual practices.</note> or <term>vibhûtis</term> <note>Manifestations of power or "glories."</note>: far from being sought for themselves, these powers constitute nothing more than simple accidents, belonging to the domain of the "great illusion" <note>Original: "grande illusion," referring to Mâyâ, the cosmic illusion of the phenomenal world.</note> like everything of a phenomenal order, and the <term>Yogî</term> only exercises them in entirely exceptional circumstances; considered otherwise, they could only be obstacles to complete realization. One see how groundless is the common opinion that makes the <term>Yogî</term> a sort of magician, or even a sorcerer; in fact, those who show off certain singular faculties,

Through true metaphysical realization, freed from all contingencies and thus essentially supra-individual <note>Refers to a state that transcends the limitations of the individual human personality or ego.</note>, the *Yogî* has become identical to this "Universal Man" <term>Universal Man</term> <note>In metaphysics, this represents the complete human being who has integrated all possible states of existence, serving as the link between the Divine and the world.</note> of whom we spoke briefly before; however, to draw out the implications of this, we would have to step outside the limits we intend to impose on ourselves at present. ## CHAPTER XIII
### THE MIMANSA

The word *mîmânsâ* literally means "profound reflection"; it applies, in a general way, to the reflective study of the *Veda* <term>Veda</term> <note>The most ancient and sacred body of scriptures in Hinduism, considered divine revelation.</note>, aiming to determine the exact meaning of the *shruti* <term>shruti</term> <note>Sanskrit for "that which is heard"; it refers to the primary authoritative texts of the Hindu tradition.</note> and to draw out the consequences implied within it, whether in the practical or intellectual order. Understood this way, the *Mimansa* comprises the last two of the six *darshanas* <term>darshanas</term> <note>Points of view or orthodox schools of Indian philosophy.</note>, which are then designated as *Purva-Mimansa* and *Uttara-Mimansa*—that is, the first and the second *Mimansa*—and which relate respectively to the two orders we have just indicated. Thus, the first *Mimansa* is also called *Karma-Mimansa*, as it concerns the domain of action <note>original: "karma"</note>, while the second is called *Brahma-Mimansa*, as it essentially concerns the knowledge of *Brahma* <note>The Supreme Reality or Absolute in Hindu metaphysics.</note>; it should be noted that it is the supreme *Brahma*, and no longer *Ishwara* <note>The personal God or creative principle, as opposed to the impersonal Absolute.</note>, who is considered here, because the point of view in question is that of pure metaphysics. This second *Mimansa* is properly the *Vedanta*; and when one speaks of the *Mimansa* without an epithet, as we do in the present chapter, it is always the first *Mimansa* that is exclusively being discussed.

The exposition of this *darshana* is attributed to Jaimini, and the method followed therein is as follows: erroneous opinions on a question are first developed, then refuted, and the true solution to the question is finally given as the conclusion of this entire discussion; this method of exposition presents a remarkable analogy with that of the Scholastic doctrine in the Western Middle Ages <note>A reference to the "disputation" method used by medieval theologians like Thomas Aquinas, where objections are raised and answered to reach a logical conclusion.</note>. As for the nature of the subjects treated, it is defined at the very beginning of Jaimini's *sutras* <term>sutras</term> <note>Aphoristic strings of text that serve as a manual for a specific school of thought.</note> as a study that must establish the proofs and the reasons for being of *dharma*, in its connection with *karya* or "that which must be accomplished." We have sufficiently insisted on the notion of *dharma* <term>dharma</term> <note>Often translated as duty, law, or righteousness; it refers to the essential order of things and the actions that conform to that order.</note>, and on what must be understood by the conformity of action to *dharma*, which is precisely what is at issue here; we shall recall that the word *karma* has a double meaning: in a general sense, it is action in all its forms, which is often opposed to *jnana* or knowledge, which further corresponds to the distinction between the two...

latter *darshanas* <term>darshanas</term> <note>Traditional "points of view" or schools of Indian philosophy.</note>; in a special and technical sense, it is ritual action <note>original: "karma"</note>, as it is prescribed in the *Veda*, and this latter sense is naturally frequent in the *Mimansa*, which aims to provide the reasons for these prescriptions and to specify their scope.

The *Mimansa* begins by considering the various *pramanas* or means of proof <term>pramanas</term> <note>The valid means by which we gain accurate knowledge, such as perception or inference.</note>, which are those indicated by the logicians, plus certain other sources of knowledge with which the logicians did not need to concern themselves in their particular field; one could, moreover, easily reconcile the different classifications of these *pramanas* by viewing them simply as more or less developed and complete, for they are in no way contradictory. A distinction is then made between several kinds of prescriptions or injunctions, the most general division being that of the direct injunction and the indirect injunction; the portion of the *Veda* containing precepts is called *brahmana* <term>brahmana</term> <note>The section of the Vedas providing instructions for rituals.</note>, as opposed to the *mantra* or ritual formula, and everything contained in the Vedic texts is either *mantra* or *brahmana*. Furthermore, there are not only precepts in the *brahmana*, since the *Upanishads* <term>Upanishads</term> <note>The final, philosophical parts of the Vedas focusing on the nature of reality and the soul.</note>, which are purely doctrinal and form the foundation of the *Vedanta*, fall into this category; but the practical *brahmana*, to which the *Mimansa* primarily attaches itself, is that which indicates the manner of performing rites, the conditions for this performance, the modalities applicable to various circumstances, and which explains the meaning of the symbolic elements entering into these rites and the *mantras* that should be employed for each specific case. 

Regarding the nature and efficacy of the *mantra*, as well as, more generally, regarding the traditional authority of the *Veda* and its "non-human" origin <note>original: "non-humaine"; this refers to the concept of *apaurusheya*, meaning that the scriptures are not the product of human authors but are eternal truths.</note>, the *Mimansa* develops the theory of the perpetuity of sound to which we alluded previously, and, more precisely, that of the original and perpetual association of articulated sound with the sense of hearing, which makes language something quite different from a more or less arbitrary convention. One also finds there a theory of the infallibility of traditional doctrine, an infallibility which must be conceived as inherent in the doctrine itself, and which, consequently, belongs in no way to human individuals; the latter only participate in it to the extent that they effectively know the doctrine and interpret it exactly, and even then, this infallibility should not be attributed to individuals as such, but always to the doctrine expressed through them. This is why only those who know the *Veda* in its entirety are qualified to compose true traditional writings, the authority of which is a participation in that of the

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the Mimansa school, specifically discussing its relationship to Vedic authority and the auxiliary sciences known as the Vedangas. primordial tradition, from which it is derived and upon which it has its exclusive foundation, without the individuality of the human author playing the slightest part: this distinction between fundamental authority and derived authority in the traditional order is that of *shruti* <term>shruti</term> <note>Sanskrit for "that which is heard"; refers to the primary, revealed tradition of the Vedas.</note> and *smriti* <term>smriti</term> <note>Sanskrit for "that which is remembered"; refers to traditional knowledge derived from human sages based on the primary revelation.</note>, which we have already indicated regarding the “Laws of *Manu*” <term>Manu</term> <note>The archetypal lawgiver in Hindu tradition, credited with the foundational social and moral code.</note>. The conception of infallibility as inherent to the doctrine alone is, moreover, common to both Hindus and Muslims; it is also, at its core, the same concept that Catholicism applies specifically to the religious point of view, for “papal infallibility” <note>original: "l’infaillibilité pontificale"</note>, if understood correctly in its principle, appears as essentially attached to a function—which is the authorized interpretation of the doctrine—and not to an individual person, who is never infallible outside the exercise of this function whose conditions are rigorously determined.

By reason of the nature of the *Mimansa* <term>Mimansa</term> <note>One of the six orthodox schools of Indian philosophy, specializing in the logic of ritual and Vedic interpretation.</note>, it is to this *darshana* <term>darshana</term> <note>A "point of view" or system of philosophy.</note> that the *Vedangas* <term>Vedangas</term> <note>The "limbs" of the Veda; six auxiliary sciences used to interpret and perform Vedic rites correctly.</note> relate most directly, those auxiliary sciences of the *Veda* that we defined earlier; one need only refer back to those definitions to realize the close link they share with the current subject. Thus, the *Mimansa* insists on the importance that exact spelling and correct pronunciation—as taught by *shiksha* <term>shiksha</term> <note>The science of phonetics and phonology.</note>—have for the understanding of the texts, and it distinguishes between different classes of *mantras* <term>mantras</term> <note>Sacred ritual formulas or chants.</note> according to their specific rhythms, which falls under *chhandas* <term>chhandas</term> <note>The science of prosody and poetic meter.</note>. On the other hand, one encounters considerations relating to *vyakarana* <term>vyakarana</term> <note>The science of grammar.</note>, that is to say, grammatical matters, such as the distinction between the regular meaning of words and their dialectal or "barbaric" <note>Referring to non-Sanskrit or non-standard linguistic influences.</note> meanings, as well as remarks on certain particular forms used in the *Veda* and on terms that have a sense there different from their usual meaning; to these must be added, on many occasions, the etymological and symbolic interpretations which are the subject of *nirukta* <term>nirukta</term> <note>The science of etymology and linguistic explanation.</note>. Finally, knowledge of *jyotisha* <term>jyotisha</term> <note>The science of astronomy and astrology.</note> is necessary to determine the time when rites must be performed, and as for *kalpa* <term>kalpa</term> <note>The science of ritual procedure and ceremony.</note>, we have seen that it summarizes the prescriptions concerning their actual performance. Furthermore, the *Mimansa* treats a great number of questions regarding jurisprudence, and this should not be surprising, since in Hindu civilization, all legislation is essentially traditional; one can notice, moreover, a certain analogy in the way legal debates on one hand, and the discussions of the *Mimansa* on the other, are conducted, and there is even an identity in the terms used to designate the successive phases of both. This resemblance is certainly not accidental, but it should not be seen as anything more than what it really is: a sign of the application of the same spirit to

Therefore, for an action, which in itself is only a momentary modification, to be able to have future and more or less distant results, it must have, at the very moment it is accomplished, an effect that is not presently perceptible, but which, by subsisting in a permanent way—at least relatively—will later produce, in its turn, the perceptible result. It is this imperceptible effect, potential in a sense, which is called *apûrva* <note>Sanskrit: "unprecedented" or "unseen." In the Mimansa school of Indian philosophy, this refers to the invisible latent power created by a ritual or action that bridges the time gap between the act and its eventual fruit.</note>, because it is superadded and not prior to the action; it can be regarded either as a posterior state of the action itself, or as an antecedent state of the result, as the effect must always be virtually contained within its cause, from which it could not otherwise proceed. Moreover, even in cases where a certain result appears to follow the action immediately in time, the intermediate existence of an *apûrva* is no less necessary, since there is still succession and not perfect simultaneity, and because the action, in itself, is always separated from its result.

In this way, action escapes instantaneity, and even, to a certain extent, the limitations of the temporal condition; indeed, the *apûrva*, the seed of all its future consequences, not being in the domain of corporeal and sensible manifestation, is outside of ordinary time, but not outside of all duration, for it still belongs to the order of contingencies. Now, the *apûrva* can, on one hand, remain attached to the being who performed the action, as henceforth being a constituent element of their individuality considered in its incorporeal part, where it will persist as long as that part itself endures; and, on the other hand, it can go beyond the bounds of this individuality to enter the domain of the potential energies of the cosmic order. In this second part, if one represents it—by an image that is undoubtedly imperfect—as a vibration emitted at a certain point, this vibration, after propagating to the confines of the domain it can reach, will return in the opposite direction to its starting point, and this, as causality requires, in the form of a reaction of the same nature as the initial action.

This is very precisely what Taoism, for its part, designates as "concordant actions and reactions": every action, like every manifestation more generally, being a rupture of equilibrium—as we said regarding the three *gunas* <note>Sanskrit: the three fundamental qualities of nature: *Sattva* (harmony), *Rajas* (activity), and *Tamas* (inertia). Their imbalance leads to the differentiation of the world.</note>—the corresponding reaction is necessary to re-establish this equilibrium, as the sum of all differentiations must always finally be equivalent to total undifferentiation. This point, where the human order and the cosmic order meet, completes the idea one can form of the relationships between *karma* <note>Sanskrit: "action" or "deed"; the law of causal necessity governing the consequences of actions.</note> and *dharma* <note>Sanskrit: "law," "order," or "essential nature"; the principle that sustains the universe.</note>; and it must be added immediately that the reaction, being a perfectly natural consequence of the action, is in no way a "sanction" in the sense

If we have dwelt at some length on this explanation, it is not simply because it provides an interesting example of a certain kind of Eastern theory, nor even because we will have the opportunity later to point out a false interpretation of it that has been given in the West; it is also, and above all, because what is at issue here has a most considerable effective scope, even practically—although, on this last point, it is appropriate to maintain a certain reserve, and it is better to be satisfied with giving very general indications, as we are doing here, leaving it to each person to draw out developments and conclusions in conformity with their own faculties and personal tendencies.

## CHAPTER XIV
### THE VEDANTA

With *Vedanta*, we are, as we have already said, in the realm of pure metaphysics; it is therefore superfluous to repeat that it is neither a philosophy nor a religion, even though Orientalists inevitably insist on seeing it as one or the other, or even, like Schopenhauer, as both at once. The name of this final *darshana* <note>Sanskrit: "point of view" or "perspective." In the context of Indian tradition, it refers to one of the six orthodox schools of thought, though they are considered complementary perspectives rather than competing philosophies.</note> etymologically means the "end of the *Veda*," and the word "end" must be understood here in the double sense, which it also possesses in English, of conclusion and of goal; indeed, the *Upanishads*, upon which it is essentially based, form the final part of the Vedic texts, and what is taught therein—to the extent that it can be—is the final and supreme goal of the whole of traditional knowledge, stripped of all the more or less particular and contingent applications to which it may give rise in various orders. The very designation of the *Upanishads* indicates that they are intended to destroy ignorance, the root of the illusion that imprisons the being within the bonds of conditioned existence, and that they achieve this effect by providing the means to approach the knowledge of *Brahma* <note>The Supreme Reality or the Absolute in Hindu metaphysics; it is the unchanging reality amidst and beyond the world.</note>; if it is only a matter of approaching this knowledge, it is because, being strictly incommunicable in its essence, it can only be effectively reached through strictly personal work, for which no external teaching, however lofty or profound it may be, has the power to substitute. The interpretation we have just given is the one upon which all qualified Hindus agree; it would obviously be ridiculous to prefer the unauthoritative conjecture of certain European authors, who claim that the *Upanishad* is the knowledge obtained by "sitting at the feet" of a preceptor; moreover, Max Müller <note>[17]</note>, while accepting this latter meaning, is forced to recognize that it indicates nothing truly characteristic, and that it would suit any of the other portions of the *Veda* just as well, since oral teaching is their common mode of regular transmission.

The incommunicable character of total and definitive knowledge arises from

Indeed, any symbolism can always suggest at least possibilities of conception, even if they cannot be entirely expressed, and this is without mentioning certain modes of transmission taking place outside and beyond all formal representation—modes the very idea of which must seem too implausible to a Westerner for it to be useful or simply possible to dwell upon them. On the other hand, it is true that comprehension—even theoretical, and starting from its most elementary levels—presupposes an indispensable personal effort and is conditioned by the specific receptive aptitudes of the one to whom a teaching is communicated; it is only too obvious that a teacher, however excellent, cannot understand on behalf of his student, and that it belongs exclusively to the student to assimilate what is placed within his reach. If this is so, it is because all true and truly assimilated knowledge is already in itself—not yet an effective realization, certainly, but at least a virtual realization, if one may join these two words which, here, contradict each other only in appearance; otherwise, one could not say with <term>Aristotle</term><note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE) was a foundational Greek philosopher. What can be taught—and even then incompletely—are only more or less indirect and mediated means of metaphysical realization, as we indicated regarding <term>Yoga</term><note>Yoga: Derived from the Sanskrit root *yuj* (to join); in this context, it refers to the metaphysical union of the individual with the Universal Principle, and the methods used to achieve it.</note>, and the first of all these means, the most indispensable, and even the only one absolutely indispensable, is theoretical knowledge itself. However, it should be added that, in total metaphysics, theory and realization are never completely separated; one can observe this at every moment in the <term>Upanishads</term><note>The Upanishads are the concluding portion of the Vedas, containing the core philosophical and metaphysical teachings of the Hindu tradition.</note>, where it is often very difficult to distinguish what relates respectively to one and the other, and where, to tell the truth,

the same things relate to both, depending on the way in which they are viewed. In a doctrine that is metaphysically complete, the perspective of realization <note>The actualization of spiritual knowledge within oneself</note> reacts upon the very exposition of the theory, which assumes it at least implicitly and can never be independent of it; for theory, having in itself only a preparatory value, must be subordinate to realization, just as the means is subordinate to the end for which it is established.

All these considerations are necessary to understand the point of view of <term>Vedanta</term><note>A major school of Indian philosophy based on the final portion of the Vedas</note>, or, better yet, its spirit, since the metaphysical point of view—not being any one "special" point of view—can only be called such in a purely analogical sense. Moreover, these considerations apply similarly to any other form that traditional metaphysics may take in other civilizations; for metaphysics, for the reasons we have already specified, is essentially one and cannot be otherwise. One cannot emphasize enough the fact that it is the <term>Upanishads</term><note>The philosophical and mystical scriptures that form the core of the Vedanta</note> which, being an integral part of the <term>Veda</term><note>The most ancient and sacred body of Hindu knowledge and scripture</note>, represent the primordial and fundamental tradition here. The Vedanta, as it emerges expressly from them, was synthetically coordinated—which does not mean "systematized"—in the <term>Brahma-sutras</term><note>A foundational text attributed to Badarayana that summarizes the teachings of the Upanishads</note>, the composition of which is attributed to <term>Badarayana</term>; he, moreover, is identified with <term>Vyasa</term><note>A legendary figure in Indian tradition; the name "Vyasa" literally means "the compiler" or "arranger," signifying a specific intellectual function of organizing traditional knowledge</note>, which is particularly significant for anyone who knows the intellectual function designated by this name. The *Brahma-sutras*, the text of which is extremely concise, have given rise to numerous commentaries, among which those of <term>Shankaracharya</term> and <term>Ramanuja</term> are by far the most important. Both of these commentaries are strictly orthodox, despite their apparent divergences, which are at root only differences of adaptation: that of Shankaracharya represents more specifically the <term>Shaivite</term><note>Centered on the principle of Shiva, representing the transformative or destructive aspect of the Divine</note> tendency, and that of Ramanuja the <term>Vaishnavite</term><note>Centered on the principle of Vishnu, representing the preservative aspect of the Divine</note> tendency. The general indications we have given in this regard will exempt us from developing this distinction for the moment, as it only concerns different paths tending toward an identical goal.

The *Vedanta*, precisely because it is purely metaphysical, presents itself essentially as *advaita-vada* or the "doctrine of non-duality" <note>original: "adwaita-vâda"</note>; we have explained the meaning of this expression by differentiating metaphysical thought from philosophical thought. To clarify its scope as much as possible, we will now say that, while "Being" is "one," the supreme Principle, designated as <term>Brahma</term><note>The Absolute or Ultimate Reality in Hindu metaphysics</note>, can only be said to be "without duality" because it is beyond all determination, even that of "Being," which is the first of all determinations.
