...encompassing all things, it cannot be characterized by any positive attribution: such is the requirement of its infinity, which is necessarily the absolute totality, containing within itself all possibilities. There can, therefore, be nothing that is truly outside of *Brahma*, for such a supposition would be equivalent to limiting it; as an immediate consequence, the world—taking this word in its broadest possible sense as the sum of universal manifestation—is not distinct from *Brahma*, or, at least, is only distinguished from it in an illusory mode. However, on the other hand, *Brahma* is absolutely distinct from the world, since one cannot apply to it any of the determinative attributes that belong to the world, the entirety of universal manifestation being rigorously naught in the face of its infinity; and it will be noted that this non-reciprocal relationship <note>The idea that while the world depends on the Absolute, the Absolute does not depend on the world</note> entails the formal condemnation of “pantheism,” as well as all “immanentism” <note>The belief that the divine is solely present in the material world rather than transcending it</note>. Furthermore, “pantheism,” if one wishes to keep a sufficiently precise and reasonable meaning for this term, is inseparable from “naturalism,” which is to say that it is clearly anti-metaphysical; it is therefore absurd to see “pantheism” in <term>Vedanta</term>, and yet this idea, as absurd as it may be, is the one most commonly held by Westerners, even by specialists: this is certainly enough to give Orientals, who know what “pantheism” actually is, a high opinion of the value of European science and the insight of its representatives!

It is evident that we cannot give even a brief overview of the doctrine as a whole; certain questions treated therein—such as, for example, the constitution of the human being viewed metaphysically—may be the subject of specific studies. We shall pause only on one point, concerning the supreme goal, which is called *moksha* or *mukti*, that is to say, “deliverance,” because the being who reaches it is freed from the bonds of conditioned existence, in whatever state or mode it may be, through perfect identification with the Universal: this is the realization of what Islamic esotericism <note>Sufism or 'Tasawwuf'</note> calls the “Supreme Identity,” and it is through this, and this alone, that a man becomes a *Yogi* in the true sense of the word. The state of the *Yogi* is therefore not the analogue of any special state, but it contains all possible states just as the principle contains all its consequences; the one who has reached it is also called *jivan-mukta*, that is to say, “delivered in life,” as opposed to the *videha-mukta* or “delivered beyond form” <note>Literally "without a body"</note>, an expression designating the being for whom realization does not occur—or rather, from the virtual state it was in, only becomes effective—after death or the dissolution of the composite being...

Moreover, in one case as in the other, the being is definitively freed from individual conditions, or from everything whose totality is called **name** and **form** <note>original: *nâma* and *rûpa*—the two components that constitute individual identity in Hindu philosophy</note>, and even from the conditions of all manifestation; it escapes the indefinite causal chain of actions and reactions, which does not happen in the simple passage to another individual state, even one occupying a higher rank than the human state in the hierarchy of degrees of existence. It is manifest, on the other hand, that action can only have consequences in the domain of action, and that its effectiveness stops precisely where its influence ends; action cannot, therefore, have the effect of liberating one from action and obtaining "deliverance"; thus, any action, whatever it may be, can at most lead only to partial realizations, corresponding to certain higher states, but still determined and conditioned. <term>Shankarâchârya <note>Adi Shankara (c. 8th century), one of the most important philosophers in the Vedanta tradition, known for his teachings on non-dualism.</note></term> expressly declares that “there is no other means of obtaining complete and final ‘deliverance’ than knowledge; action, which is not opposed to ignorance, cannot remove it, while knowledge dissipates ignorance as light dissipates darkness [18]”; and, ignorance being the root and the cause of all limitation, when it has disappeared, the individuality, which is characterized by its limitations, disappears by that very fact. This “transformation,” in the etymological sense of “passing beyond form,” changes nothing, moreover, in appearances; in the case of the **one delivered while living** <note>original: *jîvan-mukta*—someone who has achieved spiritual liberation while still inhabiting a physical body</note>, the individual appearance naturally persists without any external change, but it no longer affects the being who is clothed in it, since the latter effectively knows that it is only illusory; however, of course, knowing this effectively is quite another thing from having a purely theoretical conception of it. Following the passage we have just cited, Shankarâchârya describes the state of the **Yogi** <note>original: *Yogî*—here referring to one who has achieved union with the Absolute</note> to the extent, though very limited, that words can express or rather indicate it; these considerations form the true conclusion of the study of the nature of the human being, to which we have alluded, by showing, as the supreme and final goal of metaphysical knowledge, the highest possibilities that this being is capable of reaching.

# CHAPTER XV
## ADDITIONAL REMARKS ON THE DOCTRINE AS A WHOLE

In this presentation, which we intended to be as synthetic as possible, we have constantly tried to show—alongside the distinctive characteristics of each <term>darshana <note>original: "darshana"—a Sanskrit term meaning "viewpoint" or "perspective," referring here to the six orthodox systems of Hindu philosophy.</note></term>—how each one relates to metaphysics. Metaphysics is the common center from which all branches of the doctrine develop in various directions. This approach provided us with an opportunity to clarify several important points regarding the overall conception of this doctrine. In this regard, it must be understood that while the <term>Vedanta <note>original: "Vêdânta"—literally the "end" or "culmination" of the Vedas, representing the highest level of knowledge.</note></term> is counted as the last of the *darshanas* because it represents the completion of all knowledge, it is nonetheless, in its essence, the principle from which everything else derives; the other branches are merely its specification or application.

If a field of knowledge did not depend on metaphysics in this way, it would literally lack a principle and, consequently, could not possess any traditional character. This is the fundamental difference between scientific knowledge as understood in the West and that which, in India, corresponds to it most closely. It is clear that the viewpoint of cosmology is not equivalent to that of modern physics, and even the viewpoint of traditional logic is not the same as that of philosophical logic as envisioned, for example, by <term>Stuart Mill <note>John Stuart Mill (1806–1873), an English philosopher famous for his works on logic and empiricism.</note></term>; we have already noted these distinctions. 

Cosmology, even within the limits of the <term>Vaishêshika <note>original: "Vaishêshika"—one of the six orthodox schools, which focuses on the classification of the natural world and the constituent elements of reality.</note></term>, is not an experimental science like modern physics. Because of its connection to principles, it is—like the other doctrinal branches—far more deductive than inductive. <term>Cartesian physics <note>The scientific theories of René Descartes (1596–1650), which sought to explain the natural world through mechanical principles and mathematics.</note></term>, it is true, was also deductive, but it suffered from the great flaw of being based, in terms of principles, on nothing more than a simple philosophical hypothesis, which led to its failure.

The difference in method we have just pointed out reflects a profound difference in conception. This exists even for sciences that are truly experimental, but which, despite this, remain much more deductive

...than they are in the West, they escape all empiricism <note>empirical: knowledge based solely on observation or experience rather than on underlying principles or theory.</note>; it is only under these conditions that these sciences have a title to be regarded as traditional knowledge, even if of secondary importance and of an inferior order. Here, we are thinking especially of medicine viewed as an <term>Upaveda <note>original: "Upavêda"—a term meaning "sub-Vedas" or "secondary knowledge," referring here to the traditional medical system known as Ayurveda.</note></term>; and what we say of it applies equally to the traditional medicine of the Far East. Without losing anything of its practical character, this medicine is something much more extensive than what we are accustomed to designating by this name; besides pathology and therapeutics, it includes, notably, many considerations that would be classified in the West as physiology or even psychology, but which, naturally, are treated in an entirely different manner. The results that such a science achieves in application can, in many cases, seem extraordinary to those who form only an overly inaccurate idea of it; we believe, moreover, that it is extremely difficult for a Westerner to arrive at a sufficient knowledge in this kind of study, where methods of investigation are employed that are completely different from those to which he is accustomed.

We have just said that practical knowledge, even when it is linked to tradition and has its source there, is nonetheless only inferior knowledge; its derivation determines its subordination, which is strictly logical. Furthermore, the Easterners, who, by temperament and deep conviction, care very little for immediate applications, have never dreamed of introducing into the order of pure knowledge any concern for material or sentimental interest—the only element capable of altering this natural and normal hierarchy of knowledge. This same cause of intellectual disorder is also what, by becoming generalized in the mentality of a race or an era, primarily brings about the forgetting of pure metaphysics, for which it illegitimately substitutes more or less specialized viewpoints, while at the same time giving birth to sciences that can claim no traditional principle. These sciences are legitimate as long as they maintain themselves within just limits, but they must not be taken for anything other than what they are, that is to say, analytical, fragmentary, and relative knowledge; and thus, by radically separating itself from metaphysics, with which its own viewpoint indeed allows no relationship, Western science necessarily lost in scope what it gained in independence, and its development toward practical applications was compensated by an inevitable speculative <note>speculative: relating to pure theory or deep intellectual contemplation rather than practical application.</note> diminishment.

<summary>This page explains that traditional sciences like medicine (Upaveda) are superior to modern Western sciences because they are rooted in metaphysical principles rather than mere observation. It argues that while Western science excels in practical application, it has lost intellectual depth by separating itself from these traditional foundations.</summary>

<keywords>Upaveda, Traditional Medicine, Far East, Metaphysics, Western Science, Hierarchy of Knowledge, Empiricism, Speculative Knowledge</keywords>

These few observations complete everything we have already said regarding the profound separation between the respective viewpoints of the East <note>In this context, "the East" refers to traditional Eastern civilizations (like those of India, China, and Islam) which the author views as having maintained a link to ancient, universal truths.</note> and the West: in the East, tradition is truly the entirety of civilization, since it encompasses—through its consequences—the entire cycle of true knowledge, regardless of what order they relate to, as well as the whole of social institutions. Everything is included there in seed form from the beginning, by the very fact that tradition establishes the universal principles from which all things derive, along with their laws and conditions. Any necessary adaptation to a given era can only consist of an adequate development—following a strictly deductive and analogical <note>analogical: a method of reasoning that finds correspondences between different levels of reality, such as the relationship between the human body and the cosmos.</note> spirit—of the solutions and clarifications that are most specifically suited to the mentality of that era. 

It is understandable that, under these conditions, the influence of tradition has a force from which one cannot escape, and that any schism, whenever one occurs, leads immediately to the constitution of a pseudo-tradition <note>pseudo-tradition: a system that mimics the forms of a true tradition but lacks its genuine spiritual or metaphysical foundation.</note>; as for openly and definitively breaking all traditional ties, no individual has the desire, nor even the possibility. This also allows us to understand the nature and characteristics of the teaching through which the principles are transmitted, along with the set of disciplines suited to assimilating and integrating all things into the intellectuality <note>intellectualité: refers here to the overarching spiritual and mental framework that defines a civilization's way of thinking.</note> of a civilization.

<summary>The author explains how Eastern civilizations are entirely defined by tradition, which provides a universal framework for all knowledge and social structures. He argues that because tradition is all-encompassing, it is impossible for individuals in these societies to fully break away from it, with any deviations merely resulting in "pseudo-traditions."</summary>

# CHAPTER XVI
## TRADITIONAL TEACHING

We have said that the upper caste, that of the *Brâhmanas* <term>Brâhmanas: the priestly and scholarly caste in Hindu society, traditionally responsible for the preservation and transmission of sacred knowledge</term>, has the essential function of conserving and transmitting the traditional doctrine; this is its true reason for being, since it is upon this doctrine that the entire social order rests, which could find no other principles without which nothing is stable or lasting. Where tradition is everything, those who are its custodians must logically be everything; or at least—as the diversity of functions necessary for the social organism entails an incompatibility between them and requires their fulfillment by different individuals—these individuals all essentially depend on the holders of tradition. For if they did not effectively participate in the tradition, they could not effectively participate in collective life: this is the true and complete meaning of the spiritual and intellectual authority belonging to the *Brâhmanas*. This also explains, at the same time, the profound and unfailing attachment that unites the disciple to the master, not only in India but throughout the East <note>In this context, the "East" refers to traditional civilizations such as those of India, China, and the Islamic world.</note>, the likes of which one would seek in vain in the modern West. Indeed, the function of the instructor is truly a "spiritual paternity," and this is why the ritual and symbolic act by which it begins is a "second birth" <note>In the Hindu tradition, this refers to the *Upanayana* or initiation ceremony, after which a student is considered 'twice-born' (*dvija*).</note> for the one admitted to receive the teaching through regular transmission. It is this idea of "spiritual paternity" that is very accurately expressed by the word *guru* <note>original: "guru"</note>, which designates the instructor among the Hindus and also carries the meaning of "ancestor"; it is to this same idea that the word *sheikh* <note>original: "sheikh"</note> alludes among the Arabs, which, with the literal meaning of "old man," has an identical usage. In China, the dominant conception of the "solidarity of the race" gives the corresponding thought a different nuance, assimilating the role of the instructor to that of an "elder brother," the natural guide and support for those who follow him in the traditional way, and who will only become an "ancestor" after his death; but the expression "to be born to knowledge" is nonetheless of common use there, as it is everywhere else.

First of all, it is permissible to doubt the value and scope of an education distributed indistinctly, and in an identical form, to individuals who are most unequally gifted, and most different in aptitude and temperament, as is currently practiced among all European peoples. This system of instruction, certainly the most imperfect of all, is required by the **egalitarian** <term>egalitarian: the belief that all people are equal and should have the same rights; here, the author criticizes the forced application of this to intellectual capacities</term> mania which has destroyed not only the true notion, but even the more or less vague feeling of **hierarchy**. And yet, for people to whom "facts" must serve as the only criterion, according to the spirit of modern **experimental science**, would there be—if they were not so completely blinded by their sentimental prejudices—a fact more apparent than that of **natural inequalities**, in both the intellectual and physical orders? Next, there is another reason why the Oriental, who has not the slightest spirit of

## CHAPTER ONE
### OFFICIAL ORIENTALISM

Of **official orientalism** <term>Official Orientalism: the academic and institutionalized study of Eastern cultures, languages, and history by Western university scholars</term>, we will say only a little here, because we have already, on many occasions, pointed out the insufficiency of its methods and the falsity of its conclusions: if we have thus had it almost constantly in view, while we have hardly concerned ourselves with other Western interpretations, it is because it presents itself at least with an appearance of seriousness that the latter do not have, which obliges us to make a distinction that is to its advantage. We do not intend in any way to contest the good faith of the orientalists, which is generally beyond doubt, nor the reality of their specialized **scholarship** <term>Scholarship: translating the French *érudition*, referring here to the mastery of historical facts and linguistics as opposed to metaphysical understanding</term>; what we contest is their competence for everything that goes beyond the domain of simple scholarship. Moreover, tribute must be paid to the very laudable modesty with which some among them, being aware of the limits of their true competence, refuse to engage in a work of interpreting the doctrines; but, unfortunately, those are only a minority, and the large number is made up of those who, taking scholarship as an end in itself, as we said at the beginning, very sincerely believe that their linguistic and historical studies give them the right to speak of all sorts of things.

It is toward these latter that we think one cannot be too severe, as to the methods they employ and the results they obtain, while respecting, of course, the individuals who may deserve it in all respects, being very little responsible for their bias and their illusions. **Exclusivism** is a natural consequence of narrowness of views, of what we have called **"intellectual myopia"** <note>The author uses this metaphor to describe the specialized scholar's inability to see the broader "intellectual" or metaphysical significance of the texts they study, focusing only on the "physical" or material details of the language.</note>, and this mental defect does not seem any more curable than physical myopia; moreover, it is, like the latter, a deformation produced by the effect of certain habits that lead to it imperceptibly and without one noticing it, although one must no doubt be predisposed to it. Under these conditions, there is no reason to be surprised by the hostility that the generality of orientalists show toward those who do not submit to their methods and who do not adopt their conclusions; this is only a particular case of the consequences that the abuse <note>The text ends here, suggesting the "abuse" of the scholarly method or specialization will be elaborated on the next page.</note>

They cause this harm by obstructing all other paths that could lead much further for those capable of following them. Given the prejudices of the modern West, it is enough to turn almost everyone away from these paths—even those who might be tempted to embark on them—to solemnly declare that such a pursuit "is not scientific," simply because it does not conform to the methods and theories officially accepted and taught in the Universities. When it comes to defending oneself against any danger, one generally does not waste time looking for who is responsible; if, therefore, certain opinions are intellectually dangerous—and we believe that to be the case here—one must strive to destroy them without worrying about those who issued or defend them, whose honorability is not at all in question. Considerations of individuals, which are very little things compared to ideas, should not legitimately prevent us from combating theories that stand in the way of certain realizations. Moreover, as these realizations (to which we shall return in our conclusion) are not immediately possible, and as we are forbidden any concern for propaganda, the most effective way to combat the theories in question is not to argue indefinitely on the ground where they have placed themselves, but to reveal the reasons for their falsity while restoring the pure and simple truth, which alone essentially matters to those who can understand it.

This is where the great difference lies, upon which no agreement is possible with the specialists of scholarship <term>Scholarship: translating the French *érudition*, referring here to the academic accumulation of facts, dates, and linguistic data</term>: when we speak of truth, we do not simply mean a truth of fact—which undoubtedly has its importance, but a secondary and contingent one; what interests us in a doctrine is the truth, in the absolute sense of the word, of what is expressed therein. Conversely, those who take the viewpoint of scholarship do not concern themselves at all with the truth of ideas; at heart, they do not know what truth is, nor even if it exists, and they do not ask themselves the question. Truth is nothing to them, except in the very special case where it concerns historical truth exclusively. The same tendency asserts itself similarly among historians of philosophy: what interests them is not...

In the eyes of the partisans of this method, the first condition for being able to study metaphysical doctrines is obviously *not* to be a metaphysician; likewise, those who apply it to the "science of religions" claim more or less openly that one is disqualified from such study by the mere fact of belonging to any religion whatsoever. One might as well proclaim the exclusive competence, in any branch of knowledge, of those who have only an external and superficial knowledge of it—the very kind that scholarship alone is sufficient to give—and this is undoubtedly why, in the matter of Eastern doctrines, the opinion of Easterners is deemed null and void. There is, above all, an instinctive fear here of everything that exceeds mere scholarship and risks showing how mediocre and childish it is at its core; but this fear is reinforced by its alignment with the much more conscious interest attached to maintaining the *de facto* <note>Latin: "in fact" or "in practice."</note> monopoly established for their own benefit by the representatives of "official science" in all fields, and by the orientalists perhaps even more completely than others. ## CHAPTER II
### THE SCIENCE OF RELIGIONS

It is appropriate to say a few words here regarding what is called the "science of religions," because the field in question owes its origin precisely to <term>Indianist studies: the academic study of the history, languages, and cultures of the Indian subcontinent</term>; this immediately shows that the word "religion" is not used here in the exact sense we have previously recognized. Indeed, Burnouf <note>Eugène Burnouf (1801–1852) was an influential French scholar who helped establish Indian studies in Europe.</note>, who seems to have been the first to give this science—or so-called science—its name, neglects to include morality among the constituent elements of religion, which he thus reduces to two: doctrine and ritual. This is what allows him to include things that are in no way related to the religious point of view, for he recognizes, at least rightly so, that there is no morality in the *Veda* <note>The *Vedas* are the oldest sacred scriptures of Hinduism; the author argues they are metaphysical rather than moralistic.</note>. Such is the fundamental confusion found at the starting point of the "science of religions," which claims to unite under this same name all traditional doctrines, whatever their nature might actually be. But many other confusions have been added to these, especially since more recent scholarship has introduced into this field its formidable apparatus of exegesis, "textual criticism," and "hyper-criticism," which are better suited to impressing the naive than to leading to serious conclusions.

The so-called "science of religions" rests entirely on several postulates that are essentially preconceived ideas: for instance, it is accepted as fact that every doctrine must have begun with "naturalism" <note>Naturalism in this context is the theory that ancient religions began as a primitive personification of natural forces like thunder or rain.</note>, whereas we, on the other contrary, see in this only a deviation which, wherever it occurred, was in opposition to primordial and regular traditions. By dint of torturing texts they do not understand, these scholars always end up extracting some interpretation that conforms to this "naturalistic" spirit. This is how the entire theory of "myths" was elaborated, particularly that of the "solar myth"—the most famous of all—of which one of the main proponents was Max Müller <note>Friedrich Max Müller (1823–1900) was a German-born scholar who popularized the idea that myths were a "disease of language" and primarily about the sun.</note>, whom we have already had occasion to mention several times because he is very representative of the mentality of the <term>Orientalists: Western scholars who study the languages and civilizations of the East</term>. This theory of the "solar myth" is nothing other than the <term>astromythological: the interpretation of myths as allegories for astronomical phenomena</term> theory put forward and supported in France toward the end

<summary>The author critiques the "science of religions," arguing it is based on the false premise that all ancient traditions are religions and incorrectly interprets them through the lens of "naturalism" and "solar myths."</summary>
<keywords>science of religions, Eugène Burnouf, Veda, naturalism, solar myth, Max Müller, Orientalists, astromythology, textual criticism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the critique of the "science of religions," focusing on how scholars misinterpret symbolism as mere nature-worship and use historical methods to undermine religious traditions.</meta>

of the 18th century, by Dupuis and Volney <meta>[19]</meta>. <note>Charles-François Dupuis (1742–1809) and Constantin-François Volney (1757–1820) were French Enlightenment thinkers who pioneered the "astro-mythological" theory, claiming religions originated from observations of the stars and sun.</note> We know the application that was made of this conception to Christianity as to all other doctrines, and we have already signaled the confusion that it essentially implies: as soon as one notices in **symbolism** a correspondence with certain astronomical phenomena, one hastens to conclude that there is nothing there but a representation of these phenomena, whereas they themselves, in reality, are symbols of something that is of a completely different order, and the observed correspondence is only an application of the **analogy** which harmoniously links all the degrees of being. 

Under these conditions, it is not very difficult to find "<term>naturalism: the belief that everything arises from natural properties and causes, and supernatural or spiritual explanations are excluded or discounted</term>" everywhere, and it would even be surprising if one did not find it, given that the symbol—which necessarily belongs to the natural order—is taken for what it represents. The error is, at heart, the same as that of the "<term>nominalists: philosophers who argue that universal concepts or abstract objects do not exist, and that only individual physical things are real, while "names" are just labels</term>" who confuse the idea with the word that serves to express it; and it is in this way that modern scholars, encouraged moreover by the prejudice that leads them to imagine all civilizations as built upon the Greco-Roman type, manufacture "myths" themselves through a misunderstanding of symbols, which is the only way such myths can truly take birth.

One must understand why we qualify a study of this kind as a "so-called science," and why it is quite impossible for us to take it seriously; and it must also be added that, while affecting to give itself an air of disinterested impartiality, and even displaying the foolish pretension of "dominating all doctrines" <meta>[20]</meta>—which exceeds all just measure in this sense—this "**science of religions**" is quite simply, most of the time, a vulgar instrument of polemic in the hands of people whose true intention is to use it against religion, understood this time in its proper and habitual sense. 

This use of erudition in a negative and dissolving spirit is natural to the fanatics of the "**historical method**"; it is the very spirit of this method, essentially **anti-traditional**, at least as soon as it is taken out of its legitimate domain; and this is why all those who attach any real value to the religious point of view are rejected here as incompetent. Yet, among the specialists of the "science of religions," there are some who, in appearance at least, do not go so far: these are those who belong to the trend of "**Liberal Protestantism**"; <note>A 19th-century theological movement that sought to reconcile Christian faith with modern science and historical criticism, often emphasizing ethics over traditional dogma.</note> but these scholars, while nominally preserving the religious point of view, wish to reduce it to a simple "**moralism**," which in fact amounts to destroying it by the double...

We have already said that the "evolutionist" spirit is inherent to the "**historical method**," and one can see an application of it, among many others, in that singular theory according to which religious conceptions (or those supposed to be religious) must have necessarily passed through a series of successive phases, the main ones of which are commonly called **fetishism**, **polytheism**, and **monotheism**. This hypothesis is comparable to the one put forward in the field of linguistics, according to which languages, in the course of their development, pass successively through monosyllabic, agglutinative, and inflectional forms. <note>Monosyllabic languages (like Chinese) use single-syllable roots; agglutinative languages (like Turkish) "glue" parts together; inflectional languages (like Latin or Greek) change word endings. Modern linguistics generally views these as distinct structural types rather than evolutionary stages.</note> This is a completely baseless supposition, which is not confirmed by any fact, and to which the facts are even clearly contrary, given that one has never been able to discover the slightest indication of an actual transition from one of these forms to another. What have been taken for three successive phases, by virtue of a preconceived idea, are simply three different types to which various linguistic groups respectively belong, each always remaining within the type to which it belongs. 

The same can be said of another hypothesis of a more general order: the one that **Auguste Comte** formulated under the name of the "**law of the three stages**." <note>Auguste Comte (1798–1857) was the founder of Positivism. This is because he imagined that all possible knowledge had as its exclusive object the explanation of natural phenomena, a view which in reality applies only to scientific knowledge alone. To finish showing what should be thought of these three alleged phases of religious conceptions, we will first recall what we have already said previously: that there was never any essentially polytheistic doctrine. **Polytheism** is—like the "myths" closely linked to it—nothing but a crude deformation resulting from a profound lack of understanding; furthermore, polytheism and <term>anthropomorphism: the attribution of human characteristics, emotions, or intentions to non-human entities, especially gods.</term> only truly became widespread among the Greeks and Romans; everywhere else, they remained in the realm of individual errors. Now, as for **fetishism**, this word, of Portuguese origin, literally means "sorcery"; what it designates is therefore not religion or something more or less analogous to it, but indeed **magic**, and even of the lowest kind. Magic is by no means a form of religion, whether one supposes it to be primitive or a deviation; nor is it, as others have argued, something fundamentally opposed to religion—a kind of "counter-religion," if one may use such an expression. Finally, it is also not the source from which both religion and science emerged, according to a third opinion that is no better founded than the two previous ones; all these confusions show that those who speak of it do not really know what they are talking about. In reality, magic belongs to the domain of science, and more precisely, to experimental science; it concerns the handling of certain forces which, in the **Far East**, are called "**wandering influences**" <note>original: "influences errantes." # CHAPTER III
## THEOSOPHISM

If one must, while deploring the blindness of official <term>orientalists: Western scholars who study the languages and cultures of the East</term>, at least respect their good faith, it is no longer the same when dealing with the authors and propagators of certain theories of which we must now speak, and which can only have the effect of casting discredit upon Oriental studies and alienating serious but poorly informed minds from them, by presenting to them, as the authentic expression of the <term>doctrines of India: the traditional philosophical and metaphysical systems of the Indian subcontinent</term>, a web of ramblings and absurdities, certainly unworthy of holding one's attention. Moreover, the dissemination of these daydreams has more than just the negative, though already serious, drawback we have just mentioned; like that of many other analogous things, it is, furthermore, eminently capable of unbalancing weaker minds and less solid intelligences that take them seriously, and, in this respect, it constitutes a true danger to the general mentality—a danger whose reality is already attested to by all too many lamentable examples. These undertakings are all the less harmless because modern Westerners have a marked tendency to let themselves be taken in by everything that presents extraordinary and marvelous appearances; the development of their civilization in an exclusively practical direction, by depriving them of any effective intellectual guidance, opens the way to all <term>pseudo-scientific: claims that mimic the language of science without following its methods</term> and <term>pseudo-metaphysical: theories that use spiritual language but lack genuine intellectual depth</term> extravagances, provided they seem capable of satisfying that <note>original: "sentimentalisme"</note> sentimentality which plays such a considerable role among them, due to the very absence of true <term>intellectuality: the capacity for direct, intuitive knowledge of universal principles</term>. Furthermore, the habit of giving preponderance to experimentation in the scientific field, of attaching oneself almost exclusively to facts and attributing more value to them than to ideas, further reinforces the position of all those who, to build the most improbable theories, claim to rely on some sort of phenomena—true or supposed, often poorly controlled, and in any case poorly interpreted—and who thereby have much more chance of success with the general public than those who, wanting only to teach serious and certain doctrines, will address themselves solely to pure intelligence. Therein lies the quite natural explanation for the concordance, disconcerting at first sight, which exists, as one can...

<meta>This page continues the critique of the Theosophical Society (termed "theosophism"), specifically addressing how the movement utilizes Sanskrit terminology to appeal to Western sensibilities and its reliance on modern concepts like "evolution" and "reincarnation" rather than authentic Eastern tradition.</meta>

We set aside all the incidental absurdities with which it is surrounded; regardless, it shows how much "theosophism" is saturated with that sentimentality which is specific to Westerners. Furthermore, to see how far it pushes "moralism" and pseudo-mysticism, one only has to open any of the works where its conceptions are expressed. Indeed, when examining more and more recent works, one notices that these tendencies are becoming even more accentuated—perhaps because the leaders of the organization possess an increasingly mediocre mentality, but perhaps also because this orientation is truly the one that best serves the goal they have set for themselves. The only reason for the existence of <term>Sanskrit terminology: the use of ancient Indian sacred language (e.g., words like Karma, Dharma, or Nirvana) to provide a veneer of authority</term> within "theosophism" is to give what serves as its doctrine—for we cannot consent to call it a doctrine—an appearance designed to create an illusion for Westerners and to seduce certain individuals among them who love exoticism in form. At their core, however, these people are very happy to find there conceptions and aspirations that conform to their own, being quite incapable of understanding anything regarding authentically Oriental doctrines. This state of mind, common among what are called "people of the world," is quite comparable to that of philosophers who feel the need to employ extraordinary and pretentious words to express ideas which, in short, do not differ very deeply from those of the common crowd.

"Theosophism" attaches considerable importance to the idea of "evolution," which is very Western and very modern; and, like most branches of <term>spiritism: a 19th-century movement (often called Spiritualism in English) focused on communication with the dead</term> to which it is somewhat linked by its origins, it associates this idea with that of "reincarnation." This latter conception seems to have originated among certain socialist dreamers of the first half of the 19th century, for whom it was intended to explain the inequality of social conditions—an inequality particularly shocking in their eyes, although it is entirely natural at its root. For anyone who understands the principle of the institution of <term>castes: traditional social structures based on the inherent nature and spiritual qualities of the individual rather than mere wealth or power</term>, founded on the difference of individual natures, the question does not even arise. Moreover, theories of this kind, like those of "evolutionism," explain nothing truly; while pushing back the difficulty—even indefinitely if one wishes—they ultimately leave it entirely intact, if indeed a difficulty exists. And if there is none, they are perfectly useless. As for the claim of tracing the "reincarnationist" conception back to antiquity, it rests on nothing, if not on the misunderstanding of a few symbolic expressions, from which was born a crude interpretation of <term>metempsychosis: the ancient concept of the "transmigration of souls," which Guénon argues is fundamentally different from the modern notion of reincarnation</term>.

Pythagorean <note>Referring to the followers of the ancient Greek philosopher Pythagoras, often associated by moderns with the idea of the transmigration of souls.</note> in the sense of a kind of psychic "transformism" <note>The 19th-century precursor to the theory of evolution, suggesting that species or souls change from one form to another.</note>; it is in this same way that people have mistaken for successive earthly lives what is—not only in Hindu doctrines but even in Buddhism—an indefinite series of changes in the states of a being. In these traditions, each state possesses its own characteristic conditions, different from those of the others, and constitutes for the being a cycle of existence that it can only pass through once. Earthly existence—or even more generally, corporeal existence—represents only one particular state among an infinity of others.

The true theory of the multiple states of being is of the highest importance from a metaphysical perspective; we cannot develop it here, but we have necessarily made some allusions to it, notably regarding the *apurva* <note>original: "apûrva"; a Sanskrit term referring to the unseen or "non-prior" result of an action, acting as a causal link between an act and its eventual fruit.</note> and "concordant actions and reactions." As for "reincarnationism," which is nothing but an inept caricature of this theory, all Orientals—except perhaps a few more or less Westernized ignorant individuals whose opinion is of no value—are unanimously opposed to it. Besides, its metaphysical absurdity is very easily demonstrable: to admit that a being can pass through the same state several times amounts to assuming a limitation of Universal Possibility—that is to say, to denying the Infinite—and this negation is, in itself, contradictory to the highest degree.

It is appropriate to focus specifically on combating the idea of "reincarnation," first because it is absolutely contrary to the truth, as we have just shown in a few words, and second for another more contingent reason: this idea—popularized primarily by Spiritism <note>A movement, distinct from modern spiritualism, based on the works of Allan Kardec, focusing on mediumship and reincarnation.</note>, the most unintelligent of all "neo-spiritualist" schools and also the most widespread—is one of those that contributes most effectively to the mental imbalance we noted at the beginning of this chapter, and whose victims are unfortunately much more numerous than those who are unaware of these matters might think. 

We cannot, of course, dwell on this viewpoint here; but on the other hand, it must be added that while Spiritists strive to demonstrate the so-called "reincarnation"—as well as the immortality of the soul—"scientifically," that is to say through experimental means (which is quite incapable of providing any result in this regard), most "Theosophists" <note>Here referring specifically to members of the Theosophical Society, whom the author distinguishes from traditional Christian theosophers.</note> seem to see it as a kind of dogma or article of faith, to be accepted for sentimental reasons without any attempt to provide rational or sensory proof. This shows very clearly that it is a matter of constituting a pseudo-religion in competition with the true religions of the West, and especially with Catholicism; for, to

# CHAPTER IV
## WESTERNIZED VEDANTA

We must also mention, in a line of reasoning more or less connected to that of "theosophism," <note>The author uses this term to distinguish the modern occultist movement from historical "theosophy" or divine wisdom.</note> certain "movements" which, despite having their starting point in India itself, are nonetheless of an entirely Western inspiration; in these, a preponderant role must be attributed to those political influences to which we already alluded in the previous chapter. Their origin dates back to the first half of the 19th century, a time when Ram Mohan Roy founded the *Brahma-Samâj* <note>Literally, the "Society of Brahma" or "Society of God."</note> or "Reformed Hindu Church," the idea for which had been suggested to him by Anglican missionaries, and where a "cult" was organized, modeled exactly on the plan of Protestant services. Until then, there had never been anything to which a denomination such as "Hindu Church" or "Brahmanic Church" could be applied, as such an assimilation was made possible neither by the essential point of view of the Hindu tradition, nor by the mode of organization corresponding to it. This was, in fact, the first attempt to turn <term>Brahmanism</term> <note>The social and religious system of the Hindus based on the Vedas.</note> into a religion in the Western sense of the word, and, at the same time, there was a desire to make it a religion animated by tendencies identical to those characterizing Protestantism. 

This "reformist" movement was, as was natural, strongly encouraged and supported by the British government and by Anglo-Indian missionary societies; but it was too patently anti-traditional and too contrary to the Hindu spirit to succeed, and it was seen for nothing other than what it truly was: an instrument of foreign domination. Furthermore, by an inevitable effect of the introduction of "private judgment," <note>Original: *libre examen*. The Protestant principle of individual interpretation of scripture.</note> the *Brahma-Samâj* soon subdivided into multiple "Churches," much like the Protestantism it resembled more and more, to the point of deserving the label of "pietism"; <note>A movement within Lutheranism that emphasizes individual piety and religious experience over strict adherence to doctrine.</note> and, after various vicissitudes that are unnecessary to retrace, it ended by becoming almost entirely extinct. However, the spirit that had presided over the founding of this organization was not to be limited to a single manifestation, and other similar attempts were tried as circumstances dictated, and generally without more success; we shall only cite the *Arya-Samâj*, <note>Literally, the "Society of Nobles" or "Society of Aryans."</note> an association founded half a century ago by Dayananda Saraswati, whom some...

...called "the Luther of India," <note>This refers to Swami Dayananda Saraswati (1824–1883), the founder of the Arya Samaj, who advocated for a return to the authority of the Vedas while rejecting later Hindu developments.</note> and who was in contact with the founders of the "Theosophical Society." What is noteworthy is that there, as in the *Brahma-Samâj*, the anti-traditional tendency used as a pretext a return to primitive simplicity and to the pure doctrine of the *Veda*; to judge this claim, it is enough to know how much "moralism"—the dominant concern of all these organizations—is foreign to the *Veda*. However, Protestantism also claims to restore primitive Christianity in all its purity, and there is in this similarity something much more than a simple coincidence. Such an attitude is not lacking in cleverness for making innovations acceptable, especially in an environment strongly attached to tradition, with which it would be imprudent to break too openly. But, if one truly and sincerely admitted the fundamental principles of this tradition, one would also have to admit, by that very fact, all the developments and all the consequences that regularly derive from them; this is what the so-called "reformers" do not do, and that is why all those who have a sense of tradition easily see that the real deviation is not at all on the side where these reformers claim it to be.

Ram Mohun Roy had particularly dedicated himself to interpreting the *Vedânta* <term>Vedânta</term> <note>One of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, literally meaning the "end" or "culmination" of the Vedas; it focuses on the relationship between the individual self and the ultimate reality.</note> in accordance with his own ideas. While rightly insisting on the conception of "divine unity"—which no competent person had ever contested anyway, but which he expressed in terms much more theological than metaphysical—he distorted the doctrine in many respects to accommodate it to the Western points of view which had become his own. He turned it into something that ultimately resembled a simple philosophy tinged with religiosity, a kind of "deism" <note>The belief in a creator who does not intervene in the universe, common in 18th-century European thought.</note> dressed up in Oriental phraseology. Such an interpretation is therefore, in its very spirit, as far as possible from tradition and pure metaphysics; it represents nothing more than an individual theory without authority, and it totally ignores the realization <note>In traditional Eastern doctrines, "realization" refers to the actual spiritual attainment or direct experience of truth, rather than a mere intellectual or "book-learned" understanding.</note> which is the only true goal of the entire doctrine. 

This was the prototype of the distortions of *Vedânta*, for others were to follow later, always in the direction of a rapprochement with the West—but a rapprochement for which the East would pay the full price, to the great detriment of doctrinal truth. This was a truly foolish undertaking, diametrically opposed to the intellectual interests of both civilizations, yet the Oriental mentality, in general, is very little affected by it, for things of this kind seem quite negligible to it. Logically, it is not for the East to move closer to the West by following it in its mental deviations, as it is urged...

# CHAPTER V
## FINAL OBSERVATIONS

In speaking of Western interpretations, we have voluntarily kept to generalities as much as we could, in order to avoid raising questions about specific individuals. Such questions are often irritating and, moreover, useless when dealing solely with a doctrinal point of view <term>doctrinal point of view</term> <note>The author prioritizes the study of universal principles and formal teachings over the personal lives or historical context of the teachers themselves.</note>, as is the case here. It is very curious to see how much difficulty most Westerners have in understanding that considerations of this order prove absolutely nothing for or against the value of any given conception; this clearly shows the degree to which they push intellectual individualism, as well as the sentimentalism <note>In this context, "sentimentalism" refers to an over-reliance on emotion and moral feeling, which the author believes obscures pure intellectual or metaphysical clarity.</note> that is inseparable from it. Indeed, we know how much space the most insignificant biographical details occupy in what ought to be the history of ideas, and how common the illusion is that consists in believing that, when one knows a proper name or a date, one possesses real knowledge by that very fact; and how could it be otherwise, when one values facts more than ideas?

As for the ideas themselves, once one has come to consider them simply as the invention and property of this or that individual, and when, moreover, one is influenced and even dominated by all sorts of moral and sentimental concerns, it is only natural that the evaluation of these ideas—which are no longer envisioned in themselves and for themselves—should be affected by what one knows of the character and actions of the man to whom they are attributed. In other words, one will transfer to the ideas the sympathy or antipathy one feels for the one who conceived them, as if their truth or falsehood could depend on such contingencies. Under these conditions, one might still admit, though with some regret, that a perfectly honorable individual could have formulated or supported more or less absurd ideas; but what one will never consent to is that another individual whom one judges contemptible nevertheless possessed intellectual or even artistic value, genius, or merely talent from any point of view; and yet cases where this is so are far from rare. If there is any groundless prejudice, it is surely the one dear to the partisans of "compulsory education" <term>compulsory education</term> <note>The author likely refers to the late 19th-century educational reforms in France (the Jules Ferry laws), which linked secular education with the moral formation of citizens—a link the author finds fallacious.</note>, according to which real knowledge is inseparable from what is commonly called morality. While we are explaining possible criticisms, we must still point out, despite its lack of interest, a point of detail that might lend itself to them: we did not think it necessary to force ourselves to follow, for the Sanskrit terms we had to cite, the strange and complicated transcription usually in use among Orientalists <note>Orientalists: 19th and early 20th-century Western scholars who studied the languages and cultures of the "East."</note>. The Sanskrit alphabet has many more characters than European alphabets; therefore, one is naturally forced to represent several distinct letters with one and the same letter, whose sound is close to both, though with very perceptible differences that escape the very restricted resources of pronunciation available to Western languages. No transcription can therefore be truly exact, and it would certainly be best to abstain from it altogether; but, besides the fact that it is nearly impossible to find correct Sanskrit type for a work printed in Europe, reading these characters would be an entirely useless difficulty for those who do not know them, and who are no less capable than others of understanding Hindu doctrines. Furthermore, there are even "specialists" who, however unlikely it may seem, hardly know how to use anything but transcriptions to read Sanskrit texts, and there are editions made in this form specifically for them. Undoubtedly, it is possible to remedy, to a certain extent and through various devices, the orthographic ambiguity resulting from the too-small number of letters in the Latin alphabet; this is precisely what the Orientalists wanted to do, but the method of transcription they settled on is far from being the best possible, for it implies some

Instead, we will indicate—while maintaining a certain reserve that is indispensable in more than one respect—the actual benefit that must essentially result from a true and profound knowledge of **Eastern doctrines**.

## CONCLUSION

If a few Westerners could, by reading the preceding account, become aware of what they lack intellectually—if they could, we shall not even say understand it, but only catch a glimpse or have a presentiment of it—then this work will not have been done in vain. In saying this, we do not mean to speak solely of the invaluable advantages that those who were thus led to study **Eastern doctrines** <term>doctrines orientales: The traditional metaphysical systems of the East, which the author views as superior to Western analytical philosophy.</term> could obtain directly for themselves. In these doctrines, provided they had the required aptitudes, they would find knowledge to which there is no equivalent in the West, and alongside which the philosophies that pass for being brilliant and sublime are nothing but child's play <note>original: "amusements d'enfants." The author uses this dismissive phrase to contrast the "seriousness" of traditional Eastern realization with the "frivolity" of modern Western speculation.</note>. There is no common measure <note>original: "commune mesure." A mathematical analogy meaning the two things are so different they cannot even be compared using the same scale.</note> between truth fully assented to, through a conception of unlimited possibilities and in a realization adequate to that conception, and any hypotheses imagined by individual fancies to the scale of their essentially limited capacity. There are still other results, of a more general interest, which are moreover linked to these as more or less distant consequences; we wish to allude to the preparation—certainly a long-term goal, but nonetheless an effective one—for an intellectual rapprochement between the East and the West.

When speaking of the divergence of the West from the East, which has become more accentuated than ever in the **modern era** <term>époque moderne: For this author, the modern era represents a period of spiritual decline and deviation from universal traditions.</term>, we said that we did not think, despite appearances, that this divergence could continue indefinitely. In other words, it seems difficult to us that the West, through its mentality and the sum of its tendencies, could always move further and further away from the East, as it is doing currently, without there occurring, sooner or later, a reaction which could, under certain conditions, have the most fortunate effects. This seems to us all the more difficult because the domain in which modern Western civilization develops is, by its very nature, the most limited of all. Furthermore, the changing and unstable character peculiar to the Western mentality makes it possible not to despair of seeing it take, if the occasion arises, a completely different and even opposite direction, so that the remedy

These prejudices are carried to their highest degree among the **Germanic and Anglo-Saxon peoples**, who are thus, mentally even more than physically, the furthest removed from **Easterners**; as the **Slavic peoples** have only an intellectuality reduced to a minimum, so to speak, and as **Celticism** hardly exists anymore except as a historical memory, there remain only the so-called **Latin peoples**, and who are indeed so by the languages they speak and by the special modalities of their civilization, if not by their ethnic origins, among whom the realization of a plan like the one we have just indicated could, with some chance of success, take its starting point. <summary>The author explains his intent to interpret Eastern (specifically Indian) metaphysical doctrines for a Western audience and identifies the "Latin peoples" as the most likely starting point for an intellectual elite to bridge the gap between East and West.</summary>
<keywords>Eastern thought, orientalists, metaphysical studies, India, traditional doctrines, modern West, Latin peoples, intellectual elite, cyclical laws</keywords>

--- Page 227 ---
<meta>This page concludes the final chapter of the work, transitioning from the discussion of the Western intellectual elite's potential formation to the limitations of what can be expressed in an introductory text. It reflects on the timing of these revelations in light of recent history.</meta>

Western milieu; however, regarding the means of either the one or the other, nothing can be said at present, for it would be premature in every respect. We have only intended to envision here, we repeat, possibilities that are undoubtedly very distant, but which are nonetheless possibilities, which is sufficient reason for them to be considered. Among the preceding points, there are a few that we might have perhaps hesitated to write before recent events, <note>Guénon is likely referring to the aftermath of World War I, which he viewed as a sign of the terminal crisis of the modern West.</note> which seem to have brought these possibilities somewhat closer, or which, at the very least, may allow them to be better understood; without attaching excessive importance to **historical contingencies**, which in no way affect the truth, one must not forget that there is a question of opportunity <term>opportunity: in this context, the traditional concept of "timeliness" or "kairos," where certain truths are only revealed when the circumstances of the age allow for their reception.</term> which must often intervene in the outward formulation of this truth.

Many things are still missing for this conclusion to be complete, and these things are indeed those which concern the deepest, and therefore the most truly essential, aspects of the **Eastern doctrines** and the results that can be expected from their study for those who are capable of pursuing it far enough. What is at stake can be glimpsed, to a certain extent, through the little we have said regarding **metaphysical realization**, <note>In Guénon's work, "metaphysical realization" refers to the effective transition from theoretical knowledge to a direct, lived experience of the Infinite.</note> but we have indicated at the same time the reasons why it was not possible for us to insist upon it further, especially in a preliminary exposition such as this one; perhaps we shall return to it elsewhere, but it is there above all that one must always remember that, according to a Far-Eastern formula, "he who knows ten must only teach nine." <note>original: "celui qui sait dix ne doit enseigner que neuf." This suggests the necessity of keeping the most profound realizations "esoteric" or unspoken to protect them from distortion.</note> Be that as it may, everything that can be developed without reservation—that is to say, everything that is expressible within the purely theoretical side of **metaphysics**—is still more than sufficient so that, for those who can understand it, even if they go no further, the analytical and fragmentary speculations of the **modern West** appear as they truly are: namely, as a vain and illusory search, without principle and without a final goal, and whose mediocre results are worth neither the time nor the effort of anyone who possesses an intellectual horizon vast enough not to limit their activity within it.

<summary>Guénon concludes by acknowledging that while his proposals for a Western intellectual elite may seem distant, recent history makes them relevant. He emphasizes that the most profound aspects of metaphysics (realization) must remain largely unsaid, yet even theoretical knowledge is enough to expose the futility of modern Western philosophy.</summary>

# THE GERMAN INFLUENCE

->(CHAPTER II OF THE FOURTH PART,<-
->SUBSEQUENTLY DELETED BY THE AUTHOR)<-

It is quite curious to observe that the first Indianists <note>original: *indianistes*; early Western scholars who studied the languages and culture of India</note>, who were primarily English, often said things that were more accurate than those who came after them, despite not showing a very profound understanding. No doubt, they also committed many errors, but these at least did not have a systematic character and did not proceed from a preconceived bias, even an unconscious one. The English mentality, certainly, has no aptitude for metaphysical <term>metaphysics: For the author, this refers to the knowledge of universal, infinite principles, which he distinguishes from the limited "pseudo-metaphysics" of modern philosophy.</term> conceptions, but it also has no pretension in this regard; meanwhile, the German mentality, which is fundamentally no better gifted, harbors the greatest illusions about itself. To realize this, one only needs to compare what the two peoples have produced in terms of philosophy. The English spirit hardly leaves the practical order, represented by morality and sociology, and experimental science, represented by psychology—of which it was the inventor. When it deals with logic, it is primarily induction <note>The process of reaching a general conclusion from specific observations.</note> that it has in view and to which it gives preponderance over deduction. On the contrary, if one considers German philosophy, one finds only hypotheses and systems with metaphysical pretensions, deductions based on fantastical starting points, and ideas that wish to pass for profound when they are simply nebular. This pseudo-metaphysics—which is as far removed as possible from true metaphysics—the Germans wish to find in others, whose conceptions they always interpret according to their own. This last failing is nowhere more invincible than with them, because no other people has a turn of mind so narrowly systematic. Moreover, in this, the Germans are merely pushing to the extreme the defects common to the entire European race: their national pride leads them to behave in Europe as Europeans in general—infatuated with their imaginary superiority—behave toward the entire world. The extravagance is the same in both cases, with a simple difference of degree. It is therefore natural that the Germans imagine that their philosophers have thought everything that is...

possible for men to conceive, and they no doubt believe they are doing a great honor to other peoples by assimilating their conceptions to this philosophy of which they are so proud. This does not prevent Schopenhauer <note>Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860), a German philosopher known for his atheistic pessimism. He was one of the first Western thinkers to incorporate Indian themes into his work.</note> from having ridiculously distorted Buddhism by making it into a kind of "pessimistic" moralism, and from having given the true measure of his intellectual level by seeking "consolations" in the Vedanta <term>Vedanta: One of the six orthodox schools of Hindu philosophy, focusing on the end of the Vedas and the nature of ultimate reality (Brahman).</term>; and we see, on the other hand, contemporary orientalists like Deussen <note>Paul Deussen (1845–1919), a German scholar and friend of Friedrich Nietzsche; he was a leading authority on the Upanishads and the Vedanta in his time.</note> claiming to teach the Hindus the true doctrine of Shankaracharya <note>Adi Shankara (c. 8th century), the philosopher and theologian who consolidated the doctrine of Advaita Vedanta.</note>, to whom they simply attribute the ideas of Schopenhauer! This is because the German mentality, by the very fact that it is an excessive form of the Western mentality, is the opposite of the East and can understand nothing of it; as it nevertheless has the pretension of understanding it, it necessarily denatures it: hence these false assimilations against which we protest on every occasion, and notably this application of modern Western philosophical labels to Eastern doctrines.

When one is incapable of practicing metaphysics <term>metaphysics: For the author, this refers to the knowledge of universal, infinite principles, which he distinguishes from the limited "pseudo-metaphysics" of modern philosophy.</term>, it is certainly best not to get involved with it, and positivism <note>A philosophical system that recognizes only that which can be scientifically verified or logically proved, rejecting metaphysics and theism.</note>, despite all that is narrow and incomplete about it, still seems to us much preferable to the labored delusions of pseudo-metaphysics. The greatest fault of the German orientalists is therefore not realizing their own lack of understanding, and producing works of interpretation that have no value, but which impose themselves upon all of Europe and very easily manage to become authoritative there. This happens because other peoples have nothing to oppose them with or to offer in comparison, and also because these works surround themselves with a scholarly apparatus of erudition that strongly impresses people who have a respect for certain methods that border on superstition. These methods, moreover, are also of Germanic origin, and it would be quite unjust not to recognize the very real qualities the Germans possess in terms of erudition: the truth is that they excel in the composition of dictionaries, grammars, and those voluminous works of compilation and bibliography that require nothing more than memory and patience. It is extremely regrettable that they did not specialize entirely in this type of work, which is very useful to consult on occasion and which—a valuable thing—saves time for those who are capable of doing something else. What is hardly less regrettable is that these same methods, instead of remaining the exclusive domain of the Germans, to whose temperament they were particularly suited, have spread to all European universities, and especially to France, where they are considered to be the only ones

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of German academic methods, moving from the distortion of specific philosophies to the broader systemic issues of modern scholarship and the ideological use of racial theories like "Aryanism."</meta>

"scientific," as if scholarship and science were one and the same thing; and, in fact, as a consequence of this deplorable state of mind, scholarship has come to usurp the place of true science <note>In this context, "science" refers to "scientia" or principled, traditional knowledge, while "scholarship" (érudition) refers to the mere accumulation of facts and historical data.</note>. The abuse of scholarship cultivated for its own sake, and the false belief that it can suffice to provide an understanding of ideas—all of this, among the Germans, can still be understood and excused to a certain extent. However, among peoples who do not possess the same specialized aptitudes, one can see in this nothing more than the effect of a servile tendency toward imitation—a sign of intellectual decadence that it is high time to remedy, if we do not wish to let it transform into a definitive decline.

The Germans went about it very skillfully to prepare the intellectual supremacy they dreamed of, by imposing both their philosophy and their methods of scholarship; their orientalism <term>Orientalism: The academic study of Eastern (Oriental) societies, languages, and cultures by Westerners, often criticized for applying Western biases to Eastern realities.</term> is, as we have just said, a product of the combination of these two elements. What is remarkable is the way in which these things became instruments in the service of a national ambition; it would be quite instructive, in this regard, to study how the Germans knew how to take advantage of the fanciful hypothesis of "Aryanism" <note>Aryanism: A 19th-century theory, later used for political purposes, suggesting that Europeans and North Indians shared a common "Aryan" ancestor. The author suggests this was a pseudo-historical fabrication used for nationalist goals.</note>, which they had not, for that matter, invented themselves.

For our part, we do not believe in the existence of an "Indo-European" race, even if one is willing not to persist in calling it "Aryan," which has no meaning; but what is significant is that German scholars gave this supposed race the denomination of "Indo-Germanic," and that they took every care to make this hypothesis plausible by supporting it with multiple ethnological and, above all, philological <term>philology: The branch of knowledge that deals with the structure, historical development, and relationships of languages.</term> arguments. We do not wish to enter into that discussion here; we will only remark that the real resemblance existing between the languages of India and Persia and those of Europe is by no means proof of a community of race. To explain it, it is sufficient that the ancient civilizations we know were originally brought to Europe by certain elements connected to the source from which the Hindu and Persian civilizations directly proceeded. Indeed, it is well known how easy it is for a tiny minority, under certain conditions, to impose its language, along with its institutions, upon the mass of a foreign people, even when it is ethnically absorbed by them in a short time: a striking example is that of the establishment of the Latin language in Gaul <note>Gaul: The region of Western Europe during the Iron Age and Roman era, encompassing present-day France, Belgium, and parts of neighboring countries.</note>, where the Romans, except in a few southern regions, did not...

...were never present except in negligible quantities; the French language is indisputably of almost pure Latin origin, and yet Latin elements played only a very small part in the ethnic formation of the French nation; the same is true, moreover, for Spain. On the other hand, the hypothesis of "**Indo-Germanism**" has all the less reason to exist given that Germanic languages have no more affinity with Sanskrit <term>Sanskrit: The ancient, sacred language of India, used in its classical literature and religious texts.</term> than other European languages; it merely serves to justify the assimilation of Hindu doctrines into **German philosophy**; but, unfortunately, this supposition of an imaginary kinship does not withstand the test of facts, and in reality, nothing is more dissimilar than a German and a Hindu, intellectually as well as physically—perhaps even more so intellectually.

The conclusion that emerges from all this is that, to obtain interesting results, it would first be necessary to rid ourselves of this influence which, for too long, has weighed so heavily upon **orientalism**; and, although it may be hardly possible for certain individuals to free themselves from methods that have become inveterate mental habits, we wish to hope that, in a general way, recent events <note>Likely referring to the First World War (1914-1918), which caused a massive shift in how European intellectuals viewed German cultural and academic authority.</note> will provide a favorable opportunity for this liberation. However, let our meaning be well understood: if we wish for the disappearance of German influence in the intellectual domain, it is because we consider it harmful in itself, and independently of certain historical contingencies which change nothing in the matter; it is therefore not these contingencies that make us wish for the influence in question to disappear, but we must take advantage of the state of mind they have brought about. In the intellectual order—the only one we are concerned with here—sentimental concerns have no place; German conceptions are worth exactly today what they were worth a few years ago, and it is ridiculous to see men who had always professed a boundless admiration for German philosophy suddenly begin to disparage it under the pretext of a patriotism that has nothing to do with such matters; at heart, this is worth little more than more or less consciously altering scientific or historical truth for motives of national interest, as is precisely the reproach leveled against the Germans. For our part, we who owe nothing to Germanic intellectuality, who have never had the slightest esteem for the **pseudo-metaphysics** <note>The author uses "pseudo-metaphysics" to describe modern Western philosophy that claims to seek ultimate truths but lacks the spiritual or traditional foundations of ancient or Eastern systems.</note> in which it delights, and who have never granted to **scholarship** <note>original: "érudition"</note> and its special procedures more than a very relative value and importance, we are quite at ease in saying what we think of it; and we would have said absolutely the same thing

<note>René Guénon (1886–1951) was a French intellectual who became a founding figure in the Traditionalist School. This book, his first major work, was originally intended as a doctoral thesis but was famously rejected by the Sorbonne because it challenged the "Orientalist" academic methods of the time. Guénon argued that Western scholars often misinterpreted Eastern spirituality by treating it as a historical artifact rather than a living, metaphysical reality.</note>

<term>Hindu Doctrines</term>: In this context, Guénon refers to the vast body of metaphysical and social principles found in ancient Indian texts like the Vedas and Upanishads. He sought to present them as a coherent "Intellectual" system rather than just a religion or philosophy.

<term>Social Systems and Facts</term>: The title of the book series indicates that, at the time of publication, Guénon's work was categorized alongside sociology and political science, despite its deeply philosophical and metaphysical nature.

<summary>This is the title page of René Guénon's foundational 1921 work, which introduced his critique of Western academic perspectives on Eastern spirituality and established his reputation as a proponent of universal "Traditional" metaphysics.</summary>

It went on to become a founding text for the Perennialist or Traditionalist movement.</note>

# <term>HINDU DOCTRINES</term> <note>original: "Doctrines hindoues." Guénon used the term "doctrine" rather than "religion" or "philosophy" to emphasize that Hindu tradition is a purely intellectual and metaphysical system. He argued that Western labels like "religion" were too narrow to describe the totalizing nature of Eastern thought.</note>

->BY<-

## RENÉ GUÉNON <note>René Guénon (1886–1951) was a French author who founded the Traditionalist school of thought. This book was originally his doctoral thesis at the Sorbonne, but it was famously rejected by the prominent Orientalist Sylvain Lévi, who found Guénon's defense of living tradition to be "unscientific" compared to the philological methods then in fashion.</note>

### <term>SOCIAL SYSTEMS AND SOCIAL FACTS</term> <note>original: "Systèmes et faits sociaux." This was a prestigious academic series published by Marcel Rivière, usually reserved for sociology and economics. By placing a book on metaphysics in this series, the publisher was attempting to frame Guénon’s radical ideas within a category recognizable to the French university system of the 1920s.</note>

Having had his doctoral thesis on this subject rejected by the Sorbonne because it challenged the prevailing academic methods of the time, Guénon published this volume with Marcel Rivière. The publisher was known for sociological works, which explains why Guénon's metaphysical critique was framed as part of a series on "Social Systems."</meta>

->SOCIAL SYSTEMS AND SOCIAL FACTS<- <note>original: "Systèmes et Faits Sociaux." This was a prominent academic series published by Marcel Rivière. The term "Social Facts" (Faits Sociaux) was a cornerstone of the sociological method developed by Émile Durkheim; its presence here shows the publisher’s attempt to frame Guénon's work within contemporary social science categories.</note>

# <term>HINDU DOCTRINES</term> <note>original: "Doctrines Hindoues." Guénon specifically chose the word "doctrines" to distinguish Eastern thought from Western "philosophy" or "religion," which he believed were categories ill-suited to the Eastern intellectual tradition. He viewed these doctrines as a "Traditional" transmission of universal principles rather than individual human speculation.</note>

--- Page 313 ---
<meta>This title page introduces René Guénon's seminal work, marking his formal entrance into the critique of Western Orientalism. This volume was originally intended as a doctoral thesis at the Sorbonne, but it was rejected because Guénon refused to adhere to the purely historical and philological methods demanded by the academic establishment. Consequently, it was published as part of a series on sociology, which explains the specific branding at the top of the page.</meta>

-> SOCIAL SYSTEMS AND SOCIAL FACTS <- <note>original: "Systèmes et Faits Sociaux." This was an academic series published by Marcel Rivière. The term "Social Facts" is a direct reference to the sociological school of Émile Durkheim, which was the dominant intellectual framework in France at the time.</note>
